abstract: A class of fast, supervised learning algorithms is presented. They use lo(cid:173) cal representations, hashing, atld multiple scales of resolution to approximate functions which are piece-wise continuous. Inspired by Albus's CMAC model, the algorithms learn orders of magnitude more rapidly than typical imple(cid:173) mentations of back propagation, while often achieving comparable qualities of generalization. Furthermore, unlike most traditional function approximation methods, the algorithms are well suited for use in real time adaptive signal processing. Unlike simpler adaptive systems, such as linear predictive cod(cid:173) ing, the adaptive linear combiner, and the Kalman filter, the new algorithms are capable of efficiently capturing the structure of complicated non-linear systems. As an illustration, the algorithm is applied to the prediction of a chaotic timeseries.

paragraphs: The paper introduces supervised learning algorithms for approximating piecewise-continuous functions. Inspired by the CMAC model, they combine local representations, hashing, and several levels of resolution. This arrangement represents a function at different scales, allowing the approximation to account for both broader structure and more localized variation.

The authors report learning speeds orders of magnitude faster than typical backpropagation implementations, while often obtaining comparable generalization. The qualification matters: similar performance on new inputs is reported frequently, rather than as an unconditional guarantee. The approach targets situations where an adaptive system must update its behavior quickly enough to be useful during ongoing signal processing.

The algorithms are also described as efficiently capturing complicated nonlinear structure beyond the capabilities of the simpler adaptive systems discussed in the abstract. A prediction task involving a chaotic time series illustrates the method. The broader contribution is a representation strategy that connects rapid supervised updates with nonlinear function approximation, making learning speed a central feature of the design.
summary.tldr: Local, hashed representations at multiple resolutions enable much faster learning than typical backpropagation, often with comparable generalization.

title: Fast Learning in Multi-Resolution Hierarchies

abstract: In this paper, after some introductory remarks into the classification prob(cid:173) lem as considered in various research communities, and some discussions concerning some of the reasons for ascertaining the performances of the three chosen algorithms, viz., CART (Classification and Regression Tree), C4.5 (one of the more recent versions of a popular induction tree tech(cid:173) nique known as ID3), and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), it is proposed to compare the performances of these algorithms under two criteria: classi(cid:173) fication and generalisation. It is found that, in general, the MLP has better classification and generalisation accuracies compared with the other two algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper compares three approaches to assigning examples to categories: CART, C4.5, and a multilayer perceptron. CART and C4.5 are tree-based techniques, while the multilayer perceptron is a neural network. Bringing them into one comparison connects classification methods associated with different research communities and provides a common basis for assessing their predictive performance.

The evaluation distinguishes classification from generalisation. That distinction matters because fitting the examples used to develop a classifier and handling additional examples are separate questions. Comparing both criteria helps establish whether a method’s ability to represent the classification problem is accompanied by an ability to carry that learning beyond the examples already encountered.

The authors report that the multilayer perceptron generally achieves better accuracy on both criteria than the two tree methods. The wording describes an overall tendency in the comparison rather than an unconditional ranking for every classification problem. The stated contribution is comparative evidence favoring the neural approach across the two performance dimensions the paper considers.
summary.tldr: The comparison finds that multilayer perceptrons generally outperform CART and C4.5 in classification and generalisation accuracy.

title: Comparison of three classification techniques: CART, C4.5 and Multi-Layer Perceptrons

abstract: The dynamic behavior of a network model consisting of all-to-all excitatory coupled binary neurons with global inhibition is studied analytically and numerically. We prove that for random input signals, the output of the network consists of synchronized bursts with apparently random intermis(cid:173) sions of noisy activity. Our results suggest that synchronous bursts can be generated by a simple neuronal architecture which amplifies incoming coin(cid:173) cident signals. This synchronization process is accompanied by dampened oscillations which, by themselves, however, do not play any constructive role in this and can therefore be considered to be an epiphenomenon.

This synchronization process is accompanied by dampened oscillations which, by themselves, however, do not play any constructive role in this and can therefore be considered to be an epiphenomenon.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a simple neural network can produce synchronized bursts of activity. Its neurons are binary, every neuron excites every other neuron, and inhibition acts globally across the network. The authors analyze this architecture mathematically and numerically, connecting its wiring and input conditions to the activity it generates.

For random input signals, they prove that the network produces synchronized bursts separated by apparently random stretches of noisy activity. Their interpretation is that the architecture amplifies incoming signals that happen to coincide. Coordinated output can therefore arise through amplification of coincident inputs, without requiring the network to settle into a shared repeating frequency.

Damped oscillations accompany this synchronization, but the analysis finds that they do not contribute constructively to it. They are a side effect of the dynamics rather than the mechanism responsible for the bursts. This distinction matters when interpreting neural activity: observing oscillations alongside synchrony does not establish that the oscillations generate that synchrony, as this solvable model illustrates.
summary.tldr: A simple excitatory network with global inhibition produces synchronized bursts by amplifying coincident inputs, while accompanying oscillations are incidental.

title: Burst Synchronization without Frequency Locking in a Completely Solvable Neural Network Model

abstract: We use two co-evolving neural networks to determine new classes of protein secondary structure which are significantly more pre(cid:173) dictable from local amino sequence than the conventional secondary structure classification. Accurate prediction of the conventional secondary structure classes: alpha helix, beta strand, and coil, from primary sequence has long been an important problem in compu(cid:173) tational molecular biology. Neural networks have been a popular method to attempt to predict these conventional secondary struc(cid:173) ture classes. Accuracy has been disappointingly low. The algo(cid:173) rithm presented here uses neural networks to similtaneously exam(cid:173) ine both sequence and structure data, and to evolve new classes of secondary structure that can be predicted from sequence with significantly higher accuracy than the conventional classes. These new classes have both similarities to, and differences with the con(cid:173) ventional alpha helix, beta strand and coil.

paragraphs: This paper revisits what a protein secondary-structure predictor should predict. The usual task assigns local amino acid sequences to alpha helix, beta strand, or coil, but the authors describe the accuracy of neural predictions for these conventional classes as disappointing. They investigate whether different structure classes can be more predictable from local sequence.

The method uses two neural networks that evolve together while examining sequence and structure data. Rather than holding the target categories fixed throughout learning, it develops new secondary-structure classes alongside the ability to predict them. This makes the definition of the classification problem part of the learning process itself.

The resulting classes are substantially more predictable from local amino acid sequence than the conventional categories. They retain some similarities to helix, strand, and coil while also differing from them. The improvement therefore concerns a learned structural classification, and its meaning depends on that changed target. The contribution is a way to discover structure categories that align more closely with information available in local sequence.
summary.tldr: Two co-evolving networks discover protein structure categories that local amino acid sequences predict more accurately than conventional categories.

title: Neural Network Definitions of Highly Predictable Protein Secondary Structure Classes

abstract: This paper shows that if a large neural network is used for a pattern classification problem, and the learning algorithm finds a network with small weights that has small squared error on the training patterns, then the generalization performance depends on the size of the weights rather than the number of weights. More specifi(cid:173) cally, consider an i-layer feed-forward network of sigmoid units, in which the sum of the magnitudes of the weights associated with each unit is bounded by A. The misclassification probability con(cid:173) verges to an error estimate (that is closely related to squared error on the training set) at rate O((cA)l(l+1)/2J(log n)jm) ignoring log factors, where m is the number of training patterns, n is the input dimension, and c is a constant. This may explain the gen(cid:173) eralization performance of neural networks, particularly when the number of training examples is considerably smaller than the num(cid:173) ber of weights. It also supports heuristics (such as weight decay and early stopping) that attempt to keep the weights small during training.

paragraphs: A neural network can have many more weights than training examples and still predict well on unseen data. This paper gives a theoretical explanation for that possibility. It shows that, under stated conditions, a generalization guarantee can depend on weight magnitudes rather than on the total number of weights.

The analysis concerns feed-forward networks of sigmoid units. For each unit, the sum of the absolute values of its associated weights is bounded. The learning algorithm must also find a network with small squared training error. Under these conditions, the probability of misclassification approaches an estimate related to training error, with a rate involving the weight bound, network depth, input dimension, and sample count.

The result shifts attention from counting parameters to controlling how large their values become. Its assumptions matter: a large network alone does not receive the guarantee. The paper also provides theoretical support for weight decay and early stopping, since these training heuristics seek to keep weights small while obtaining a useful fit.
summary.tldr: For sigmoid networks with bounded weights and small training error, generalization guarantees can depend on weight size rather than parameter count.

title: For Valid Generalization the Size of the Weights is More Important than the Size of the Network

abstract: This paper presents a method for obtaining class membership probability esti- mates for multiclass classiﬁcation problems by coupling the probability estimates produced by binary classiﬁers. This is an extension for arbitrary code matrices of a method due to Hastie and Tibshirani for pairwise coupling of probability estimates. Experimental results with Boosted Naive Bayes show that our method produces calibrated class membership probability estimates, while having similar classiﬁcation accuracy as loss-based decoding, a method for obtaining the most likely class that does not generate probability estimates.

This is an extension for arbitrary code matrices of a method due to Hastie and Tibshirani for pairwise coupling of probability estimates. Experimental results with Boosted Naive Bayes show that our method produces calibrated class membership probability estimates, while having similar classiﬁcation accuracy as loss-based decoding, a method for obtaining the most likely class that does not generate probability estimates.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to obtain probabilities for several classes from classifiers that each solve a binary problem. Combining binary decisions can identify a predicted class, but the authors seek a fuller output: an estimated probability of membership for every class. Their method couples the probability estimates produced by the binary classifiers.

The approach extends an earlier method for coupling pairwise probabilities to arbitrary code matrices. These matrices describe how the multiclass problem is expressed through binary tasks. Supporting arbitrary matrices broadens the arrangements of binary classifiers whose outputs can be brought together into multiclass probability estimates.

Experiments using Boosted Naive Bayes show calibrated class-membership estimates while preserving classification accuracy similar to loss-based decoding. Calibration concerns whether the estimated probabilities correspond to observed membership frequencies. The comparison matters because loss-based decoding selects the most likely class without producing probabilities. In the reported experiments, coupling supplies this additional probabilistic information with similar accuracy, rather than achieving its benefit through a claimed increase in classification accuracy.
summary.tldr: Coupling binary probability estimates produces calibrated multiclass probabilities with accuracy similar to loss-based decoding in the reported experiments.

title: Reducing multiclass to binary by coupling probability estimates

abstract: A new family of kernels for statistical learning is introduced that ex- ploits the geometric structure of statistical models. Based on the heat equation on the Riemannian manifold deﬁned by the Fisher informa- tion metric, information diffusion kernels generalize the Gaussian kernel of Euclidean space, and provide a natural way of combining generative statistical modeling with non-parametric discriminative learning. As a special case, the kernels give a new approach to applying kernel-based learning algorithms to discrete data. Bounds on covering numbers for the new kernels are proved using spectral theory in differential geometry, and experimental results are presented for text classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces kernels that use the geometry of statistical models to define similarity for learning. Its starting point is the Fisher information metric, which gives the space of statistical models a geometric structure. The authors then use the heat equation on that space to construct a family of information diffusion kernels.

These kernels generalize the Gaussian kernel from ordinary Euclidean space to the geometry associated with statistical models. This creates a connection between generative modeling and nonparametric discriminative learning: a statistical model supplies the structure from which a learning kernel is built. A special case provides a new way to apply kernel algorithms to discrete data.

The paper contributes both theoretical analysis and an application. Using spectral theory from differential geometry, the authors prove bounds on covering numbers for the kernels, addressing their mathematical complexity. They also present text-classification experiments. Together, these contributions develop the construction, analyze its properties, and illustrate its use on discrete observations without asserting a particular comparative improvement in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Information diffusion kernels use statistical-model geometry to connect generative modeling with kernel-based discriminative learning.

title: Information Diffusion Kernels

abstract: It has been suggested that the primary goal of the sensory system is to represent input in such a way as to reduce the high degree of redun- dancy. Given a noisy neural representation, however, solely reducing redundancy is not desirable, since redundancy is the only clue to reduce the effects of noise. Here we propose a model that best balances redun- dancy reduction and redundant representation. Like previous models, our model accounts for the localized and oriented structure of simple cells, but it also predicts a different organization for the population. With noisy, limited-capacity units, the optimal representation becomes an overcom- plete, multi-scale representation, which, compared to previous models, is in closer agreement with physiological data. These results offer a new perspective on the expansion of the number of neurons from retina to V1 and provide a theoretical model of incorporating useful redundancy into efficient neural representations. 1 Introduction Efficient coding theory posits that one of the primary goals of sensory coding is to eliminate redundancy from raw sensory signals, ideally representing the input by a set of statistically independent features [1]. Models for learning efficient codes, such as sparse coding [2] or ICA [3], predict the localized, oriented, and band-pass characteristics of simple cells. In this framework, units are assumed to be non-redundant and so the number of units should be identical to the dimensionality of the data. Redundancy, however, can be beneficial if it is used to compensate for inherent noise in the system [4]. The models above assume that the system noise is low and negligible so that redundancy in the representation is not necessary. This is equivalent to assuming that the representational capacity of individual units is unlimited. Real neurons, however, have limited capacity [5], and this should place constraints on how a neural population can best encode a sensory signal. In fact, there are important characteristics of simple cells, such as the multi-scale representation, that cannot be explained by efficient coding theory. The aim of this study is to evaluate how the optimal representation changes when the system is constrained by limited capacity units. We propose a model that best balances redundancy reduction and redundant representation given the limited capacity units. In contrast to the efficient coding models, it is possible to have a larger number of units than the intrinsic dimensionality of the data. This further allows to introduce redundancy in the population, enabling precise reconstruction using the imprecise representation of a single unit.

paragraphs: Efficient sensory coding often emphasizes removing redundancy from inputs. This paper argues that noise changes the objective: redundant information can help compensate for an imprecise neural representation. It proposes a model that balances redundancy reduction with useful repetition when individual units have limited capacity.

Under these noisy, limited-capacity conditions, the optimal representation becomes overcomplete and spans multiple scales. Overcompleteness means that the population can contain more units than the intrinsic dimensionality of the input. This permits a population to reconstruct information precisely even when the representation supplied by any one unit is imprecise.

Like earlier models, the proposed model accounts for the localized and oriented structure of simple cells. It also predicts a different population organization that agrees more closely with physiological data than previous models. These results offer a theoretical perspective on why neuron numbers expand from the retina to V1. The explanatory force comes from treating limited capacity and noise as constraints that can make redundancy useful.
summary.tldr: With noisy, limited-capacity units, a model balancing compression and useful redundancy favors overcomplete, multiscale representations closer to physiological observations.

title: Sparse Coding of Natural Images Using an Overcomplete Set of Limited Capacity Units

abstract: We describe an approach to building brain-computer interfaces (BCI) based on graphical models for probabilistic inference and learning. We show how a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) can be used to infer probability distributions over brain- and body-states during planning and execution of actions. The DBN is learned directly from observed data and allows measured signals such as EEG and EMG to be interpreted in terms of internal states such as intent to move, preparatory activity, and movement execution. Unlike traditional classification-based approaches to BCI, the proposed approach (1) allows continuous tracking and predic- tion of internal states over time, and (2) generates control signals based on an entire probability distribution over states rather than binary yes/no decisions. We present preliminary results of brain- and body-state es- timation using simultaneous EEG and EMG signals recorded during a self-paced left/right hand movement task.

paragraphs: This paper models a brain-computer interface as inference about changing brain and body states. It uses a dynamic Bayesian network learned directly from observations to interpret EEG and EMG signals. The internal states include intention to move, preparation for movement, and movement execution, connecting measured activity to stages of an action.

The network maintains probability distributions over these states during planning and execution. This supports continuous tracking and prediction over time and lets control signals depend on the whole distribution. That distinction matters because the interface can represent uncertainty among possible internal states instead of reducing every observation to a binary decision about whether an event is occurring.

The authors present preliminary state-estimation results from simultaneous EEG and EMG recordings during a self-paced task involving left or right hand movements. The findings illustrate the proposed probabilistic interpretation of brain and body activity in that setting. The contribution is a temporal framework for interface control, with the reported evidence specifically characterized as preliminary rather than a completed demonstration of broad practical performance.
summary.tldr: A learned dynamic Bayesian network tracks uncertain brain and body states over time to support brain-computer interface control.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Brain-Computer Interfaces

abstract: A recently proposed formulation of the stochastic planning and control problem as one of parameter estimation for suitable artiﬁcial statistical models has led to the adoption of inference algorithms for this notoriously hard problem. At the algorithmic level, the focus has been on developing Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithms. In this paper, we begin by making the crucial observation that the stochastic control problem can be reinterpreted as one of trans-dimensional inference. With this new interpretation, we are able to propose a novel reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm that is more efﬁcient than its EM counterparts. Moreover, it enables us to implement full Bayesian policy search, without the need for gradients and with one single Markov chain. The new approach involves sampling directly from a distribution that is proportional to the reward and, consequently, performs better than classic simulations methods in situations where the reward is a rare event.

paragraphs: Stochastic planning can be expressed as parameter estimation in an artificial statistical model. This perspective makes inference algorithms available for learning policies, or rules for choosing actions. The paper builds on that connection by observing that the control problem can be viewed as inference across spaces of different dimensions.

That interpretation leads to a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which can move between dimensions during sampling. The authors present it as more efficient than the expectation-maximization approaches previously emphasized for this formulation. It also supports fully Bayesian policy search using a single Markov chain and does not require gradients.

A key feature is sampling directly from a distribution proportional to reward. This focuses inference on outcomes according to their reward contribution, which matters when rewarding events are rare. The paper reports better performance than classic simulation methods in that situation. The contribution is therefore both a reinterpretation of control as trans-dimensional inference and an algorithm whose sampling distribution addresses rare rewards.
summary.tldr: Reversible jump MCMC enables gradient-free Bayesian policy search and improves on classic simulation methods when rewards are rare events.

title: Bayesian Policy Learning with Trans-Dimensional MCMC

abstract: We study consistency properties of surrogate loss functions for general multiclass classification problems, defined by a general loss matrix. We extend the notion of classification calibration, which has been studied for binary and multiclass 0-1 classification problems (and for certain other specific learning problems), to the general multiclass setting, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a surrogate loss to be classification calibrated with respect to a loss matrix in this setting. We then introduce the notion of \emph{classification calibration dimension} of a multiclass loss matrix, which measures the smallest size' of a prediction space for which it is possible to design a convex surrogate that is classification calibrated with respect to the loss matrix. We derive both upper and lower bounds on this quantity, and use these results to analyze various loss matrices. In particular, as one application, we provide a different route from the recent result of Duchi et al.\ (2010) for analyzing the difficulty of designing low-dimensional' convex surrogates that are consistent with respect to pairwise subset ranking losses. We anticipate the classification calibration dimension may prove to be a useful tool in the study and design of surrogate losses for general multiclass learning problems.

We then introduce the notion of \emph{classification calibration dimension} of a multiclass loss matrix, which measures the smallest size' of a prediction space for which it is possible to design a convex surrogate that is classification calibrated with respect to the loss matrix. paragraphs: The paper studies when optimizing a substitute training loss remains aligned with the actual costs of multiclass prediction. Those costs are specified by a loss matrix, allowing different mistakes to have different consequences. The authors extend classification calibration to this general setting and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a surrogate loss to satisfy it.

They then define classification calibration dimension: the smallest prediction-space dimension in which a convex, calibrated surrogate can be constructed for a given loss matrix. This turns a design question into a measurable property of the learning problem. The issue is how much representational space a suitable convex surrogate needs.

Upper and lower bounds on this dimension allow the authors to analyze several loss matrices. One application concerns the difficulty of constructing low-dimensional consistent convex surrogates for pairwise subset ranking. The resulting framework supplies a way to investigate both possibilities and obstacles in surrogate design, with broader usefulness presented as a prospect.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes calibrated multiclass surrogate losses and bounds the prediction-space dimension needed to construct convex ones.

title: Classification Calibration Dimension for General Multiclass Losses

abstract: We advocate the use of a new distribution family—the transelliptical—for robust inference of high dimensional graphical models. The transelliptical family is an extension of the nonparanormal family proposed by Liu et al. (2009). Just as the nonparanormal extends the normal by transforming the variables using univariate functions, the transelliptical extends the elliptical family in the same way. We propose a nonparametric rank-based regularization estimator which achieves the parametric rates of convergence for both graph recovery and parameter estima- tion. Such a result suggests that the extra robustness and ﬂexibility obtained by the semiparametric transelliptical modeling incurs almost no efﬁciency loss. We also discuss the relationship between this work with the transelliptical component analysis proposed by Han and Liu (2012).

The transelliptical family is an extension of the nonparanormal family proposed by Liu et al. (2009). Just as the nonparanormal extends the normal by transforming the variables using univariate functions, the transelliptical extends the elliptical family in the same way. We propose a nonparametric rank-based regularization estimator which achieves the parametric rates of convergence for both graph recovery and parameter estima- tion. paragraphs: This paper introduces the transelliptical distribution family for robust estimation of high-dimensional graphical models. The construction extends elliptical distributions by allowing separate univariate transformations of the variables. It follows the same broad idea by which nonparanormal models extend normal distributions, but starts from a broader underlying family.

The authors propose a regularized estimator based on ranks rather than a fully specified parametric distribution. Their theoretical result is that it achieves parametric convergence rates for both recovering the graph and estimating model parameters. These are distinct goals: identifying the graph’s structure and accurately estimating the quantities that describe the model.

Matching those rates suggests that the added robustness and modeling flexibility come with almost no loss of statistical efficiency. That is a conclusion about convergence rates, not a claim that all finite-sample behavior is identical. The paper also discusses connections to transelliptical component analysis, placing graph estimation alongside another use of the same distribution family.
summary.tldr: Rank-based estimation for transelliptical graphical models achieves parametric convergence rates while allowing greater distributional flexibility and robustness.

title: Transelliptical Graphical Models

abstract: We develop an inference and optimal design procedure for recovering synaptic weights in neural microcircuits. We base our procedure on data from an experiment in which populations of putative presynaptic neurons can be stimulated while a subthreshold recording is made from a single postsynaptic neuron. We present a realistic statistical model which accounts for the main sources of variability in this experiment and allows for large amounts of information about the biological system to be incorporated if available. We then present a simpler model to facilitate online experimental design which entails the use of efficient Bayesian inference. The optimized approach results in equal quality posterior estimates of the synaptic weights in roughly half the number of experimental trials under experimentally realistic conditions, tested on synthetic data generated from the full model.

The goal is to infer connection strengths from these responses while making efficient use of experimental trials.

The authors first develop a detailed statistical model that accounts for major sources of experimental variability. It can also incorporate substantial biological information when such information is available. They then introduce a simpler model that supports efficient Bayesian inference during the experiment. This computational simplification enables online design, connecting current uncertainty about synaptic weights with the choice of subsequent experimental conditions.

Tests use synthetic data generated from the full model under experimentally realistic conditions. The optimized procedure achieves posterior estimates of comparable quality with roughly half as many trials. This result supports the potential efficiency of jointly designing experiments and estimating connections, with the reported trial reduction established in the stated synthetic setting.
summary.tldr: Bayesian inference and online experimental design recover comparable synaptic-weight estimates with roughly half as many trials in realistic synthetic tests.

title: Bayesian Inference and Online Experimental Design for Mapping Neural Microcircuits

abstract: We introduce the Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC), a measure of non-linear dependence between random variables of arbitrary dimension based on the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi Maximum Correlation Coefficient. RDC is defined in terms of correlation of random non-linear copula projections; it is invariant with respect to marginal distribution transformations, has low computational cost and is easy to implement: just five lines of R code, included at the end of the paper.

paragraphs: The Randomized Dependence Coefficient, or RDC, measures nonlinear dependence between random variables that may have arbitrary dimension. Its starting point is the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi maximum correlation coefficient. The paper turns that motivation into a measure built from random nonlinear projections and correlations between the resulting representations.

These projections use copula representations, connecting the construction to dependence apart from the individual marginal distributions. The stated invariance to marginal distribution transformations means the measure is designed to preserve its assessment when those marginal descriptions change. This property matters when the relationship between variables is the object of interest, rather than the particular distributions each variable follows on its own.

The authors emphasize practicality alongside the statistical construction. RDC has low computational cost and can be implemented in five lines of R code, which the paper supplies. The contribution therefore combines a nonlinear, multidimensional dependence measure with a compact implementation. Its appeal lies in making a maximum-correlation-inspired approach accessible for computation while retaining the stated invariance property.
summary.tldr: RDC measures nonlinear dependence through random copula projections, combining marginal-transformation invariance with low computational cost.

title: The Randomized Dependence Coefficient

abstract: The explosion in the amount of data available for analysis often necessitates a transition from batch to incremental clustering methods, which process one element at a time and typically store only a small subset of the data. In this paper, we initiate the formal analysis of incremental clustering methods focusing on the types of cluster structure that they are able to detect. We find that the incremental setting is strictly weaker than the batch model, proving that a fundamental class of cluster structures that can readily be detected in the batch setting is impossible to identify using any incremental method. Furthermore, we show how the limitations of incremental clustering can be overcome by allowing additional clusters.

In this paper, we initiate the formal analysis of incremental clustering methods focusing on the types of cluster structure that they are able to detect. We find that the incremental setting is strictly weaker than the batch model, proving that a fundamental class of cluster structures that can readily be detected in the batch setting is impossible to identify using any incremental method. Furthermore, we show how the limitations of incremental clustering can be overcome by allowing additional clusters.

paragraphs: Large datasets often make it useful to cluster observations incrementally, processing one item at a time and retaining only a small portion of the data. This paper asks what kinds of cluster structure such methods can identify. Its focus is on the capabilities of the incremental setting itself, rather than only the performance of one particular algorithm.

The authors prove that the incremental model is strictly weaker than the batch model they study. They identify a fundamental class of cluster structures that can be recovered in the batch setting but cannot be identified by any incremental method in their setting. This establishes a structural obstacle that cannot simply be resolved by choosing a better incremental algorithm.

The paper then shows that permitting additional clusters can overcome the identified limitations. The number of clusters is therefore an important part of the comparison between incremental and batch processing. Allowing more clusters changes what incremental methods can recover, providing a theoretical reason to consider extra clusters when moving from batch analysis to incremental processing.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a gap between incremental and batch clustering and shows that allowing extra clusters can overcome the identified limitations.

title: Incremental Clustering: The Case for Extra Clusters

abstract: A basic problem in the design of privacy-preserving algorithms is the \emph{private maximization problem}: the goal is to pick an item from a universe that (approximately) maximizes a data-dependent function, all under the constraint of differential privacy. This problem has been used as a sub-routine in many privacy-preserving algorithms for statistics and machine learning. Previous algorithms for this problem are either range-dependent---i.e., their utility diminishes with the size of the universe---or only apply to very restricted function classes. This work provides the first general purpose, range-independent algorithm for private maximization that guarantees approximate differential privacy. Its applicability is demonstrated on two fundamental tasks in data mining and machine learning.

Previous algorithms for this problem are either range-dependent---i.e., their utility diminishes with the size of the universe---or only apply to very restricted function classes. This work provides the first general purpose, range-independent algorithm for private maximization that guarantees approximate differential privacy. Its applicability is demonstrated on two fundamental tasks in data mining and machine learning.

paragraphs: Private maximization asks an algorithm to choose an item with a high data-dependent score while satisfying differential privacy. Because this selection problem appears inside many statistical and machine-learning procedures, improvements to it can matter beyond a single application. The challenge is to preserve selection quality while respecting the privacy constraint.

The paper identifies a limitation of previous approaches: their utility either deteriorates as the universe of possible items grows, or their applicability is confined to restricted function classes. It introduces what the authors describe as the first general-purpose, range-independent algorithm for this problem. Here, range independence addresses the dependence of utility on the size of the item universe.

The privacy guarantee is approximate differential privacy, a qualification that is part of the stated result. The authors demonstrate applicability to two fundamental tasks in data mining and machine learning. The main contribution is therefore a broadly applicable private-selection mechanism whose utility avoids the identified universe-size dependence, rather than a claim that privacy has no cost or that computation is independent of universe size.
summary.tldr: A general-purpose private-maximization algorithm avoids utility dependence on the item-universe size while guaranteeing approximate differential privacy.

title: The Large Margin Mechanism for Differentially Private Maximization

abstract: While robust parameter estimation has been well studied in parametric density estimation, there has been little investigation into robust density estimation in the nonparametric setting. We present a robust version of the popular kernel density estimator (KDE). As with other estimators, a robust version of the KDE is useful since sample contamination is a common issue with datasets. What ``robustness'' means for a nonparametric density estimate is not straightforward and is a topic we explore in this paper. To construct a robust KDE we scale the traditional KDE and project it to its nearest weighted KDE in the $L^2$ norm. Because the squared $L^2$ norm penalizes point-wise errors superlinearly this causes the weighted KDE to allocate more weight to high density regions. We demonstrate the robustness of the SPKDE with numerical experiments and a consistency result which shows that asymptotically the SPKDE recovers the uncontaminated density under sufficient conditions on the contamination.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation estimates a probability density from samples without choosing a fixed parametric family. Contaminated samples can distort that estimate, motivating a robust alternative. The paper also examines what robustness should mean in this nonparametric setting, where the object being recovered is an entire density rather than a small set of parameters.

The proposed method scales a conventional kernel density estimate and projects it onto the nearest weighted kernel density estimate using the L2 norm. Squared L2 error penalizes larger pointwise discrepancies more than proportionally. In this construction, that causes the weighted estimate to assign greater weight to regions of high density.

The authors support the method with numerical experiments and a consistency result. Under sufficient conditions on the contamination, the estimator asymptotically recovers the uncontaminated density. This is a conditional recovery guarantee as the sample size grows, rather than a claim of removing arbitrary contamination. The contribution connects a simple scaling-and-projection operation with a precise route to robust nonparametric density estimation.
summary.tldr: Scaling and projecting a kernel density estimate yields a robust estimator with asymptotic recovery guarantees under sufficient contamination conditions.

title: Robust Kernel Density Estimation by Scaling and Projection in Hilbert Space

abstract: The global Markov property for Gaussian graphical models ensures graph separation implies conditional independence. Specifically if a node set $S$ graph separates nodes $u$ and $v$ then $X_u$ is conditionally independent of $X_v$ given $X_S$. The opposite direction need not be true, that is, $X_u \perp X_v \mid X_S$ need not imply $S$ is a node separator of $u$ and $v$. When it does, the relation $X_u \perp X_v \mid X_S$ is called faithful. In this paper we provide a characterization of faithful relations and then provide an algorithm to test faithfulness based only on knowledge of other conditional relations of the form $X_i \perp X_j \mid X_S$.

paragraphs: In a Gaussian graphical model, graph separation implies a corresponding conditional independence. If a set of nodes separates two other nodes, their variables are independent once the separating variables are given. This is the direction guaranteed by the global Markov property, linking graph structure to probabilistic relationships.

The reverse implication can fail. Knowing that two variables are conditionally independent given a set of variables does not necessarily show that the corresponding nodes are separated by that set. The paper calls a conditional independence relation faithful when this reverse connection to separation holds. Its subject is therefore the reliability of interpreting a particular independence as evidence about the graph.

The authors characterize faithful relations and give an algorithm for testing faithfulness using knowledge of other conditional independence relations. This provides a way to assess the structural meaning of an independence through additional probabilistic relationships. The contribution clarifies when the connection between graphical separation and conditional independence can be used in both directions for the relation being tested.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when conditional independence reflects graph separation and provides a faithfulness test based on other independence relations.

title: Testing Unfaithful Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Neural population activity often exhibits rich variability. This variability is thought to arise from single-neuron stochasticity, neural dynamics on short time-scales, as well as from modulations of neural firing properties on long time-scales, often referred to as non-stationarity. To better understand the nature of co-variability in neural circuits and their impact on cortical information processing, we introduce a hierarchical dynamics model that is able to capture inter-trial modulations in firing rates, as well as neural population dynamics. We derive an algorithm for Bayesian Laplace propagation for fast posterior inference, and demonstrate that our model provides a better account of the structure of neural firing than existing stationary dynamics models, when applied to neural population recordings from primary visual cortex.

paragraphs: Activity across a population of neurons varies in several ways. The paper distinguishes single-neuron randomness, short-timescale neural dynamics, and slower changes in firing properties. Those slower changes, called non-stationarity, motivate a model that can describe both ongoing population dynamics and changes in firing rates between experimental trials.

The authors introduce a hierarchical dynamics model to represent these sources of temporal structure together. Its hierarchy allows inter-trial firing-rate modulation to coexist with neural population dynamics. They also derive a Bayesian Laplace propagation algorithm for fast posterior inference, providing a computational procedure for estimating the model from observed activity.

Applied to population recordings from primary visual cortex, the model gives a better account of neural firing structure than existing stationary dynamics models. This supports including between-trial modulation when explaining the recordings studied. The broader significance is methodological: a model that allows firing properties to change can characterize shared neural variability more faithfully than one whose dynamics assume stationarity in this setting.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical dynamics model captures between-trial firing changes and better explains visual-cortex recordings than stationary dynamics models.

title: Unlocking neural population non-stationarities using hierarchical dynamics models

abstract: Discrete Fourier transforms provide a significant speedup in the computation of convolutions in deep learning. In this work, we demonstrate that, beyond its advantages for efficient computation, the spectral domain also provides a powerful representation in which to model and train convolutional neural networks (CNNs).We employ spectral representations to introduce a number of innovations to CNN design. First, we propose spectral pooling, which performs dimensionality reduction by truncating the representation in the frequency domain. This approach preserves considerably more information per parameter than other pooling strategies and enables flexibility in the choice of pooling output dimensionality. This representation also enables a new form of stochastic regularization by randomized modification of resolution. We show that these methods achieve competitive results on classification and approximation tasks, without using any dropout or max-pooling. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of complex-coefficient spectral parameterization of convolutional filters. While this leaves the underlying model unchanged, it results in a representation that greatly facilitates optimization. We observe on a variety of popular CNN configurations that this leads to significantly faster convergence during training.

paragraphs: The paper explores frequency-domain representations as a way to design and train convolutional neural networks. Fourier transforms already accelerate convolution, but the authors investigate their value beyond computation. They use spectral representations to change how networks reduce resolution, apply regularization, and represent their trainable filters.

Spectral pooling reduces dimensionality by truncating the frequency-domain representation. The authors report that it retains considerably more information per parameter than other pooling strategies and permits flexible output dimensions. Random changes in resolution also provide a form of stochastic regularization. These methods achieve competitive classification and approximation results without using dropout or max-pooling.

A separate contribution represents convolutional filters with complex-valued spectral coefficients. This changes the parameterization while leaving the underlying model unchanged, allowing the study to distinguish representational effects on optimization from changes to the model itself. Across several popular CNN configurations, the authors observe significantly faster training convergence. Together, the results show how the choice of representation can affect both information retention and the ease of optimization.
summary.tldr: Frequency-domain pooling, regularization, and filter parameterization provide competitive CNN results and faster observed training convergence.

title: Spectral Representations for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We focus on the adversarial multi-armed bandit problem. The EXP3 algorithm of Auer et al. (2003) was shown to have a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T N \log N})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $N$ is the number of available actions (arms). More recently, Audibert and Bubeck (2009) improved the bound by a logarithmic factor via an entirely different method. In the present work, we provide a new set of analysis tools, using the notion of convex smoothing, to provide several novel algorithms with optimal guarantees. First we show that regularization via the Tsallis entropy matches the minimax rate of Audibert and Bubeck (2009) with an even tighter constant; it also fully generalizes EXP3. Second we show that a wide class of perturbation methods lead to near-optimal bandit algorithms as long as a simple condition on the perturbation distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is met: one needs that the hazard function of $\mathcal{D}$ remain bounded. The Gumbel, Weibull, Frechet, Pareto, and Gamma distributions all satisfy this key property; interestingly, the Gaussian and Uniform distributions do not.

paragraphs: The paper develops analysis tools and algorithms for adversarial multi-armed bandits, where a learner repeatedly chooses among actions. Performance is assessed through regret over T rounds with N available actions. The authors use convex smoothing to study algorithm design, connecting different ways of softening the choice among competing actions.

One result concerns regularization with Tsallis entropy. The resulting approach generalizes EXP3 and matches the previously established minimax regret rate with a tighter constant. This places an established algorithm inside a broader family while showing that a particular regularization choice can achieve the optimal rate described in the abstract.

Failure to satisfy this condition is not itself a proof of poor performance; the result identifies a class for which the analysis supplies guarantees.
summary.tldr: Convex smoothing yields optimal bandit algorithms and a bounded-hazard sufficient condition for near-optimal random-perturbation methods.

title: Fighting Bandits with a New Kind of Smoothness

abstract: Many practical perception systems exist within larger processes which often include interactions with users or additional components that are capable of evaluating the quality of predicted solutions. In these contexts, it is beneficial to provide these oracle mechanisms with multiple highly likely hypotheses rather than a single prediction. In this work, we pose the task of producing multiple outputs as a learning problem over an ensemble of deep networks -- introducing a novel stochastic gradient descent based approach to minimize the loss with respect to an oracle. Our method is simple to implement, agnostic to both architecture and loss function, and parameter-free. Our approach achieves lower oracle error compared to existing methods on a wide range of tasks and deep architectures. We also show qualitatively that solutions produced from our approach often provide interpretable representations of task ambiguity.

In these contexts, it is beneficial to provide these oracle mechanisms with multiple highly likely hypotheses rather than a single prediction. In this work, we pose the task of producing multiple outputs as a learning problem over an ensemble of deep networks -- introducing a novel stochastic gradient descent based approach to minimize the loss with respect to an oracle. Our method is simple to implement, agnostic to both architecture and loss function, and parameter-free. paragraphs: Some perception systems operate inside larger processes where a user or another component can evaluate candidate predictions. In those settings, producing several plausible hypotheses can be useful. The paper treats this as a learning problem for an ensemble of deep networks, with the goal of producing alternatives that work well when such an evaluator is available.

The authors introduce a stochastic-gradient approach that minimizes loss with respect to an oracle. This makes the usefulness of the ensemble's candidate set the training target. They describe the method as simple to implement, independent of the particular network architecture and loss function, and parameter-free.

Across the evaluated tasks and architectures, the approach achieves lower oracle error than existing methods. Qualitative examples also show that its different solutions often give interpretable representations of ambiguity in the task. These results concern the quality of alternatives available to an oracle, matching the intended setting where a downstream evaluator can assess the proposed solutions.
summary.tldr: Stochastic multiple-choice learning trains deep ensembles to offer useful alternative predictions and reduces oracle error across evaluated tasks.

title: Stochastic Multiple Choice Learning for Training Diverse Deep Ensembles

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GAN) approximate a target data distribution by jointly optimizing an objective function through a "two-player game" between a generator and a discriminator. Despite their empirical success, however, two very basic questions on how well they can approximate the target distribution remain unanswered. First, it is not known how restricting the discriminator family affects the approximation quality. Second, while a number of different objective functions have been proposed, we do not understand when convergence to the global minima of the objective function leads to convergence to the target distribution under various notions of distributional convergence. In this paper, we address these questions in a broad and unified setting by defining a notion of adversarial divergences that includes a number of recently proposed objective functions. We show that if the objective function is an adversarial divergence with some additional conditions, then using a restricted discriminator family has a moment-matching effect. Additionally, we show that for objective functions that are strict adversarial divergences, convergence in the objective function implies weak convergence, thus generalizing previous results.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial learning trains a generator against a discriminator to approximate a data distribution. This paper asks what that competition actually guarantees. It examines how limiting the discriminator's available functions changes approximation quality, and when improving the training objective means that the generated distribution is approaching the target in a mathematical sense.

The authors introduce adversarial divergences, a shared mathematical framework encompassing several proposed adversarial objectives. Within this framework, they show that restricting the discriminator has a moment-matching effect when additional conditions hold. In plain language, the restriction makes agreement on certain statistical summaries central to the comparison between generated and target data.

A second result connects objective convergence to distributional convergence: for strict adversarial divergences, convergence of the objective implies weak convergence of distributions. The significance is conditional and precise. Appropriate objectives can make progress in their numerical value meaningful as distributional progress, while the discriminator analysis explains how its expressive restrictions shape what the learning problem measures.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how restricted discriminators shape GAN approximation and when objective convergence implies weak distributional convergence.

title: Approximation and Convergence Properties of Generative Adversarial Learning

abstract: At the heart of deep learning we aim to use neural networks as function approximators - training them to produce outputs from inputs in emulation of a ground truth function or data creation process. In many cases we only have access to input-output pairs from the ground truth, however it is becoming more common to have access to derivatives of the target output with respect to the input -- for example when the ground truth function is itself a neural network such as in network compression or distillation. Generally these target derivatives are not computed, or are ignored. This paper introduces Sobolev Training for neural networks, which is a method for incorporating these target derivatives in addition the to target values while training. By optimising neural networks to not only approximate the function’s outputs but also the function’s derivatives we encode additional information about the target function within the parameters of the neural network. Thereby we can improve the quality of our predictors, as well as the data-efficiency and generalization capabilities of our learned function approximation. We provide theoretical justifications for such an approach as well as examples of empirical evidence on three distinct domains: regression on classical optimisation datasets, distilling policies of an agent playing Atari, and on large-scale applications of synthetic gradients. In all three domains the use of Sobolev Training, employing target derivatives in addition to target values, results in models with higher accuracy and stronger generalisation.

paragraphs: Neural networks commonly learn a target function from examples of its inputs and outputs. Sometimes its derivatives are available too, describing how outputs change as inputs change. This paper introduces Sobolev Training, which uses both target values and target derivatives during training, incorporating information that ordinary value-matching training may ignore.

Matching derivatives teaches the network about the target function's local behavior as well as its output at particular inputs. This situation arises naturally when the target is another neural network, as in compression or distillation. The additional training signal can improve approximation quality, data efficiency, and generalization by encoding more information about the function being learned.

The authors provide theoretical justification and empirical evidence across three domains: regression on classical optimization datasets, distillation of Atari-playing policies, and large-scale synthetic-gradient applications. In all three, adding derivative targets yields higher accuracy and stronger generalization. The findings support using available derivative information as an additional source of supervision for function approximation.
summary.tldr: Sobolev Training matches target derivatives as well as outputs, improving accuracy and generalization across three tested domains.

title: Sobolev Training for Neural Networks

abstract: Influence maximization is the problem of selecting $k$ nodes in a social network to maximize their influence spread. The problem has been extensively studied but most works focus on the submodular influence diffusion models. In this paper, motivated by empirical evidences, we explore influence maximization in the non-submodular regime. In particular, we study the general threshold model in which a fraction of nodes have non-submodular threshold functions, but their threshold functions are closely upper- and lower-bounded by some submodular functions (we call them $\varepsilon$-almost submodular). We first show a strong hardness result: there is no $1/n^{\gamma/c}$ approximation for influence maximization (unless P = NP) for all networks with up to $n^{\gamma}$ $\varepsilon$-almost submodular nodes, where $\gamma$ is in (0,1) and $c$ is a parameter depending on $\varepsilon$. This indicates that influence maximization is still hard to approximate even though threshold functions are close to submodular. We then provide $(1-\varepsilon)^{\ell}(1-1/e)$ approximation algorithms when the number of $\varepsilon$-almost submodular nodes is $\ell$. Finally, we conduct experiments on a number of real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate that our approximation algorithms outperform other baseline algorithms.
originalAbstract: Influence maximization is the problem of selecting $k$ nodes in a social network to maximize their influence spread. The problem has been extensively studied but most works focus on the submodular influence diffusion models. In this paper, motivated by empirical evidences, we explore influence maximization in the non-submodular regime. In particular, we study the general threshold model in which a fraction of nodes have non-submodular threshold functions, but their threshold functions are closely upper- and lower-bounded by some submodular functions (we call them $\varepsilon$-almost submodular). We first show a strong hardness result: there is no $1/n^{\gamma/c}$ approximation for influence maximization (unless P = NP) for all networks with up to $n^{\gamma}$ $\varepsilon$-almost submodular nodes, where $\gamma$ is in (0,1) and $c$ is a parameter depending on $\varepsilon$. This indicates that influence maximization is still hard to approximate even though threshold functions are close to submodular. We then provide $(1-\varepsilon)^{\ell}(1-1/e)$ approximation algorithms when the number of $\varepsilon$-almost submodular nodes is $\ell$. Finally, we conduct experiments on a number of real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate that our approximation algorithms outperform other baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects a fixed number of starting nodes to make influence spread as widely as possible through a network. Much prior work assumes submodularity, a diminishing-returns property that helps make approximation tractable. This paper studies threshold diffusion when some nodes violate that property, although their threshold functions remain closely bounded by submodular functions.

The authors call these functions epsilon-almost submodular. They establish a strong conditional hardness result: unless P equals NP, no algorithm achieves the stated approximation factor across all networks with the specified growing number of such nodes. Thus, local functions being close to submodular does not by itself preserve easy approximation of overall influence spread.

They also provide algorithms with approximation factor (1 − epsilon)^ell times (1 − 1/e), where ell counts the almost-submodular nodes. This guarantee makes the dependence on both deviation and node count explicit. Experiments on real-world datasets show these algorithms outperforming the evaluated baselines. Together, the results identify a theoretical obstacle and provide approximation methods whose guarantees reflect how much non-submodularity the network contains.
summary.tldr: Influence maximization can remain hard near submodularity, but the paper gives approximation guarantees depending on the number of almost-submodular nodes.

title: Influence Maximization with $\varepsilon$-Almost Submodular Threshold Functions

abstract: Many machine learning tools for regression are based on recursive partitioning of the covariate space into smaller regions, where the regression function can be estimated locally. Among these, regression trees and their ensembles have demonstrated impressive empirical performance. In this work, we shed light on the machinery behind Bayesian variants of these methods. In particular, we study Bayesian regression histograms, such as Bayesian dyadic trees, in the simple regression case with just one predictor. We focus on the reconstruction of regression surfaces that are piecewise constant, where the number of jumps is unknown. We show that with suitably designed priors, posterior distributions concentrate around the true step regression function at a near-minimax rate. These results {\sl do not} require the knowledge of the true number of steps, nor the width of the true partitioning cells. Thus, Bayesian dyadic regression trees are fully adaptive and can recover the true piecewise regression function nearly as well as if we knew the exact number and location of jumps. Our results constitute the first step towards understanding why Bayesian trees and their ensembles have worked so well in practice. As an aside, we discuss prior distributions on balanced interval partitions and how they relate to an old problem in geometric probability. Namely, we relate the probability of covering the circumference of a circle with random arcs whose endpoints are confined to a grid, a new variant of the original problem.

Crucially, the procedure does not need advance knowledge of how many constant pieces exist or how wide their intervals are.

The result gives a precise sense in which these trees adapt to unknown complexity: they recover the function nearly as well as a procedure informed about the jumps. This is an initial theoretical explanation for Bayesian trees' practical success within the studied setting. The paper also connects priors over balanced interval partitions to a geometric probability problem involving random arcs covering a circle.
summary.tldr: With suitable priors, Bayesian dyadic regression trees adapt to unknown steps in a one-predictor regression function at a near-optimal rate.

title: Bayesian Dyadic Trees and Histograms for Regression

abstract: Despite impressive recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL), its deployment in real-world physical systems is often complicated by unexpected events, limited data, and the potential for expensive failures. In this paper, we describe an application of RL “in the wild” to the task of regulating temperatures and airflow inside a large-scale data center (DC). Adopting a data-driven, model-based approach, we demonstrate that an RL agent with little prior knowledge is able to effectively and safely regulate conditions on a server floor after just a few hours of exploration, while improving operational efficiency relative to existing PID controllers.

The paper studies reinforcement learning for this task inside a large-scale data center. Its motivation is practical: unexpected events, limited data, and costly failures can complicate the deployment of learning-based control.

The authors adopt a data-driven, model-based approach. This places a model within the control strategy and uses experience from the system to support learning. The agent starts with little prior knowledge, making the amount of exploration needed especially relevant. The reported demonstration shows that it can effectively and safely regulate conditions on a server floor after only a few hours of exploration.

The agent also improves operational efficiency relative to the existing PID controllers. These findings connect learning speed, operational control, and efficiency within the same deployment. Their significance is the demonstrated use of reinforcement learning in a real physical system under the practical constraints highlighted by the authors. The safety and efficiency claims describe the reported data-center application.
summary.tldr: A model-based reinforcement-learning controller learns to regulate a data-center server floor safely and efficiently after a few hours of exploration.

title: Data center cooling using model-predictive control

abstract: We consider a generalization of mixed regression where the response is an additive combination of several mixture components. Standard mixed regression is a special case where each response is generated from exactly one component. Typical approaches to the mixture regression problem employ local search methods such as Expectation Maximization (EM) that are prone to spurious local optima. On the other hand, a number of recent theoretically-motivated \emph{Tensor-based methods} either have high sample complexity, or require the knowledge of the input distribution, which is not available in most of practical situations. In this work, we study a novel convex estimator \emph{MixLasso} for the estimation of generalized mixed regression, based on an atomic norm specifically constructed to regularize the number of mixture components. Our algorithm gives a risk bound that trades off between prediction accuracy and model sparsity without imposing stringent assumptions on the input/output distribution, and can be easily adapted to the case of non-linear functions. In our numerical experiments on mixtures of linear as well as nonlinear regressions, the proposed method yields high-quality solutions in a wider range of settings than existing approaches.

This paper considers a broader setting where several components can contribute additively to the same response. That change allows the prediction model to represent combined contributions while retaining ordinary mixed regression as a special case.

The proposed estimator, MixLasso, uses a convex objective with an atomic norm designed to regularize the number of mixture components. This addresses difficulties associated with local-search approaches such as EM, which can encounter spurious local optima. The authors also contrast their approach with tensor-based methods that may need many samples or knowledge of the input distribution.

Together, these results support the estimator's combination of component control, convex formulation, and flexibility in the regression functions.
summary.tldr: MixLasso uses convex atomic-norm regularization to estimate additive mixtures of regression components while balancing accuracy and sparsity.

title: MixLasso: Generalized Mixed Regression via Convex Atomic-Norm Regularization

abstract: There are now several large scale deployments of differential privacy used to collect statistical information about users. However, these deployments periodically recollect the data and recompute the statistics using algorithms designed for a single use. As a result, these systems do not provide meaningful privacy guarantees over long time scales. Moreover, existing techniques to mitigate this effect do not apply in the ``local model'' of differential privacy that these systems use. In this paper, we introduce a new technique for local differential privacy that makes it possible to maintain up-to-date statistics over time, with privacy guarantees that degrade only in the number of changes in the underlying distribution rather than the number of collection periods. We use our technique for tracking a changing statistic in the setting where users are partitioned into an unknown collection of groups, and at every time period each user draws a single bit from a common (but changing) group-specific distribution. We also provide an application to frequency and heavy-hitter estimation.

paragraphs: Repeated collection creates a privacy problem even when each individual collection uses a private algorithm. Applying a method designed for one use over many periods can weaken the overall guarantee until it becomes uninformative. This paper addresses that accumulation in the local differential privacy setting used by large-scale statistical collection systems.

The proposed technique maintains current statistics while making privacy degradation depend on the number of changes in the underlying distribution, rather than the number of collection periods. The distinction matters when measurements are frequent but the population's statistical behavior changes less often. Continued collection can then be analyzed in terms of actual distributional change.

The authors study users divided into an unknown set of groups. Each period, every user draws one bit from a changing distribution shared by their group. They apply the technique to tracking a statistic in this setting and also to frequency and heavy-hitter estimation. The result provides a framework for ongoing private monitoring whose privacy accounting reflects evolving data rather than simply counting repeated collection events.
summary.tldr: A local privacy technique ties long-term privacy degradation to distribution changes instead of the number of data collections.

title: Local Differential Privacy for Evolving Data

abstract: A typical biological neuron, such as a pyramidal neuron of the neocortex, receives thousands of afferent synaptic inputs on its dendrite tree and sends the efferent axonal output downstream. In typical artificial neural networks, dendrite trees are modeled as linear structures that funnel weighted synaptic inputs to the cell bodies. However, numerous experimental and theoretical studies have shown that dendritic arbors are far more than simple linear accumulators. That is, synaptic inputs can actively modulate their neighboring synaptic activities; therefore, the dendritic structures are highly nonlinear. In this study, we model such local nonlinearity of dendritic trees with our dendritic neural network (DENN) structure and apply this structure to typical machine learning tasks. Equipped with localized nonlinearities, DENNs can attain greater model expressivity than regular neural networks while maintaining efficient network inference. Such strength is evidenced by the increased fitting power when we train DENNs with supervised machine learning tasks. We also empirically show that the locality structure can improve the generalization performance of DENNs, as exemplified by DENNs outranking naive deep neural network architectures when tested on 121 classification tasks from the UCI machine learning repository.

paragraphs: Artificial neurons typically combine weighted inputs linearly before further processing. Biological dendrites can behave differently: nearby synaptic inputs can influence one another, creating local nonlinear interactions. This paper takes that observation as inspiration for dendritic neural networks, or DENNs, which explicitly model such local nonlinearities.

The proposed structure aims to increase what a network can represent while retaining efficient inference. Its additional expressive power comes from interactions within the input-processing structure of a neuron. In supervised learning experiments, the authors observe increased fitting power, supporting the claim that these localized nonlinearities can represent relationships that regular neural networks capture less effectively.

The paper also investigates whether the locality of those interactions helps performance on unseen data. Across 121 classification tasks from the UCI repository, DENNs outrank the naive deep network architectures used in the comparison. This provides empirical support for improved generalization in those tests. The contribution thus links a biologically motivated architectural change to both greater fitting capacity and reported improvements in classification performance.
summary.tldr: Dendritic neural networks add localized nonlinear input interactions, increasing fitting power and improving generalization in the reported classification comparisons.

title: Improved Expressivity Through Dendritic Neural Networks

abstract: Data-driven approaches to solving robotic tasks have gained a lot of traction in recent years. However, most existing policies are trained on large-scale datasets collected in curated lab settings. If we aim to deploy these models in unstructured visual environments like people's homes, they will be unable to cope with the mismatch in data distribution. In such light, we present the first systematic effort in collecting a large dataset for robotic grasping in homes. First, to scale and parallelize data collection, we built a low cost mobile manipulator assembled for under 3K USD. Second, data collected using low cost robots suffer from noisy labels due to imperfect execution and calibration errors. To handle this, we develop a framework which factors out the noise as a latent variable. Our model is trained on 28K grasps collected in several houses under an array of different environmental conditions. We evaluate our models by physically executing grasps on a collection of novel objects in multiple unseen homes. The models trained with our home dataset showed a marked improvement of 43.7% over a baseline model trained with data collected in lab. Our architecture which explicitly models the latent noise in the dataset also performed 10% better than one that did not factor out the noise. We hope this effort inspires the robotics community to look outside the lab and embrace learning based approaches to handle inaccurate cheap robots.
