Together, these findings support collecting data in deployment-like environments and accounting for the inaccuracies of inexpensive robots.
summary.tldr: Home-collected grasping data and explicit modeling of hardware-induced label noise improve grasping performance in unseen homes.

title: Robot Learning in Homes: Improving Generalization and Reducing Dataset Bias

abstract: We consider the graph matching/similarity problem of determining how similar two given graphs $G_0,G_1$ are and recovering the permutation $\pi$ on the vertices of $G_1$ that minimizes the symmetric difference between the edges of $G_0$ and $\pi(G_1)$. Graph matching/similarity has applications for pattern matching, vision, social network anonymization, malware analysis, and more. We give the first efficient algorithms proven to succeed in the correlated Erdös-Rényi model (Pedarsani and Grossglauser, 2011). Specifically, we give a polynomial time algorithm for the graph similarity/hypothesis testing task which works for every constant level of correlation between the two graphs that can be arbitrarily close to zero. We also give a quasi-polynomial ($n^{O(\log n)}$ time) algorithm for the graph matching task of recovering the permutation minimizing the symmetric difference in this model. This is the first algorithm to do so without requiring as additional input a ``seed'' of the values of the ground truth permutation on at least $n^{\Omega(1)}$ vertices. Our algorithms follow a general framework of counting the occurrences of subgraphs from a particular family of graphs allowing for tradeoffs between efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks a correspondence between vertices that makes two graphs' edge sets agree as closely as possible. A related similarity task asks whether graphs exhibit the relevant relationship without necessarily recovering that correspondence. The paper provides algorithms with success guarantees for both tasks in the correlated Erdős–Rényi random graph model.

For similarity testing, the algorithm runs in polynomial time and works at every fixed positive correlation level, including constants arbitrarily close to zero. Recovering the matching requires quasi-polynomial time, n raised to a quantity proportional to log n. The matching algorithm does not require an additional seed specifying the true correspondence for a polynomial-sized collection of vertices.

Both algorithms use counts of subgraphs drawn from a particular family. This common framework permits tradeoffs between computational efficiency and accuracy. The distinction between the two runtime guarantees matters: testing similarity is polynomial-time here, while recovering the full correspondence has the larger quasi-polynomial bound. Their proven success is tied to the stated random graph model.
summary.tldr: Subgraph counting enables polynomial-time similarity testing and seed-free quasi-polynomial matching in correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs.

title: (Nearly) Efficient Algorithms for the Graph Matching Problem on Correlated Random Graphs

abstract: One-bit compressed sensing (1bCS) is a method of signal acquisition under extreme measurement quantization that gives important insights on the limits of signal compression and analog-to-digital conversion. The setting is also equivalent to the problem of learning a sparse hyperplane-classifier. In this paper, we propose a generic approach for signal recovery in nonadaptive 1bCS that leads to improved sample complexity for approximate recovery for a variety of signal models, including nonnegative signals and binary signals. We construct 1bCS matrices that are universal - i.e. work for all signals under a model - and at the same time recover very general random sparse signals with high probability. In our approach, we divide the set of samples (measurements) into two parts, and use the first part to recover the superset of the support of a sparse vector. The second set of measurements is then used to approximate the signal within the superset. While support recovery in 1bCS is well-studied, recovery of superset of the support requires fewer samples, which then leads to an overall reduction in sample complexity for approximate recovery.

paragraphs: One-bit compressed sensing studies signal recovery when each measurement is reduced to a single bit. The problem also corresponds to learning a sparse hyperplane classifier. This paper develops a general recovery strategy for nonadaptive measurements, aiming to reduce how many observations are needed to approximately reconstruct sparse signals.

The method splits measurements into two groups. The first identifies a superset of the signal’s support: a collection of coordinates containing all the nonzero entries, potentially alongside extra coordinates. The second approximates the signal within that collection. Finding this larger candidate set requires fewer measurements than identifying the exact support, which reduces the total cost of approximate recovery.

The authors construct universal measurement matrices that work for every signal within a model, alongside high-probability recovery results for very general random sparse signals. Improvements cover multiple signal models, including nonnegative and binary signals. The key insight is that approximate reconstruction can benefit from an intermediate localization step that deliberately permits extra candidate coordinates instead of demanding exact support identification.
summary.tldr: Recovering a superset of nonzero coordinates before estimating their values reduces measurement requirements in one-bit compressed sensing.

title: Superset Technique for Approximate Recovery in One-Bit Compressed Sensing

abstract: We introduce a new family of non-linear neural network activation functions that mimic the properties induced by the widely-used Mat\'ern family of kernels in Gaussian process (GP) models. This class spans a range of locally stationary models of various degrees of mean-square differentiability. We show an explicit link to the corresponding GP models in the case that the network consists of one infinitely wide hidden layer. In the limit of infinite smoothness the Mat\'ern family results in the RBF kernel, and in this case we recover RBF activations. Mat\'ern activation functions result in similar appealing properties to their counterparts in GP models, and we demonstrate that the local stationarity property together with limited mean-square differentiability shows both good performance and uncertainty calibration in Bayesian deep learning tasks. In particular, local stationarity helps calibrate out-of-distribution (OOD) uncertainty. We demonstrate these properties on classification and regression benchmarks and a radar emitter classification task.

The family covers locally stationary models with different degrees of mean-square differentiability, providing a way to vary smoothness through the activation choice. The goal includes improving how Bayesian neural networks express uncertainty.

The authors establish an explicit connection to corresponding Gaussian-process models for a network with one infinitely wide hidden layer. At the infinite-smoothness limit, the Matérn family becomes the RBF kernel, and the proposed construction recovers RBF activations. This gives the activation family a defined theoretical relationship to established probabilistic models under that architectural limit.

Local stationarity specifically helps calibrate uncertainty on out-of-distribution inputs. The evaluations include classification and regression benchmarks and a radar emitter classification task, supporting activation design as a useful tool for shaping uncertainty behavior in the Bayesian deep-learning settings tested.
summary.tldr: Matérn-inspired activations connect neural networks to Gaussian-process properties and improve uncertainty calibration in evaluated Bayesian learning tasks.

title: Stationary Activations for Uncertainty Calibration in Deep Learning

abstract: Implicitly defined, continuous, differentiable signal representations parameterized by neural networks have emerged as a powerful paradigm, offering many possible benefits over conventional representations. However, current network architectures for such implicit neural representations are incapable of modeling signals with fine detail, and fail to represent a signal's spatial and temporal derivatives, despite the fact that these are essential to many physical signals defined implicitly as the solution to partial differential equations. We propose to leverage periodic activation functions for implicit neural representations and demonstrate that these networks, dubbed sinusoidal representation networks or SIRENs, are ideally suited for representing complex natural signals and their derivatives. We analyze SIREN activation statistics to propose a principled initialization scheme and demonstrate the representation of images, wavefields, video, sound, and their derivatives. Further, we show how SIRENs can be leveraged to solve challenging boundary value problems, such as particular Eikonal equations (yielding signed distance functions), the Poisson equation, and the Helmholtz and wave equations. Lastly, we combine SIRENs with hypernetworks to learn priors over the space of SIREN functions.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe signals through continuous, differentiable functions parameterized by networks. Capturing fine detail is only part of the challenge: for many physical signals, derivatives in space and time are also essential. The paper introduces sinusoidal representation networks, or SIRENs, using periodic activation functions to represent both complex signals and their derivatives.

The authors analyze the statistics of SIREN activations to develop a principled initialization scheme. They demonstrate representations of images, wavefields, video, sound, and derivatives. This combination matters because a representation that reproduces signal values must also handle derivatives well when those derivatives are central to the problem being solved.

The paper further applies SIRENs to challenging boundary value problems involving particular Eikonal equations, the Poisson equation, and Helmholtz and wave equations. The Eikonal applications yield signed distance functions. Finally, SIRENs are combined with hypernetworks to learn priors over their function space. Together, these demonstrations connect the architecture to signal representation, equation solving, and learning structure across a family of represented functions.
summary.tldr: SIRENs use periodic activations and principled initialization to represent detailed signals and their derivatives and solve several boundary value problems.

title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions

abstract: Graph neural networks have shown superior performance in a wide range of applications providing a powerful representation of graph-structured data. Recent works show that the representation can be further improved by auxiliary tasks. However, the auxiliary tasks for heterogeneous graphs, which contain rich semantic information with various types of nodes and edges, have less explored in the literature. Our methods can be applied to any graph neural networks in a plug-in manner without manual labeling or additional data. This paper builds such tasks from meta-paths, which describe composite relationships formed by sequences of different edge types.

title: Self-supervised Auxiliary Learning with Meta-paths for Heterogeneous Graphs

abstract: We address the problem of fitting 3D human models to 3D scans of dressed humans. Classical methods optimize both the data-to-model correspondences and the human model parameters (pose and shape), but are reliable only when initialised close to the solution. Some methods initialize the optimization based on fully supervised correspondence predictors, which is not differentiable end-to-end, and can only process a single scan at a time. Our main contribution is LoopReg, an end-to-end learning framework to register a corpus of scans to a common 3D human model. The key idea is to create a self-supervised loop. A backward map, parameterized by a Neural Network, predicts the correspondence from every scan point to the surface of the human model. A forward map, parameterized by a human model, transforms the corresponding points back to the scan based on the model parameters (pose and shape), thus closing the loop. Formulating this closed loop is not straightforward because it is not trivial to force the output of the NN to be on the surface of the human model -- outside this surface the human model is not even defined. To this end, we propose two key innovations. First, we define the canonical surface implicitly as the zero level set of a distance field in R3, which in contrast to more common UV parameterizations does not require cutting the surface, does not have discontinuities, and does not induce distortion. Second, we diffuse the human model to the 3D domain. This allows to map the NN predictions forward, even when they slightly deviate from the zero level set. Results demonstrate that we can train LoopReg mainly self-supervised -- following a supervised warm-start, the model becomes increasingly more accurate as additional unlabelled raw scans are processed. Our code and pre-trained models can be downloaded for research.

Results show increasing accuracy as additional unlabeled raw scans are processed, supporting the use of this loop to learn registration from a growing scan collection.
summary.tldr: LoopReg learns human-scan registration through a closed correspondence loop, improving with unlabeled scans after a supervised warm-start.

title: LoopReg: Self-supervised Learning of Implicit Surface Correspondences, Pose and Shape for 3D Human Mesh Registration

abstract: Deep neural networks are known to be overconfident when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs which clearly do not belong to any class. This is a problem in safety-critical applications since a reliable assessment of the uncertainty of a classifier is a key property, allowing to trigger human intervention or to transfer into a safe state. In this paper, we are aiming for certifiable worst case guarantees for OOD detection by enforcing not only low confidence at the OOD point but also in an $l_\infty$-ball around it. For this purpose, we use interval bound propagation (IBP) to upper bound the maximal confidence in the $l_\infty$-ball and minimize this upper bound during training time. We show that non-trivial bounds on the confidence for OOD data generalizing beyond the OOD dataset seen at training time are possible. Moreover, in contrast to certified adversarial robustness which typically comes with significant loss in prediction performance, certified guarantees for worst case OOD detection are possible without much loss in accuracy.

paragraphs: A classifier can assign high confidence to an input that belongs to none of its classes. This is especially troublesome when uncertainty should trigger human review or a safe operating state. The paper addresses whether low confidence on such out-of-distribution inputs can be protected against adversarial changes.

The training objective covers both an out-of-distribution example and a surrounding neighborhood defined by a maximum per-coordinate perturbation. Interval bound propagation computes an upper bound on the largest confidence anywhere in that neighborhood. Training minimizes this bound, so the objective addresses the worst case within the specified region rather than only the confidence at its center.

The authors show that meaningful confidence bounds can extend to out-of-distribution data beyond the examples used during training. They also find that certified worst-case detection can be achieved with little loss in classification accuracy. The guarantees concern confidence within the bounded neighborhoods, and the results demonstrate that this form of certification can have a modest accuracy cost.
summary.tldr: Training on certified confidence bounds enables robust out-of-distribution detection with little reported loss in classification accuracy.

title: Certifiably Adversarially Robust Detection of Out-of-Distribution Data

abstract: Consider an oracle which takes a point x and returns the minimizer of a convex function f in an l_2 ball of radius r around x. It is straightforward to show that roughly r^{-1}\log(1/epsilon) calls to the oracle suffice to find an \epsilon-approximate minimizer of f in an l_2 unit ball. Perhaps surprisingly, this is not optimal: we design an accelerated algorithm which attains an epsilon-approximate minimizer with roughly r^{-2/3} \log(1/epsilon) oracle queries, and give a matching lower bound. Further, we implement ball optimization oracles for functions with a locally stable Hessian using a variant of Newton's method and, in certain cases, stochastic first-order methods. The resulting algorithms apply to a number of problems of practical and theoretical import, improving upon previous results for logistic and l_infinity regression and achieving guarantees comparable to the state-of-the-art for l_p regression.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to solve a convex optimization problem when a particular local solver is available. Given a point, this solver returns the best solution within a Euclidean ball of radius r around it. The question is how many calls to that local solver are needed to find an approximately optimal solution over a unit ball.

A straightforward approach needs roughly r⁻¹ log(1/ε) calls to reach accuracy ε. The authors develop an accelerated procedure that reduces this to roughly r⁻²ᐟ³ log(1/ε) calls. They also establish a matching lower bound, showing that the improved dependence reaches the limit identified by their oracle analysis.

The paper then connects this abstract solver to implementable methods. For functions whose Hessian is locally stable, it constructs ball solvers using a Newton variant and, in certain cases, stochastic first-order methods. The resulting algorithms improve previous results for logistic and maximum-norm regression, while providing guarantees comparable to leading results for p-norm regression.
summary.tldr: An accelerated convex optimization algorithm uses fewer local ball-minimization calls, with a matching lower bound and applications to regression.

title: Acceleration with a Ball Optimization Oracle

abstract: The recent advances in image generation have been achieved by style-based image generators. Such approaches learn to disentangle latent factors in different image scales and encode latent factors as “style” to control image synthesis. However, existing approaches cannot further disentangle fine-grained semantics from each other, which are often conveyed from feature channels. In this paper, we propose a novel image synthesis approach by learning Semantic-aware relative importance for feature channels in Generative Adversarial Networks (SariGAN). Such a model disentangles latent factors according to the semantic of feature channels by channel-/group- wise fusion of latent codes and feature channels. Particularly, we learn to cluster feature channels by semantics and propose an adaptive group-wise Normalization (AdaGN) to independently control the styles of different channel groups. For example, we can adjust the statistics of channel groups for a human face to control the open and close of the mouth, while keeping other facial features unchanged. We propose to use adversarial training, a channel grouping loss, and a mutual information loss for joint optimization, which not only enables high-fidelity image synthesis but leads to superior interpretable properties. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the SOTA style-based approaches in both unconditional image generation and conditional image inpainting tasks.

paragraphs: Style-based generators provide control over image synthesis, but their controls may not separate fine-grained semantic attributes. SariGAN addresses that problem by connecting latent factors to the meanings carried by feature channels. The aim is to make changes correspond more cleanly to particular visual properties within an image.

The contribution links image quality with the organization of internal features: learned semantic groups become a mechanism for controlling distinct aspects of the generated image.
summary.tldr: SariGAN groups feature channels by semantics and controls their normalization to produce more interpretable, fine-grained image edits.

title: Learning Semantic-aware Normalization for Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Domain adaptation aims at knowledge transfer from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Current domain adaptation methods have made substantial advances in adapting discrete domains. However, this can be unrealistic in real-world applications, where target data usually comes in an online and continually evolving manner as small batches, posing challenges to classic domain adaptation paradigm: (1) Mainstream domain adaptation methods are tailored to stationary target domains, and can fail in non-stationary environments. (2) Since the target data arrive online, the agent should also maintain competence on previous target domains, i.e. to adapt without forgetting. To tackle these challenges, we propose a meta-adaptation framework which enables the learner to adapt to continually evolving target domain without catastrophic forgetting. Our framework comprises of two components: a meta-objective of learning representations to adapt to evolving domains, enabling meta-learning for unsupervised domain adaptation; and a meta-adapter for learning to adapt without forgetting, reserving knowledge from previous target data. Experiments validate the effectiveness our method on evolving target domains.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from labeled source data to an unlabeled target domain. Many methods treat the target as stationary, but practical target data can arrive in small batches and change continually. This paper studies adaptation in that evolving setting, where learning from new data must also preserve competence on previous target domains.

The proposed framework uses meta-adaptation with two components. A meta-objective trains representations for adaptation to changing domains, extending meta-learning to unsupervised domain adaptation. A meta-adapter learns how to adapt while retaining knowledge from earlier target data. Together, these components address responsiveness to new domains and the risk of catastrophic forgetting.

Experiments validate the method's effectiveness on evolving target domains. The stated contribution is a framework organized around continuing change and knowledge retention throughout adaptation. This matters because success on the latest target batch alone would not satisfy the paper's objective: the learner should also maintain abilities acquired from earlier portions of the target stream.
summary.tldr: A meta-adaptation framework learns to handle continually changing unlabeled target domains while retaining knowledge from earlier target data.

title: Learning to Adapt to Evolving Domains

abstract: Self-supervised Learning (SSL) including the mainstream contrastive learning has achieved great success in learning visual representations without data annotations. However, most of methods mainly focus on the instance level information (\ie, the different augmented images of the same instance should have the same feature or cluster into the same class), but there is a lack of attention on the relationships between different instances. In this paper, we introduced a novel SSL paradigm, which we term as relational self-supervised learning (ReSSL) framework that learns representations by modeling the relationship between different instances. Specifically, our proposed method employs sharpened distribution of pairwise similarities among different instances as \textit{relation} metric, which is thus utilized to match the feature embeddings of different augmentations. Moreover, to boost the performance, we argue that weak augmentations matter to represent a more reliable relation, and leverage momentum strategy for practical efficiency. Experimental results show that our proposed ReSSL significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both performance and training efficiency.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning often emphasizes making different augmented views of the same image agree. This paper shifts attention toward relationships between different images. Its framework, relational self-supervised learning or ReSSL, learns representations by using the pattern of similarities among instances as a training signal.

ReSSL represents those relationships with a sharpened distribution of pairwise similarities. That distribution is used to match feature embeddings across augmentations, encouraging consistency in how instances relate to one another. The authors argue that weak augmentation helps produce a more reliable relational signal. They also incorporate a momentum strategy to make the approach practically efficient.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods in both performance and training efficiency. These findings support using relationships across examples as useful supervision beyond agreement between views of an individual example. The method's design also highlights that augmentation strength affects the reliability of the relational information being used to train the representation.
summary.tldr: ReSSL learns visual representations by matching relationships among images, using weak augmentation to make those relationships more reliable.

title: ReSSL: Relational Self-Supervised Learning with Weak Augmentation

abstract: What is the minimum necessary information required by a neural net $D(\cdot)$ from an image $x$ to accurately predict its class? Extracting such information in the input space from $x$ can allocate the areas $D(\cdot)$ mainly attending to and shed novel insights to the detection and defense of adversarial attacks. In this paper, we propose ''class-disentanglement'' that trains a variational autoencoder $G(\cdot)$ to extract this class-dependent information as $x - G(x)$ via a trade-off between reconstructing $x$ by $G(x)$ and classifying $x$ by $D(x-G(x))$, where the former competes with the latter in decomposing $x$ so the latter retains only necessary information for classification in $x-G(x)$. We apply it to both clean images and their adversarial images and discover that the perturbations generated by adversarial attacks mainly lie in the class-dependent part $x-G(x)$. The decomposition results also provide novel interpretations to classification and attack models. Inspired by these observations, we propose to conduct adversarial detection and adversarial defense respectively on $x - G(x)$ and $G(x)$, which consistently outperform the results on the original $x$. In experiments, this simple approach substantially improves the detection and defense against different types of adversarial attacks.

The authors seek to expose that information directly in image space, so the resulting decomposition can illuminate classification behavior and adversarial attacks. Their approach, called class-disentanglement, separates an image into a reconstructed component and a residual.

In the reported experiments, both choices consistently outperform their counterparts operating on the original image. The results connect an interpretable decomposition of class-related information with practical improvements in detecting and defending against different adversarial attack types.
summary.tldr: Class-disentanglement separates images into complementary components that improve adversarial detection and defense in the reported experiments.

title: Class-Disentanglement and Applications in Adversarial Detection and Defense

abstract: In natural language processing, most models try to learn semantic representations merely from texts. The learned representations encode the “distributional semantics” but fail to connect to any knowledge about the physical world. In contrast, humans learn language by grounding concepts in perception and action and the brain encodes “grounded semantics” for cognition. Inspired by this notion and recent work in vision-language learning, we design a two-stream model for grounding language learning in vision. The model includes a VGG-based visual stream and a Bert-based language stream. The two streams merge into a joint representational space. Through cross-modal contrastive learning, the model first learns to align visual and language representations with the MS COCO dataset. The model further learns to retrieve visual objects with language queries through a cross-modal attention module and to infer the visual relations between the retrieved objects through a bilinear operator with the Visual Genome dataset. After training, the model’s language stream is a stand-alone language model capable of embedding concepts in a visually grounded semantic space. This semantic space manifests principal dimensions explainable with human intuition and neurobiological knowledge. Word embeddings in this semantic space are predictive of human-defined norms of semantic features and are segregated into perceptually distinctive clusters. Furthermore, the visually grounded language model also enables compositional language understanding based on visual knowledge and multimodal image search with queries based on images, texts, or their combinations.

title: Explainable Semantic Space by Grounding Language to Vision with Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning

abstract: In this paper, we tackle the problem of novel visual category discovery, i.e., grouping unlabelled images from new classes into different semantic partitions by leveraging a labelled dataset that contains images from other different but relevant categories. This is a more realistic and challenging setting than conventional semi-supervised learning. We propose a two-branch learning framework for this problem, with one branch focusing on local part-level information and the other branch focusing on overall characteristics. To transfer knowledge from the labelled data to the unlabelled, we propose using dual ranking statistics on both branches to generate pseudo labels for training on the unlabelled data. We further introduce a mutual knowledge distillation method to allow information exchange and encourage agreement between the two branches for discovering new categories, allowing our model to enjoy the benefits of global and local features. We comprehensively evaluate our method on public benchmarks for generic object classification, as well as the more challenging datasets for fine-grained visual recognition, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Novel category discovery groups unlabeled images into semantic categories using labeled images from different but related classes. The challenge is to transfer useful visual knowledge even though the labeled examples do not belong to the categories being discovered. This paper addresses that setting with two complementary views of each image.

One branch focuses on local parts, while the other captures overall characteristics. Dual ranking statistics generate pseudo-labels in both branches, allowing knowledge from labeled data to guide training on unlabeled images. A mutual knowledge distillation procedure then exchanges information between the branches and encourages them to agree about the emerging categories.

The design brings local and global features together during discovery rather than relying on either representation alone. Evaluation covers public benchmarks for generic object categories and more challenging fine-grained recognition datasets. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across that evaluation, supporting the usefulness of combining complementary visual information with mutual guidance when discovering classes absent from the labeled dataset.
summary.tldr: Two mutually teaching branches combine local and global visual information to discover new categories from unlabeled images.

title: Novel Visual Category Discovery with Dual Ranking Statistics and Mutual Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Recently, the information-theoretical framework has been proven to be able to obtain non-vacuous generalization bounds for large models trained by Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) with isotropic noise. In this paper, we optimize the information-theoretical generalization bound by manipulating the noise structure in SGLD. We prove that with constraint to guarantee low empirical risk, the optimal noise covariance is the square root of the expected gradient covariance if both the prior and the posterior are jointly optimized. This validates that the optimal noise is quite close to the empirical gradient covariance. Technically, we develop a new information-theoretical bound that enables such an optimization analysis. We then apply matrix analysis to derive the form of optimal noise covariance. Presented constraint and results are validated by the empirical observations.

We prove that with constraint to guarantee low empirical risk, the optimal noise covariance is the square root of the expected gradient covariance if both the prior and the posterior are jointly optimized. This validates that the optimal noise is quite close to the empirical gradient covariance. Technically, we develop a new information-theoretical bound that enables such an optimization analysis. We then apply matrix analysis to derive the form of optimal noise covariance. Presented constraint and results are validated by the empirical observations.

paragraphs: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics adds noise during gradient-based training. Existing information-theoretic analyses can provide informative generalization bounds when that noise is isotropic, meaning it has the same variance in every direction. This paper asks whether changing the directional structure of the noise can improve such a bound.

The authors develop a new information-theoretic bound that permits optimization over noise covariance. They then use matrix analysis to characterize the optimum. When the prior and posterior are optimized jointly, and a constraint is imposed to maintain low empirical risk, the optimal covariance is the matrix square root of the expected gradient covariance.

This is a conditional result about optimizing the proposed bound while controlling training performance. It connects the preferred noise structure to variation in the gradients, rather than treating all directions identically. The authors interpret it as supporting noise close to the empirical gradient covariance. Empirical observations validate the presented constraint and results, providing support for the relationship derived in the analysis.
summary.tldr: Under joint prior–posterior optimization and a low-training-risk constraint, an SGLD generalization bound favors noise covariance tied to gradient covariance.

title: Optimizing Information-theoretical Generalization Bound via Anisotropic Noise of SGLD

abstract: Generative modeling has evolved to a notable field of machine learning. Deep polynomial neural networks (PNNs) have demonstrated impressive results in unsupervised image generation, where the task is to map an input vector (i.e., noise) to a synthesized image. However, the success of PNNs has not been replicated in conditional generation tasks, such as super-resolution. Existing PNNs focus on single-variable polynomial expansions which do not fare well to two-variable inputs, i.e., the noise variable and the conditional variable. In this work, we introduce a general framework, called CoPE, that enables a polynomial expansion of two input variables and captures their auto- and cross-correlations. We exhibit how CoPE can be trivially augmented to accept an arbitrary number of input variables. CoPE is evaluated in five tasks (class-conditional generation, inverse problems, edges-to-image translation, image-to-image translation, attribute-guided generation) involving eight datasets. The thorough evaluation suggests that CoPE can be useful for tackling diverse conditional generation tasks. The source code of CoPE is available at https://github.com/grigorisg9gr/polynomial_nets_for_conditional_generation.

The paper identifies a mismatch in existing polynomial neural networks: their success at generating images from noise relies on single-variable expansions, while conditional generation involves both noise and a conditioning input. Simply having a successful unconditional generator does not resolve how those inputs should interact.

CoPE addresses this by expanding two input variables together. Its formulation captures relationships within each input and across the two inputs, making their interaction part of the polynomial representation. The framework can also be extended to accept an arbitrary number of input variables, broadening the kinds of conditioning information it can accommodate.

The evaluation covers eight datasets and five task categories: class-conditioned generation, inverse problems, edges-to-image translation, image-to-image translation, and attribute-guided generation. The reported evidence suggests usefulness across diverse conditional tasks. The central contribution is a general way to represent multiple interacting inputs in polynomial generators, with empirical support across these different settings.
summary.tldr: CoPE extends polynomial neural networks to conditional generation by explicitly modeling relationships within and between multiple inputs.

title: Conditional Generation Using Polynomial Expansions

abstract: As machine learning models grow more complex and their applications become more high-stakes, tools for explaining model predictions have become increasingly important. This has spurred a flurry of research in model explainability and has given rise to feature attribution methods such as LIME and SHAP. Despite their widespread use, evaluating and comparing different feature attribution methods remains challenging: evaluations ideally require human studies, and empirical evaluation metrics are often data-intensive or computationally prohibitive on real-world datasets. In this work, we address this issue by releasing XAI-BENCH: a suite of synthetic datasets along with a library for benchmarking feature attribution algorithms. Unlike real-world datasets, synthetic datasets allow the efficient computation of conditional expected values that are needed to evaluate ground-truth Shapley values and other metrics. The synthetic datasets we release offer a wide variety of parameters that can be configured to simulate real-world data. We demonstrate the power of our library by benchmarking popular explainability techniques across several evaluation metrics and across a variety of settings. The versatility and efficiency of our library will help researchers bring their explainability methods from development to deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/abacusai/xai-bench.

Comparing these explanations is difficult: human evaluations can be needed, and quantitative measures on real-world data may demand extensive data or computation. XAI-BENCH addresses this evaluation problem through synthetic datasets and a library for benchmarking attribution methods.

The key advantage of the synthetic setting is that conditional expected values can be computed efficiently. These quantities support the calculation of ground-truth Shapley values and other evaluation measures, providing reference information against which explanations can be assessed. The datasets expose configurable parameters so researchers can construct varied settings intended to resemble aspects of real-world data.

The authors demonstrate the library by comparing popular explanation techniques across multiple measures and settings. This makes the resource useful for investigating how an explanation method behaves as the evaluation conditions change. The contribution is a controllable, computationally efficient experimental foundation for explainability research. It addresses the difficulty of obtaining evaluation references while retaining flexibility in the types of synthetic data used.
summary.tldr: XAI-BENCH uses configurable synthetic data to make reference attribution values and other explanation-quality measures efficient to compute.

title: Synthetic Benchmarks for Scientific Research in Explainable Machine Learning

abstract: It is well-known that modern neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples. To mitigate this problem, a series of robust learning algorithms have been proposed. However, although the robust training error can be near zero via some methods, all existing algorithms lead to a high robust generalization error. In this paper, we provide a theoretical understanding of this puzzling phenomenon from the perspective of expressive power for deep neural networks. Specifically, for binary classification problems with well-separated data, we show that, for ReLU networks, while mild over-parameterization is sufficient for high robust training accuracy, there exists a constant robust generalization gap unless the size of the neural network is exponential in the data dimension $d$. This result holds even if the data is linear separable (which means achieving standard generalization is easy), and more generally for any parameterized function classes as long as their VC dimension is at most polynomial in the number of parameters. Moreover, we establish an improved upper bound of $\exp({\mathcal{O}}(k))$ for the network size to achieve low robust generalization error when the data lies on a manifold with intrinsic dimension $k$ ($k \ll d$). Nonetheless, we also have a lower bound that grows exponentially with respect to $k$ --- the curse of dimensionality is inevitable. By demonstrating an exponential separation between the network size for achieving low robust training and generalization error, our results reveal that the hardness of robust generalization may stem from the expressive power of practical models.

paragraphs: A network can resist adversarial perturbations on its training examples yet remain vulnerable on new data. This paper investigates that gap through expressive power: whether a model is large enough to represent a classifier that generalizes robustly. Its theoretical setting concerns binary classification with well-separated data.

An accompanying lower bound still grows exponentially in k. These results identify representational capacity as a possible source of robust generalization difficulty, including settings where ordinary generalization is easy, and show why lower intrinsic dimension helps without eliminating the theoretical dimensionality barrier.
summary.tldr: Theoretical bounds reveal an exponential model-size separation between robust training and robust generalization in the studied classification settings.

title: Why Robust Generalization in Deep Learning is Difficult: Perspective of Expressive Power

abstract: The dynamic membrane potential threshold, as one of the essential properties of a biological neuron, is a spontaneous regulation mechanism that maintains neuronal homeostasis, i.e., the constant overall spiking firing rate of a neuron. As such, the neuron firing rate is regulated by a dynamic spiking threshold, which has been extensively studied in biology. Existing work in the machine learning community does not employ bioinspired spiking threshold schemes. This work aims at bridging this gap by introducing a novel bioinspired dynamic energy-temporal threshold (BDETT) scheme for spiking neural networks (SNNs). The proposed BDETT scheme mirrors two bioplausible observations: a dynamic threshold has 1) a positive correlation with the average membrane potential and 2) a negative correlation with the preceding rate of depolarization. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed BDETT on robot obstacle avoidance and continuous control tasks under both normal conditions and various degraded conditions, including noisy observations, weights, and dynamic environments. We find that the BDETT outperforms existing static and heuristic threshold approaches by significant margins in all tested conditions, and we confirm that the proposed bioinspired dynamic threshold scheme offers homeostasis to SNNs in complex real-world tasks.

paragraphs: A spiking neuron fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold. In biological neurons, that threshold can change to help maintain a stable overall firing rate, a property called homeostasis. This paper brings that regulatory idea into spiking neural networks through a bioinspired dynamic energy-temporal threshold scheme, BDETT.

BDETT follows two biological observations. The threshold is positively related to average membrane potential and negatively related to the preceding rate of depolarization. In plain terms, the firing threshold responds both to the neuron’s average internal state and to how quickly that state was rising. This makes the threshold part of the neuron’s changing behavior rather than a fixed setting.

The authors evaluate BDETT on robot obstacle avoidance and continuous control. Tests include normal operation and degraded conditions involving noisy observations, noisy weights, and changing environments. BDETT significantly outperforms static and heuristic threshold approaches in every tested condition. The results also support its ability to provide homeostasis in these tasks, connecting biologically motivated firing regulation with practical control performance.
summary.tldr: BDETT adapts spiking thresholds using biological principles, improving control performance and firing-rate stability in the tested conditions.

title: Biologically Inspired Dynamic Thresholds for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: There have been multiple works that try to ascertain explanations for decisions of black box models on particular inputs by perturbing the input or by sampling around it, creating a neighborhood and then fitting a sparse (linear) model (e.g. LIME). Many of these methods are unstable and so more recent work tries to find stable or robust alternatives. However, stable solutions may not accurately represent the behavior of the model around the input. Thus, the question we ask in this paper is are we approximating the local boundary around the input accurately? In particular, are we sampling the right neighborhood so that a linear approximation of the black box is faithful to its true behavior around that input given that the black box can be highly non-linear (viz. deep relu network with many linear pieces). It is difficult to know the correct neighborhood width (or radius) as too small a width can lead to a bad condition number of the inverse covariance matrix of function fitting procedures resulting in unstable predictions, while too large a width may lead to accounting for multiple linear pieces and consequently a poor local approximation. We in this paper propose a simple approach that is robust across neighborhood widths in recovering faithful local explanations. In addition to a naive implementation of our approach which can still be accurate, we propose a novel adaptive neighborhood sampling scheme (ANS) that we formally show can be much more sample and query efficient. We then empirically evaluate our approach on real data where our explanations are significantly more sample and query efficient than the competitors, while also being faithful and stable across different widths.

paragraphs: Many explanations of black-box predictions fit a simple linear model to samples near the input of interest. The paper asks whether those samples cover an appropriate neighborhood. An explanation can be stable across repeated runs while still failing to describe how the original model behaves locally.

Neighborhood size creates a practical tension. Sampling too narrowly can make the fitting problem numerically ill-conditioned and predictions unstable. Sampling too broadly can combine several different linear regions of a nonlinear model, leaving a single linear explanation poorly matched to the input's surroundings. The authors propose an approach that recovers faithful local explanations across different neighborhood widths.

They also develop adaptive neighborhood sampling, or ANS, and formally show that it can require substantially fewer samples and black-box queries than a naive implementation of their approach. Experiments on real data find significant efficiency improvements over competitors while retaining fidelity and stability across widths. The contribution connects explanation quality with sampling design: choosing where to query the model is part of producing a useful local account of its behavior.
summary.tldr: Adaptive neighborhood sampling produces faithful, stable local explanations with fewer samples and black-box queries in the reported experiments.

title: Is this the Right Neighborhood? Accurate and Query Efficient Model Agnostic Explanations

abstract: The stochastic multi-armed bandit setting has been recently studied in the non-stationary regime, where the mean payoff of each action is a non-decreasing function of the number of rounds passed since it was last played. This model captures natural behavioral aspects of the users which crucially determine the performance of recommendation platforms, ad placement systems, and more. Even assuming prior knowledge of the mean payoff functions, computing an optimal planning in the above model is NP-hard, while the state-of-the-art is a $1/4$-approximation algorithm for the case where at most one arm can be played per round. We first focus on the setting where the mean payoff functions are known. In this setting, we significantly improve the best-known guarantees for the planning problem by developing a polynomial-time $(1-{1}/{e})$-approximation algorithm (asymptotically and in expectation), based on a novel combination of randomized LP rounding and a time-correlated (interleaved) scheduling method. Furthermore, our algorithm achieves improved guarantees -- compared to prior work -- for the case where more than one arms can be played at each round. Moving to the bandit setting, when the mean payoff functions are initially unknown, we show how our algorithm can be transformed into a bandit algorithm with sublinear regret.

paragraphs: In this bandit setting, an action's expected payoff can increase the longer it has gone unused. Choosing an action therefore affects both the reward available now and its opportunity to recharge. This captures behavior relevant to recommendations and advertising, but it creates a difficult scheduling problem: optimal planning is NP-hard even when the payoff functions are already known.

For known payoff functions, the paper combines randomized rounding of a linear program with an interleaved scheduling method that coordinates choices over time. The resulting polynomial-time algorithm achieves a 1 − 1/e approximation asymptotically and in expectation. This improves on the previous 1/4 guarantee for the setting allowing at most one action per round.

The algorithm also improves prior guarantees when several actions can be selected in each round. Finally, the authors transform the planner into a bandit algorithm for initially unknown payoff functions, obtaining sublinear regret. That extension connects better scheduling with learning the recharging behavior from experience, while retaining the stated theoretical performance guarantees.
summary.tldr: A randomized scheduling method improves approximation guarantees for recharging-payoff bandits and extends to unknown payoffs with sublinear regret.

title: Non-Stationary Bandits under Recharging Payoffs: Improved Planning with Sublinear Regret

abstract: Fully decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning has shown great potentials for many real-world cooperative tasks, where the global information, \textit{e.g.}, the actions of other agents, is not accessible. Although independent Q-learning is widely used for decentralized training, the transition probabilities are non-stationary since other agents are updating policies simultaneously, which leads to non-guaranteed convergence of independent Q-learning. To deal with non-stationarity, we first introduce stationary ideal transition probabilities, on which independent Q-learning could converge to the global optimum. Further, we propose a fully decentralized method, I2Q, which performs independent Q-learning on the modeled ideal transition function to reach the global optimum. The modeling of ideal transition function in I2Q is fully decentralized and independent from the learned policies of other agents, helping I2Q be free from non-stationarity and learn the optimal policy. Empirically, we show that I2Q can achieve remarkable improvement in a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks.

paragraphs: In fully decentralized cooperative reinforcement learning, agents cannot access global information such as the actions of other agents. Independent Q-learning is a natural option, but each agent learns while the others change their policies. Consequently, the transition probabilities it experiences keep changing, and convergence of ordinary independent Q-learning is not guaranteed.

The paper introduces stationary ideal transition probabilities under which independent Q-learning could converge to the global optimum. I2Q then models this ideal transition function and performs independent Q-learning on it. Crucially, that modeling is fully decentralized and independent of the policies learned by other agents, addressing the source of non-stationarity identified by the authors.

The proposed route to optimal learning therefore rests on the modeled ideal transitions rather than directly treating the changing interaction process as stationary. Empirically, I2Q achieves substantial improvements across a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks. These results support the approach of changing the transition model used for learning while preserving the decentralized information setting.
summary.tldr: I2Q models stationary ideal transitions to address non-stationarity in fully decentralized cooperative Q-learning.

title: I2Q: A Fully Decentralized Q-Learning Algorithm

abstract: Humans learn from visual inputs at multiple timescales, both rapidly and flexibly acquiring visual knowledge over short periods, and robustly accumulating online learning progress over longer periods. Modeling these powerful learning capabilities is an important problem for computational visual cognitive science, and models that could replicate them would be of substantial utility in real-world computer vision settings. In this work, we establish benchmarks for both real-time and life-long continual visual learning. Our real-time learning benchmark measures a model's ability to match the rapid visual behavior changes of real humans over the course of minutes and hours, given a stream of visual inputs. Our life-long learning benchmark evaluates the performance of models in a purely online learning curriculum obtained directly from child visual experience over the course of years of development. We evaluate a spectrum of recent deep self-supervised visual learning algorithms on both benchmarks, finding that none of them perfectly match human performance, though some algorithms perform substantially better than others. Interestingly, algorithms embodying recent trends in self-supervised learning -- including BYOL, SwAV and MAE -- are substantially worse on our benchmarks than an earlier generation of self-supervised algorithms such as SimCLR and MoCo-v2. We present analysis indicating that the failure of these newer algorithms is primarily due to their inability to handle the kind of sparse low-diversity datastreams that naturally arise in the real world, and that actively leveraging memory through negative sampling -- a mechanism eschewed by these newer algorithms -- appears useful for facilitating learning in such low-diversity environments. We also illustrate a complementarity between the short and long timescales in the two benchmarks, showing how requiring a single learning algorithm to be locally context-sensitive enough to match real-time learning changes while stable enough to avoid catastrophic forgetting over the long term induces a trade-off that human-like algorithms may have to straddle. Taken together, our benchmarks establish a quantitative way to directly compare learning between neural networks models and human learners, show how choices in the mechanism by which such algorithms handle sample comparison and memory strongly impact their ability to match human learning abilities, and expose an open problem space for identifying more flexible and robust visual self-supervision algorithms.

summary.tldr: Two human-learning benchmarks reveal weaknesses in self-supervised algorithms on sparse visual streams and a trade-off between rapid adaptation and long-term retention.

title: How Well Do Unsupervised Learning Algorithms Model Human Real-time and Life-long Learning?

abstract: While neural network binary classifiers are often evaluated on metrics such as Accuracy and $F_1$-Score, they are commonly trained with a cross-entropy objective. How can this training-evaluation gap be addressed? While specific techniques have been adopted to optimize certain confusion matrix based metrics, it is challenging or impossible in some cases to generalize the techniques to other metrics. Adversarial learning approaches have also been proposed to optimize networks via confusion matrix based metrics, but they tend to be much slower than common training methods. In this work, we propose a unifying approach to training neural network binary classifiers that combines a differentiable approximation of the Heaviside function with a probabilistic view of the typical confusion matrix values using soft sets. Our theoretical analysis shows the benefit of using our method to optimize for a given evaluation metric, such as $F_1$-Score, with soft sets, and our extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our approach in several domains.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often trained to minimise cross-entropy but assessed using accuracy or F1 score. These objectives measure different things, creating a gap between what training directly rewards and what evaluation ultimately values. Existing ways to optimise particular evaluation metrics can be difficult to extend to other metrics, while adversarial alternatives can be slow.

The paper proposes a shared approach for metrics built from confusion matrix entries, such as counts of correct and incorrect positive predictions. It combines a differentiable approximation to the Heaviside threshold function with a probabilistic interpretation of those entries through soft sets. This replaces the abrupt classification threshold with a formulation that supports gradient-based optimisation of the desired metric.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting the benefit of optimising an evaluation metric through this soft-set construction, including F1 score. They also report effective results across several experimental domains. The approach matters because it connects the training objective more directly to the criterion used to judge the classifier, while offering a common construction across confusion-matrix-based metrics.
summary.tldr: A differentiable soft-set formulation lets binary classifiers train more directly toward confusion-matrix-based evaluation metrics such as F1.

title: Bridging the Gap: Unifying the Training and Evaluation of Neural Network Binary Classifiers

abstract: Forecasting future world events is a challenging but valuable task. Forecasts of climate, geopolitical conflict, pandemics and economic indicators help shape policy and decision making. In these domains, the judgment of expert humans contributes to the best forecasts. Given advances in language modeling, can these forecasts be automated? To this end, we introduce Autocast, a dataset containing thousands of forecasting questions and an accompanying news corpus. Questions are taken from forecasting tournaments, ensuring high quality, real-world importance, and diversity. The news corpus is organized by date, allowing us to precisely simulate the conditions under which humans made past forecasts (avoiding leakage from the future). Motivated by the difficulty of forecasting numbers across orders of magnitude (e.g. global cases of COVID-19 in 2022), we also curate IntervalQA, a dataset of numerical questions and metrics for calibration. We test language models on our forecasting task and find that performance is far below a human expert baseline. However, performance improves with increased model size and incorporation of relevant information from the news corpus. In sum, Autocast poses a novel challenge for large language models and improved performance could bring large practical benefits.

paragraphs: Forecasting future events requires judging uncertain developments, often with substantial expert input. This paper introduces Autocast to test whether language models can help automate that task, using thousands of questions drawn from forecasting tournaments and an accompanying news corpus.

The news is organized by date so experiments can reproduce the information available when a historical forecast was made, avoiding leakage from later events. The authors also introduce IntervalQA, a numerical-question dataset with calibration metrics, motivated by quantities that vary across orders of magnitude.

Tested language models perform far below a human-expert baseline. Larger models and access to relevant news improve results, but do not close the reported gap. The abstract does not provide forecast scores. The contribution is a challenging evaluation resource and an initial assessment of capabilities, rather than evidence that language models already match experts on consequential future-event predictions.
summary.tldr: Autocast benchmarks future-event forecasting while controlling access to time-stamped news.

title: Forecasting Future World Events With Neural Networks

abstract: The standard assumption in reinforcement learning (RL) is that agents observe feedback for their actions immediately. However, in practice feedback is often observed in delay. This paper studies online learning in episodic Markov decision process (MDP) with unknown transitions, adversarially changing costs, and unrestricted delayed bandit feedback. More precisely, the feedback for the agent in episode $k$ is revealed only in the end of episode $k + d^k$, where the delay $d^k$ can be changing over episodes and chosen by an oblivious adversary. We present the first algorithms that achieve near-optimal $\sqrt{K + D}$ regret, where $K$ is the number of episodes and $D = \sum_{k=1}^K d^k$ is the total delay, significantly improving upon the best known regret bound of $(K + D)^{2/3}$.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents often must act before feedback from earlier decisions arrives. This paper studies that problem in episodic Markov decision processes with unknown transitions and adversarially changing costs. Feedback is limited to the bandit setting and can arrive after a different delay for each episode.

Specifically, feedback for episode k appears only at the end of episode k plus its delay. Delays are unrestricted and may be chosen by an oblivious adversary. This creates a learning problem in which the agent must cope simultaneously with uncertainty about environmental transitions, changing costs, and information that remains unavailable while subsequent episodes take place.

The authors provide algorithms with near-optimal regret scaling as the square root of K+D, where K counts episodes and D sums their delays. This improves the previously known dependence of (K+D) to the two-thirds power. The result makes the cumulative cost of delayed information explicit: the bound depends on total delay as well as the number of episodes, while achieving a sharper growth rate in their combined quantity.
summary.tldr: New algorithms achieve near-optimal square-root regret dependence on episodes plus total delay in adversarial episodic reinforcement learning.

title: Near-Optimal Regret for Adversarial MDP with Delayed Bandit Feedback

abstract: It has been observed that visual classification models often rely mostly on spurious cues such as the image background, which hurts their robustness to distribution changes. To alleviate this shortcoming, we propose to monitor the model's relevancy signal and direct the model to base its prediction on the foreground object.This is done as a finetuning step, involving relatively few samples consisting of pairs of images and their associated foreground masks. Specifically, we encourage the model's relevancy map (i) to assign lower relevance to background regions, (ii) to consider as much information as possible from the foreground, and (iii) we encourage the decisions to have high confidence. When applied to Vision Transformer (ViT) models, a marked improvement in robustness to domain-shifts is observed. Moreover, the foreground masks can be obtained automatically, from a self-supervised variant of the ViT model itself; therefore no additional supervision is required. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hila-chefer/RobustViT.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can base predictions on background cues that happen to correlate with the correct label. When those correlations change, performance can suffer. This paper proposes using a model's relevance map during fine-tuning to encourage predictions that depend more on the foreground object.

The fine-tuning procedure uses relatively few image-and-mask pairs. It encourages three behaviors: assigning less relevance to background regions, using information from as much of the foreground as possible, and making confident predictions. The relevance map therefore becomes a target for training, connecting where the model finds evidence with the classification behavior the authors want to promote.

Applied to vision transformers, the approach produces a marked improvement in robustness to domain shifts in the reported evaluation. The foreground masks can also be generated automatically by a self-supervised variant of the vision transformer itself, avoiding additional supervision for those masks. The results suggest that directing the model's relevance toward foreground evidence can be a useful way to improve robustness through a relatively small fine-tuning intervention.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning vision transformers to emphasize foreground relevance improves reported robustness to domain shifts, using masks that can be generated automatically.

title: Optimizing Relevance Maps of Vision Transformers Improves Robustness

abstract: The matrix completion problem seeks to recover a $d\times d$ ground truth matrix of low rank $r\ll d$ from observations of its individual elements. Real-world matrix completion is often a huge-scale optimization problem, with $d$ so large that even the simplest full-dimension vector operations with $O(d)$ time complexity become prohibitively expensive. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is one of the few algorithms capable of solving matrix completion on a huge scale, and can also naturally handle streaming data over an evolving ground truth. Unfortunately, SGD experiences a dramatic slow-down when the underlying ground truth is ill-conditioned; it requires at least $O(\kappa\log(1/\epsilon))$ iterations to get $\epsilon$-close to ground truth matrix with condition number $\kappa$. In this paper, we propose a preconditioned version of SGD that preserves all the favorable practical qualities of SGD for huge-scale online optimization while also making it agnostic to $\kappa$. For a symmetric ground truth and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) loss, we prove that the preconditioned SGD converges to $\epsilon$-accuracy in $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ iterations, with a rapid linear convergence rate as if the ground truth were perfectly conditioned with $\kappa=1$. In our numerical experiments, we observe a similar acceleration forill-conditioned matrix completion under the root mean square error (RMSE) loss, Euclidean distance matrix (EDM) completion under pairwise square loss, and collaborative filtering under the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix from observations of individual entries. At enormous scales, even operations on a full vector can be too expensive. Stochastic gradient descent is attractive because it supports inexpensive updates and streaming observations, including settings where the underlying matrix evolves. However, poor conditioning can dramatically slow its convergence.

The authors propose a preconditioned version of stochastic gradient descent that retains these practical advantages while removing dependence on the condition number from the stated convergence rate. For a symmetric target matrix and root mean square error loss, they prove that reaching error ε takes O(log(1/ε)) iterations, compared with the condition-number-dependent iteration requirement described for ordinary SGD.

This result makes the analyzed method converge as rapidly as if the target were perfectly conditioned. Numerical experiments also show acceleration for ill-conditioned matrix completion, Euclidean distance matrix completion, and collaborative filtering with their respective stated losses. Those experiments extend the practical evidence beyond the specific symmetric-matrix setting covered by the theorem.
summary.tldr: Preconditioned SGD removes condition-number dependence from a matrix-completion convergence guarantee while retaining suitability for huge streaming problems.

title: Accelerating SGD for Highly Ill-Conditioned Huge-Scale Online Matrix Completion

abstract: Commercial adoption of automatic music composition requires the capability of generating diverse and high-quality music suitable for the desired context (e.g., music for romantic movies, action games, restaurants, etc.). In this paper, we introduce combinatorial music generation, a new task to create varying background music based on given conditions. Combinatorial music generation creates short samples of music with rich musical metadata, and combines them to produce a complete music. In addition, we introduce ComMU, the first symbolic music dataset consisting of short music samples and their corresponding 12 musical metadata for combinatorial music generation. Notable properties of ComMU are that (1) dataset is manually constructed by professional composers with an objective guideline that induces regularity, and (2) it has 12 musical metadata that embraces composers' intentions. Our results show that we can generate diverse high-quality music only with metadata, and that our unique metadata such as track-role and extended chord quality improves the capacity of the automatic composition. We highly recommend watching our video before reading the paper (https://pozalabs.github.io/ComMU/).

paragraphs: This paper introduces combinatorial music generation, a task for creating varied background music that fits requested conditions. The approach generates short musical samples with descriptive metadata and combines those samples into complete music. This organization connects control over individual musical pieces with the broader goal of producing music suited to a particular context.

To support the task, the authors introduce ComMU, a symbolic music dataset containing short samples and twelve associated musical metadata fields. Professional composers manually construct the dataset using an objective guideline intended to encourage regularity. The metadata also captures aspects of composers’ intentions, giving generation systems information about how samples are meant to function musically.

The reported results show that metadata alone can guide the generation of diverse, high-quality music. The authors also find that particular metadata, including track role and extended chord quality, improves automatic composition capability. These findings support the usefulness of musically informative conditioning: the dataset supplies both composable material and structured descriptions that help direct its generation.
summary.tldr: ComMU pairs composer-created musical samples with twelve metadata fields to support controllable generation and combination of background music.

title: ComMU: Dataset for Combinatorial Music Generation

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables the collaborative training of machine learning models among various parties without the need for sensitive information exchange. Nonetheless, retaining data in individual clients introduces fundamental challenges to achieving performance on par with centrally trained models. Our study provides an extensive review of federated learning applied to visual recognition. It underscores the critical role of thoughtful architectural design choices in achieving optimal performance, a factor often neglected in the FL literature. Many existing FL solutions are tested on shallow or simple networks, which may not accurately reflect real-world applications. This practice restricts the transferability of research findings to large-scale visual recognition models. Through an in-depth analysis of diverse cutting-edge architectures such as convolutional neural networks, transformers, and MLP-mixers, we experimentally demonstrate that architectural choices can substantially enhance FL systems' performance, particularly when handling heterogeneous data. We study visual recognition models from five different architectural families on four challenging FL datasets. We also re-investigate the inferior performance convolution-based architectures in the FL setting and analyze the influence of normalization layers on the FL performance. Our findings emphasize the importance of architectural design for computer vision tasks in practical scenarios, effectively narrowing the performance gap between federated and centralized learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple parties train a shared model while retaining their data locally. For visual recognition, differences between clients' data can make matching centralized training difficult. This paper examines architectural design as an important part of that challenge, arguing that conclusions drawn from shallow or simple networks may transfer poorly to larger recognition systems.

The study evaluates models from five architectural families on four federated-learning datasets, including convolutional networks, transformers, and MLP-mixers. It investigates how these choices affect performance under heterogeneous data. It also revisits the weaker performance of convolution-based architectures in federated settings and studies the influence of normalization layers.

The experiments show that architecture can substantially improve federated visual-recognition performance and narrow the gap with centralized learning. This makes the model itself an important design choice when evaluating federated methods, alongside the collaborative training procedure. The findings support studying architectures representative of practical visual-recognition systems, since a result obtained with a simplified network may not capture how a larger model behaves.
summary.tldr: Experiments across five architecture families show that model design can substantially improve federated visual recognition under heterogeneous client data.

title: Handling Data Heterogeneity via Architectural Design for Federated Visual Recognition

abstract: In consequential domains, it is often impossible to compel individuals to take treatment, so that optimal policy rules are merely suggestions in the presence of human non-adherence to treatment recommendations. In these same domains, there may be heterogeneity both in who responds in taking-up treatment, and heterogeneity in treatment efficacy. For example, in social services, a persistent puzzle is the gap in take-up of beneficial services among those who may benefit from them the most. When in addition the decision-maker has distributional preferences over both access and average outcomes, the optimal decision rule changes. We study identification, doubly-robust estimation, and robust estimation under potential violations of positivity. We consider fairness constraints such as demographic parity in treatment take-up, and other constraints, via constrained optimization. Our framework can be extended to handle algorithmic recommendations under an often-reasonable covariate-conditional exclusion restriction, using our robustness checks for lack of positivity in the recommendation. We develop a two-stage, online learning-based algorithm for solving over parametrized policy classes under general constraints to obtain variance-sensitive regret bounds. We assess improved recommendation rules in a stylized case study of optimizing recommendation of supervised release in the PSA-DMF pretrial risk-assessment tool while reducing surveillance disparities.
