paragraphs: Evaluating a latent representation involves understanding how much diversity its points contain and how that diversity changes with the scale of observation. This paper uses metric-space magnitude, a mathematical quantity describing a space's effective size across scales. Magnitude also captures geometric properties associated with curvature, density, and entropy.

The authors develop a family of diversity measures based on this quantity. They also formalize a way to compare the magnitude functions of finite metric spaces, allowing different representations to be assessed through their multiscale structure. The measures are efficiently computable and provably stable under data perturbations, giving the comparison a mathematical foundation beyond a single diversity score.

The work evaluates these measures for automated diversity estimation, detection of mode collapse, and assessment of generative models producing text, images, and graphs. The authors report superior performance across the investigated domains and tasks. These results support magnitude as a practical tool for examining whether representations or generated outputs preserve varied structure, with comparisons that incorporate multiple scales of distance.
summary.tldr: Magnitude-based measures provide stable, efficient comparisons of representation diversity across multiple scales.

title: Metric Space Magnitude for Evaluating the Diversity of Latent Representations

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative machine learning, while preserving user data privacy. Despite its potential, standard FL algorithms lack support for diverse heterogeneous device prototypes, which vary significantly in model and dataset sizes---from small IoT devices to large workstations. This limitation is only partially addressed by existing knowledge distillation (KD) techniques, which often fail to transfer knowledge effectively across a broad spectrum of device prototypes with varied capabilities. This failure primarily stems from two issues: the dilution of informative logits from more capable devices by those from less capable ones, and the use of a single integrated logits as the distillation target across all devices, which neglects their individual learning capacities and and the unique contributions of each device. To address these challenges, we introduce TAKFL, a novel KD-based framework that treats the knowledge transfer from each device prototype's ensemble as a separate task, independently distilling each to preserve its unique contributions and avoid dilution. TAKFL also incorporates a KD-based self-regularization technique to mitigate the issues related to the noisy and unsupervised ensemble distillation process. To integrate the separately distilled knowledge, we introduce an adaptive task arithmetic knowledge integration process, allowing each student model to customize the knowledge integration for optimal performance. Additionally, we present theoretical results demonstrating the effectiveness of task arithmetic in transferring knowledge across heterogeneous device prototypes with varying capacities. Comprehensive evaluations of our method across both computer vision (CV) and natural language processing (NLP) tasks demonstrate that TAKFL achieves state-of-the-art results in a variety of datasets and settings, significantly outperforming existing KD-based methods. Our code is released at https://github.com/MMorafah/TAKFL and the project website is available at https://mmorafah.github.io/takflpage .

paragraphs: Federated learning must sometimes coordinate devices with very different model capacities and dataset sizes. Knowledge distillation can share their knowledge, but merging all teacher outputs can dilute informative signals from stronger devices. Giving every student the same merged target also overlooks differences in what each student can learn and what each device contributes.

TAKFL treats knowledge transfer from each device prototype's ensemble as a separate task. It distills those tasks independently, preserving their distinct contributions, and uses distillation-based self-regularization to mitigate noise in the unsupervised ensemble-distillation process. An adaptive task-arithmetic step then combines the separately distilled knowledge in a way customized to each student model.

The paper provides theoretical results supporting task arithmetic for knowledge transfer across devices of varying capacities. Evaluations on computer-vision and natural-language-processing tasks report state-of-the-art results and significant improvements over existing distillation-based methods. The contribution is a separation between acquiring knowledge from different sources and deciding how a particular student should integrate it, making device diversity central to the transfer process.
summary.tldr: TAKFL separately distills knowledge from different device prototypes and adaptively combines it for each student's learning capacity.

title: Towards Diverse Device Heterogeneous Federated Learning via Task Arithmetic Knowledge Integration

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become widespread across diverse applications, concerns about the security and safety of LLM interactions have intensified. Numerous guardrail models and benchmarks have been developed to ensure LLM content safety. However, existing guardrail benchmarks are often built upon ad hoc risk taxonomies that lack a principled grounding in standardized safety policies, limiting their alignment with real-world operational requirements. Moreover, they tend to overlook domain-specific risks, while the same risk category can carry different implications across different domains. To bridge these gaps, we introduce PolyGuard, the first massive multi-domain safety policy-grounded guardrail dataset. PolyGuard offers: (1) broad domain coverage across eight safety-critical domains, such as finance, law, and codeGen; (2) policy-grounded risk construction based on authentic, domain-specific safety guidelines; (3) diverse interaction formats, encompassing declarative statements, questions, instructions, and multi-turn conversations; (4) advanced benign data curation via detoxification prompting to challenge over-refusal behaviors; and (5) \textbf{attack-enhanced instances} that simulate adversarial inputs designed to bypass guardrails. Based on PolyGuard, we benchmark 19 advanced guardrail models and uncover a series of findings, such as: (1) All models achieve varied F1 scores, with many demonstrating high variance across risk categories, highlighting their limited domain coverage and insufficient handling of domain-specific safety concerns; (2) As models evolve, their coverage of safety risks broadens, but performance on common risk categories may decrease; (3) All models remain vulnerable to optimized adversarial attacks. The policy-grounded \dataset establishes the first principled and comprehensive guardrail benchmark. We believe that \dataset and the unique insights derived from our evaluations will advance the development of policy-aligned and resilient guardrail systems.

paragraphs: PolyGuard evaluates language-model guardrails using risks grounded in authentic safety guidelines for specific domains. The authors argue that ad hoc risk categories can miss operational requirements and overlook how the same risk has different implications in different settings. Their dataset covers eight safety-critical domains, including finance, law, and code generation.

The benchmark includes statements, questions, instructions, and multi-turn conversations. It also contains benign examples curated through detoxification prompting to challenge excessive refusal, alongside adversarial examples designed to bypass safeguards. These components test both sides of guardrail behavior: recognizing problematic interactions and allowing harmless ones, across multiple formats and domain-specific policy requirements.

Evaluation of 19 guardrail models finds substantial variation across risk categories, indicating uneven domain coverage. The authors also observe that newer models can cover more kinds of risk while losing performance on common categories. Every evaluated model remains vulnerable to optimized adversarial attacks. These findings show why policy-grounded, domain-aware evaluation matters: broader coverage alone does not establish consistent performance or resistance to deliberate attempts to evade a guardrail.
summary.tldr: PolyGuard benchmarks guardrails against domain-specific safety policies and finds uneven risk coverage and adversarial vulnerabilities across all 19 evaluated models.

title: PolyGuard: Massive Multi-Domain Safety Policy-Grounded Guardrail Dataset

abstract: Fair classification is a critical challenge that has gained increasing importance due to international regulations and its growing use in high-stakes decision-making settings. Existing methods often rely on adversarial learning or distribution matching across sensitive groups; however, adversarial learning can be unstable, and distribution matching can be computationally intensive. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach based on the characteristic function distance. Our method ensures that the learned representation contains minimal sensitive information while maintaining high effectiveness for downstream tasks. By utilizing characteristic functions, we achieve a more stable and efficient solution compared to traditional methods. Additionally, we introduce a simple relaxation of the objective function that guarantees fairness in common classification models with no performance degradation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently matches or achieves better fairness and predictive accuracy than existing methods. Moreover, our method maintains robustness and computational efficiency, making it a practical solution for real-world applications.

paragraphs: Fair classifiers need representations that remain useful for prediction while carrying little sensitive information. Existing approaches often rely on adversarial learning or matching distributions across sensitive groups. This paper targets the instability of adversarial training and the computational expense of distribution matching by using a distance based on characteristic functions.

The proposed objective uses that distance to minimize sensitive information in the learned representation while preserving downstream predictive effectiveness. The authors present it as a more stable and efficient approach than traditional alternatives. They also introduce a simple relaxation of the objective that guarantees fairness without performance degradation for common classification models, with the guarantee scoped to those models.

On benchmark datasets, the method consistently matches or improves on existing approaches in both fairness and predictive accuracy. The experiments also support its robustness and computational efficiency. The practical significance is the combination of a representation-learning objective with a simpler classifier-oriented relaxation: the paper seeks fairness improvements that remain compatible with useful prediction and manageable training costs.
summary.tldr: Characteristic-function-based representation learning improves fairness and accuracy in benchmarks, with a relaxed objective guaranteeing fairness without performance loss for common classifiers.

title: Simple and Effective Specialized Representations for Fair Classifiers

abstract: Although diffusion-based models can generate high-quality and high-resolution video sequences from textual or image inputs, they lack explicit integration of geometric cues when controlling scene lighting and visual appearance across frames. To address this limitation, we propose IllumiCraft, an end-to-end diffusion framework accepting three complementary inputs: (1) high-dynamic-range (HDR) video maps for detailed lighting control; (2) synthetically relit frames with randomized illumination changes (optionally paired with a static background reference image) to provide appearance cues; and (3) 3D point tracks that capture precise 3D geometry information. By integrating the lighting, appearance, and geometry cues within a unified diffusion architecture, IllumiCraft generates temporally coherent videos aligned with user-defined prompts. It supports the background-conditioned and text-conditioned video relighting and provides better fidelity than existing controllable video generation methods.

paragraphs: IllumiCraft targets video generation in which lighting and appearance must remain controlled across frames. The paper identifies a gap in diffusion-based video systems: they can generate high-quality sequences from text or images, but do not explicitly integrate geometric information when controlling illumination. This motivates treating lighting, appearance, and geometry as coordinated inputs.

Synthetically relit frames with randomized illumination changes provide appearance cues, optionally accompanied by a static background reference image. Three-dimensional point tracks supply geometric information. A unified diffusion architecture combines these inputs to generate videos that remain temporally coherent and follow user-defined prompts.

The system supports video relighting conditioned on either a background or text, and the paper reports higher fidelity than existing controllable video generation methods. Its contribution is the joint use of explicit geometry and illumination cues across a sequence. This gives the model information about scene structure alongside instructions about how that scene should look under changing light.
summary.tldr: IllumiCraft combines lighting maps, appearance cues, and 3D point tracks for temporally coherent, controllable video relighting.

title: IllumiCraft: Unified Geometry and Illumination Diffusion for Controllable Video Generation

abstract: This paper introduces \textsc{InfantAgent-Next}, a generalist agent capable of interacting with computers in a multimodal manner, encompassing text, images, audio, and video. Unlike existing approaches that either build intricate workflows around a single large model or only provide workflow modularity, our agent integrates tool-based and pure vision agents within a highly modular architecture, enabling different models to collaboratively solve decoupled tasks in a step-by-step manner. Our generality is demonstrated by our ability to evaluate not only pure vision-based real-world benchmarks (i.e., OSWorld), but also more general or tool-intensive benchmarks (e.g., GAIA and SWE-Bench). Specifically, we achieve a $\mathbf{7.27\\%}$ accuracy gain over Claude-Computer-Use on OSWorld. Codes and evaluation scripts are included in the supplementary material and will be released as open-source.

paragraphs: Computer interaction tasks can involve different kinds of information and different ways of taking action. InfantAgent-Next introduces a generalist agent designed to handle text, images, audio, and video within one modular architecture. Its central contribution is a way to coordinate capabilities across models while solving a task step by step.

The architecture integrates agents that use tools with agents that operate through vision. Tasks are separated into components that different models can solve collaboratively. This extends modularity beyond rearranging workflow stages: the system brings together distinct interaction approaches so that computer use can include both visual operation and tool-intensive work.

The authors demonstrate this breadth through evaluation on OSWorld, which involves vision-based computer interaction, and on GAIA and SWE-Bench, which cover more general or tool-intensive tasks. On OSWorld, they report a 7.27% accuracy gain over Claude-Computer-Use. The evidence therefore combines coverage across benchmark types with a specific improvement in visual computer interaction, supporting the usefulness of the integrated modular design.
summary.tldr: InfantAgent-Next coordinates tool-based and vision agents in a modular multimodal system, reporting improved OSWorld accuracy.

title: InfantAgent-Next: A Multimodal Generalist Agent for Automated Computer Interaction

abstract: Federated Generalized Category Discovery (Fed-GCD) requires a global model to classify seen classes and discover novel classes when data are siloed across heterogeneous clients. Existing GCD work often makes unrealistic assumptions, such as the need for prior knowledge of the number of novel classes or the assumption of uniform class distribution. We present Federated Local Prior Alignment (FedLPA), which eliminates these unrealistic assumptions by grounding learning in client-local structure and aligning predictions to client-local priors. Each client builds a similarity graph refined with reliable seen-class signals and discovers client-specific concepts and prototypes via Infomap. Leveraging the discovered concept structures, we introduce Local Prior Alignment (LPA): a self-distillation loss that matches the batch-mean prediction to an empirical prior computed from current concept assignments. The iterative process of local structure discovery and dynamic prior adaptation enables robust generalized category discovery under severe data heterogeneity. Our framework significantly outperforms existing federated generalized category discovery approaches on fine-grained and standard benchmarks, as demonstrated by extensive experimental results.

paragraphs: Federated generalized category discovery requires a shared model to recognize known classes and identify new ones while data remain distributed across clients. Different clients may have very different class mixtures. FedLPA addresses this setting without requiring advance knowledge of the number of novel classes or assuming a uniform class distribution.

Each client constructs a similarity graph and refines it using reliable information about known classes. Infomap then identifies client-specific concepts and their prototypes. These discovered structures provide a local basis for estimating the class proportions that predictions should reflect, instead of imposing a common distribution on every client.

Local Prior Alignment uses a self-distillation loss to match average predictions within a batch to an empirical prior derived from current concept assignments. Repeating discovery and prior adaptation lets those targets change as the local structure becomes clearer. Experiments on standard and fine-grained benchmarks report significant improvements over existing federated discovery approaches. The central idea is to make heterogeneous local structure part of the learning process.
summary.tldr: FedLPA discovers client-local concepts and adapts prediction priors to improve federated category discovery under heterogeneous data distributions.

title: FedLPA: Local Prior Alignment for Heterogeneous Federated Generalized Category Discovery

abstract: In domains such as molecular and protein generation, physical systems exhibit inherent symmetries that are critical to model. Two main strategies have emerged for learning invariant distributions: designing equivariant network architectures and using data augmentation to approximate equivariance. While equivariant architectures preserve symmetry by design, they often involve greater complexity and pose optimization challenges. Data augmentation, on the other hand, offers flexibility but may fall short in fully capturing symmetries. Our framework enhances both approaches by reducing training variance and providing a provably lower-variance gradient estimator. We achieve this by interpreting data augmentation as a Monte Carlo estimator of the training gradient and applying Rao–Blackwellization. This leads to more stable optimization, faster convergence, and reduced variance, all while requiring only a single forward and backward pass per sample. We also present a practical implementation of this estimator—incorporating the loss and sampling procedure—through a method we call Orbit Diffusion. Theoretically, we guarantee that our loss admits equivariant minimizers. Empirically, Orbit Diffusion achieves state-of-the-art results on GEOM-QM9 for molecular conformation generation, improves crystal structure prediction, and advances text-guided crystal generation on the Perov-5 and MP-20 benchmarks. Additionally, it enhances protein designability in protein structure generation. Code is available at https://github.com/vinhsuhi/Orbit-Diffusion.git.

summary.tldr: Orbit Diffusion uses a provably lower-variance gradient estimator to improve symmetry-aware diffusion training and several scientific generation tasks.

title: Rao-Blackwell Gradient Estimators for Equivariant Denoising Diffusion

abstract: A key challenge in automated formal reasoning is the intractable search space, which grows exponentially with the depth of the proof. This branching is caused by the large number of candidate proof tactics which can be applied to a given goal. Nonetheless, many of these tactics are semantically similar or lead to an execution error, wasting valuable resources in both cases. We address the problem of effectively pruning this search, using only synthetic data generated from previous proof attempts. We first demonstrate that it is possible to generate semantically aware tactic representations which capture the effect on the proving environment, likelihood of success, and execution time. We then propose a novel filtering mechanism which leverages these representations to select semantically diverse and high quality tactics, using Determinantal Point Processes. Our approach, 3D-Prover, is designed to be general, and to augment any underlying tactic generator. We demonstrate the effectiveness of 3D-Prover on the miniF2F and LeanDojo benchmarks by augmenting popular open source proving LLMs. We show that our approach leads to an increase in the overall proof rate, as well as a significant improvement in the tactic success rate, execution time and diversity. We make our code available at https://github.com/sean-lamont/3D-Prover.

paragraphs: Automated theorem provers must choose among many possible tactics at every step. As proofs become longer, these choices produce an enormous search space. Some candidate tactics accomplish essentially the same thing, while others fail during execution. Trying all of them spends resources without exploring proportionately more useful possibilities.

3D-Prover learns representations of tactics from synthetic data collected during earlier proof attempts. These representations capture what a tactic does to the proving environment, its likelihood of succeeding, and its execution time. A filtering mechanism then uses determinantal point processes to select candidates that combine quality with semantic diversity. The selection therefore considers both individual usefulness and how much candidates overlap.

The authors augment existing open-source proving language models and evaluate them on miniF2F and LeanDojo. They report higher proof rates alongside improvements in tactic success, execution time, and diversity. The contribution is a way to spend proof-search resources more effectively, designed to work alongside an underlying tactic generator.
summary.tldr: 3D-Prover improves proof search by selecting promising tactics that also explore meaningfully different possibilities.

title: 3D-Prover: Diversity Driven Theorem Proving With Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) for Combinatorial Optimization (CO) is an emerging paradigm for solving combinatorial problems using neural networks. In this paper, we address a central challenge of SSL for CO: solving problems with discrete constraints. We design an end-to-end differentiable framework that enables us to solve discrete constrained optimization problems with neural networks. Concretely, we leverage algorithmic techniques from the literature on convex geometry and Carathéodory's theorem to decompose neural network outputs into convex combinations of polytope corners that correspond to feasible sets. This decomposition-based approach enables self-supervised training but also ensures efficient quality-preserving rounding of the neural net output into feasible solutions. Extensive experiments in cardinality-constrained optimization show that our approach can consistently outperform neural baselines. We further provide worked-out examples of how our method can be applied beyond cardinality-constrained problems to a diverse set of combinatorial optimization tasks, including finding independent sets in graphs, and solving matroid-constrained problems.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn to solve combinatorial optimization problems, but their continuous outputs must ultimately become discrete decisions that satisfy constraints. This creates a central difficulty for self-supervised training: the representation used for learning needs a reliable connection to valid final solutions. The paper develops a differentiable framework around that connection.

Its approach uses convex geometry and Carathéodory’s theorem to express a network output as a weighted combination of corners of a polytope. Those corners correspond to feasible sets. Representing the output through valid discrete alternatives supports self-supervised learning while also providing a way to round it into a feasible solution efficiently and with preserved solution quality.

Experiments on problems with cardinality constraints, which restrict the number of selected elements, show consistent improvements over neural baselines. The authors also work through applications to graph independent sets and matroid constraints. These examples extend the framework’s scope beyond the experimentally emphasized setting, showing how the same geometric strategy can be applied to additional constrained combinatorial tasks.
summary.tldr: A geometric decomposition links differentiable neural training to efficient rounding into feasible discrete solutions.

title: Geometric Algorithms for Neural Combinatorial Optimization with Constraints

abstract: In real-world applications, node features in graphs often contain noise from various sources, leading to significant performance degradation in GNNs. Although several methods have been developed to enhance robustness, they rely on the unrealistic assumption that noise in node features is independent of the graph structure and node labels, thereby limiting their applicability. To this end, we introduce a more realistic noise scenario, dependency-aware noise on graphs (DANG), where noise in node features create a chain of noise dependencies that propagates to the graph structure and node labels. We propose a novel robust GNN, DA-GNN, which captures the causal relationships among variables in the data generating process (DGP) of DANG using variational inference. In addition, we present new benchmark datasets that simulate DANG in real-world applications, enabling more practical research on robust GNNs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DA-GNN consistently outperforms existing baselines across various noise scenarios, including both DANG and conventional noise models commonly considered in this field.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can lose accuracy when node attributes are noisy. The paper argues that common robustness methods make an overly restrictive assumption: feature noise is independent of graph structure and node labels. In the proposed dependency-aware noise setting, corruption participates in a chain of dependencies extending to both structure and labels.

The authors formalize this setting as DANG and develop DA-GNN to model it. The model uses variational inference to capture causal relationships among variables in the assumed data-generating process. This gives the learning method a way to account for linked sources of corruption, rather than treating noisy attributes as isolated from the rest of the graph.

The paper also introduces benchmark datasets that simulate these dependencies in real-world application settings. Experiments report that DA-GNN consistently outperforms existing baselines under both DANG and conventional noise models. The results support studying robustness through the relationships among corrupted quantities, with the benchmark contribution making this broader noise setting available for further evaluation.
summary.tldr: DA-GNN models dependencies connecting feature noise, graph structure, and labels, improving reported robustness across dependent and conventional noise settings.

title: Training Robust Graph Neural Networks by Modeling Noise Dependencies

abstract: Heterogeneity poses a fundamental challenge for many real-world large-scale decision-making problems but remains largely understudied. In this paper, we study the _fully heterogeneous_ setting of a prominent class of such problems, known as weakly-coupled Markov decision processes (WCMDPs). Each WCMDP consists of $N$ arms (or subproblems), which have distinct model parameters in the fully heterogeneous setting, leading to the curse of dimensionality when $N$ is large. We show that, under mild assumptions, an efficiently computable policy achieves an $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ optimality gap in the long-run average reward per arm for fully heterogeneous WCMDPs as $N$ becomes large. This is the _first asymptotic optimality result_ for fully heterogeneous average-reward WCMDPs. Our main technical innovation is the construction of projection-based Lyapunov functions that certify the convergence of rewards and costs to an optimal region, even under full heterogeneity.

paragraphs: The paper studies large decision problems made up of many weakly coupled Markov decision processes, called arms. In its fully heterogeneous setting, every arm may have different model parameters. This diversity makes the combined problem difficult as the number of arms grows, because the overall decision space suffers from the curse of dimensionality.

The authors show that an efficiently computable policy approaches optimal long-run average reward per arm under mild assumptions. Its optimality gap is of order one divided by the square root of the number of arms. Thus, the guarantee becomes tighter as the system grows, despite allowing all arms to differ from one another.

The proof introduces projection-based Lyapunov functions that certify convergence of rewards and costs toward an optimal region. This supplies a way to analyze stability and performance without requiring homogeneous arms. The authors identify the result as the first asymptotic optimality guarantee for fully heterogeneous average-reward problems of this type. The guarantee is conditional on the stated assumptions and concerns the per-arm average as system size increases.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, an efficient policy becomes asymptotically optimal for weakly coupled decision processes whose arms all have distinct parameters.

title: Projection-based Lyapunov method for fully heterogeneous weakly-coupled MDPs

abstract: Language models must be adapted to understand and follow user instructions. Reinforcement learning is widely used to facilitate this —typically using fixed criteria such as "helpfulness" and "harmfulness". In our work, we instead propose using flexible, instruction-specific criteria as a means of broadening the impact that reinforcement learning can have in eliciting instruction following. We propose "Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback" (RLCF). From instructions, we extract checklists and evaluate how well responses satisfy each item—using both AI judges and specialized verifier programs—then combine these scores to compute rewards for RL. We compare RLCF with other alignment methods on top of a strong instruction following model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on five widely-studied benchmarks — RLCF is the only method to help on every benchmark, including a 4-point boost in hard satisfaction rate on FollowBench, a 6-point increase on InFoBench, and a 3-point rise in win rate on Arena-Hard. We show that RLCF can also be used off-policy to improve Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and OLMo 2 7B Instruct. These results establish rubrics as a key tool for improving language models' support of queries that express a multitude of needs. We release our our dataset of rubrics (WildChecklists), models, and code to the public.

paragraphs: A user instruction can contain several requirements that broad reward criteria such as helpfulness do not describe individually. This paper proposes Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback, or RLCF, to make training rewards reflect the particular requirements of each instruction. The central idea is to judge a response against a tailored checklist.

RLCF extracts checklist items from instructions, then evaluates how well responses satisfy them. It uses both AI judges and specialized verification programs, combining their item-level scores into a reinforcement-learning reward. This gives the training process a way to respond to multiple needs expressed within the same query.

Starting from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, RLCF was the only compared alignment method to improve all five evaluated benchmarks. Reported gains include four points in FollowBench hard satisfaction rate, six points on InFoBench, and three points in Arena-Hard win rate. Off-policy use also improved Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and OLMo 2 7B Instruct. The results support instruction-specific rubrics as a useful alignment tool, with the WildChecklists dataset, models, and code released publicly.
summary.tldr: RLCF turns instruction-specific checklists into reinforcement-learning rewards and improves all five evaluated benchmarks on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

title: Checklists Are Better Than Reward Models For Aligning Language Models

abstract: Recently, deep learning-based pan-sharpening algorithms have achieved notable advancements over traditional methods. However, deep learning-based methods incur substantial computational overhead during inference, especially with large images. This excessive computational demand limits the applicability of these methods in real-world scenarios, particularly in the absence of dedicated computing devices such as GPUs and TPUs. To address these challenges, we propose Pan-LUT, a novel learnable look-up table (LUT) framework for pan-sharpening that strikes a balance between performance and computational efficiency for large remote sensing images. Our method makes it possible to process 15K$\times$15K remote sensing images on a 24GB GPU. To finely control the spectral transformation, we devise the PAN-guided look-up table (PGLUT) for channel-wise spectral mapping. To effectively capture fine-grained spatial details, we introduce the spatial details look-up table (SDLUT). Furthermore, to adaptively aggregate channel information for generating high-resolution multispectral images, we design an adaptive output look-up table (AOLUT). Our model contains fewer than 700K parameters and processes a 9K$\times$9K image in under 1 ms using one RTX 2080 Ti GPU, demonstrating significantly faster performance compared to other methods. Experiments reveal that Pan-LUT efficiently processes large remote sensing images in a lightweight manner, bridging the gap to real-world applications. Furthermore, our model surpasses SOTA methods in full-resolution scenes under real-world conditions, highlighting its effectiveness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Pan-sharpening aims to produce high-resolution multispectral imagery, but deep-learning approaches can become expensive on large remote-sensing images. Pan-LUT tackles this computational burden with learned look-up tables. Its design divides the transformation into specialized components that handle spectral information, spatial detail, and the final combination of channels.

A PAN-guided table controls spectral mapping separately for each channel. A spatial-details table captures fine image structure, and an adaptive output table combines channel information to form the high-resolution multispectral result. This division gives the framework distinct mechanisms for preserving spectral behavior and recovering spatial detail while keeping the overall model small.

The authors report fewer than 700,000 parameters and processing of a 9K-by-9K image in under one millisecond on an RTX 2080 Ti. They also report handling 15K-by-15K images on a 24GB GPU. Experiments show faster processing and better performance than state-of-the-art methods in full-resolution real-world scenes. These results support learned look-up tables as an efficient approach to very large remote-sensing images under the reported hardware conditions.
summary.tldr: Pan-LUT uses specialized learned look-up tables to produce high-resolution multispectral images with low model size and fast reported inference.

title: Pan-LUT: Efficient Pan-sharpening via Learnable Look-Up Tables

abstract: The interpretation of genomic sequences is crucial for understanding biological processes. To handle the growing volume of DNA sequence data, Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) have been developed by adapting architectures and training paradigms from Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite their remarkable performance in DNA sequence classification tasks, there remains a lack of systematic understanding regarding the training and task-adaptation processes of GFMs. Moreover, existing GFMs cannot achieve state-of-the-art performance on both short and long-context tasks and lacks multimodal abilities. By revisiting pre-training architectures and post-training techniques, we propose **Omni-DNA**, a family of models spanning 20M to 1.1B parameters that supports sequence understanding, long-context genomic reasoning, and natural-language annotation. **Omni-DNA** establishes new state-of-the-art results on 18 of 26 evaluations drawn from Nucleotide Transformer and Genomic Benchmarks. When jointly fine-tuning on biologically related tasks, **Omni-DNA** consistently outperform existing models and demonstrate multi-tasking abilities. To enable processing of arbitrary sequence lengths, we introduce **SEQPACK**—an adaptive compression operator that packs historical tokens into a learned synopsis using a position-aware learnable sampling mechanism, enabling transformer-based models to process ultra-long sequences with minimal memory and computational requirements. Our approach demonstrates superior performance on enhancer-target interaction tasks, capturing distant regulatory interactions at the 450kbp range more effectively than existing models. Finally, we present a new dataset termed **seq2func**, enabling Omni-DNA to generate accurate and functionally meaningful interpretations of DNA sequences, unlocking new possibilities for genomic analysis and discovery.

title: Omni-DNA: A Genomic Model Supporting Sequence Understanding, Long-context, and Textual Annotation

abstract: Concept-based models are an emerging paradigm in deep learning that constrains the inference process to operate through human-interpretable variables, facilitating explainability and human interaction. However, these architectures, on par with popular opaque neural models, fail to account for the true causal mechanisms underlying the target phenomena represented in the data. This hampers their ability to support causal reasoning tasks, limits out-of-distribution generalization, and hinders the implementation of fairness constraints. To overcome these issues, we propose Causally reliable Concept Bottleneck Models (C$^2$BMs), a class of concept-based architectures that enforce reasoning through a bottleneck of concepts structured according to a model of the real-world causal mechanisms. We also introduce a pipeline to automatically learn this structure from observational data and unstructured background knowledge (e.g., scientific literature). Experimental evidence suggests that C$^2$BMs are more interpretable, causally reliable, and improve responsiveness to interventions w.r.t. standard opaque and concept-based models, while maintaining their accuracy.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through intermediate variables that people can understand. That visibility supports explanation and human interaction, but understandable variables do not automatically capture how the underlying phenomenon works. The paper argues that ignoring causal relationships can limit causal reasoning, generalization beyond the training distribution, and the implementation of fairness constraints.

The proposed Causally reliable Concept Bottleneck Models organize their intermediate concepts according to a model of real-world causal mechanisms. Prediction therefore passes through concepts whose relationships have an explicit causal structure. The authors also introduce a pipeline for learning this structure using observational data together with unstructured background knowledge, such as scientific literature.

Experimental evidence suggests that these models improve interpretability, causal reliability, and responses to interventions compared with standard opaque and concept-based models, while maintaining prediction accuracy. The significance is that the model's explanation layer also structures its reasoning. The reported results support the value of combining interpretable concepts with causal organization, rather than treating interpretability alone as sufficient for reliable intervention behavior.
summary.tldr: Causally structured concept bottlenecks show improved interpretability and intervention behavior while maintaining predictive accuracy in experiments.

title: Causally Reliable Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Biological brains learn continually from a stream of unlabeled data, while integrating specialized information from sparsely labeled examples without compromising their ability to generalize. Meanwhile, machine learning methods are susceptible to catastrophic forgetting in this natural learning setting, as supervised specialist fine-tuning degrades performance on the original task. We introduce task-modulated contrastive learning (TMCL), which takes inspiration from the biophysical machinery in the neocortex, using predictive coding principles to integrate top-down information continually and without supervision. We follow the idea that these principles build a view-invariant representation space, and that this can be implemented using a contrastive loss. Then, whenever labeled samples of a new class occur, new affine modulations are learned that improve separation of the new class from all others, without affecting feedforward weights. By co-opting the view-invariance learning mechanism, we then train feedforward weights to match the unmodulated representation of a data sample to its modulated counterparts. This introduces modulation invariance into the representation space, and, by also using past modulations, stabilizes it. Our experiments show improvements in both class-incremental and transfer learning over state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches, as well as over comparable supervised approaches, using as few as 1% of available labels. Taken together, our work suggests that top-down modulations play a crucial role in balancing stability and plasticity.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to absorb new information without losing previously useful abilities. This becomes especially difficult when most incoming examples lack labels and only occasional examples identify a new class. The paper introduces task-modulated contrastive learning, or TMCL, to incorporate that sparse supervision while preserving a stable representation.

TMCL first uses contrastive learning to encourage different views of an example to receive consistent representations. When labeled examples introduce a class, it learns affine modulations that improve the class’s separation without immediately changing the feedforward weights. It then trains those weights to bring an example’s ordinary representation into agreement with its modulated versions. Reusing earlier modulations helps stabilize the representation as learning continues.

Experiments report improvements in class-incremental and transfer learning over leading unsupervised methods and comparable supervised methods, using as little as 1% of available labels. These findings support the proposed role of top-down modulation: it supplies specialized information that can subsequently be consolidated into a more general representation, helping balance adaptation with retention.
summary.tldr: TMCL consolidates sparsely supervised modulations into stable representations, improving continual and transfer learning with few labels.

title: Contrastive Consolidation of Top-Down Modulations Achieves Sparsely Supervised Continual Learning

abstract: Recently, convolutional filters have been increasingly adopted in sequential recommendation for their ability to capture local sequential patterns. However, most of these models complement convolutional filters with self-attention. This is because convolutional filters alone, generally fixed filters, struggle to capture global interactions necessary for accurate recommendation. We propose \textbf{T}ime-\textbf{V}ariant Convolutional Filters for Sequential \textbf{Rec}ommendation (TV-Rec), a model inspired by graph signal processing, where time-variant graph filters capture position-dependent temporal variations in user sequences. By replacing both fixed kernels and self-attention with time-variant filters, TV-Rec achieves higher expressive power and better captures complex interaction patterns in user behavior. This design not only eliminates the need for self-attention but also reduces computation while accelerating inference. Extensive experiments on six public benchmarks show that TV-Rec outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 7.49\%.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation uses a person's interaction history to predict what they may want next. Convolutional filters can capture local patterns in that history, but fixed filters struggle with broader interactions. Many existing models therefore add self-attention. TV-Rec explores whether filters that change with sequence position can provide the needed expressiveness more efficiently.

Inspired by graph signal processing, TV-Rec uses time-variant graph filters to capture position-dependent changes in user sequences. These filters replace both fixed convolution kernels and self-attention. The design lets the filtering operation vary across the history, helping the model represent complex behavior patterns while reducing computation and speeding up inference.

Across six public benchmarks, the authors report an average improvement of 7.49% over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support time-variant filtering as an effective architecture for the evaluated recommendation tasks. The central contribution is showing how a more expressive filter design can address the global-interaction weakness that otherwise motivates adding attention, while also providing the reported computational benefits.
summary.tldr: TV-Rec replaces fixed convolutions and self-attention with position-dependent filters, improving reported recommendation quality and inference efficiency.

title: TV-Rec: Time-Variant Convolutional Filter for Sequential Recommendation

abstract: For a well trained Boosting classifier, we are interested in how to save the testing time, i.e., to make the decision without evaluating all the base learners. To address this problem, in previous work the base learners are sequentially calculated and early stopping is allowed if the decision function has been confident enough to output its value. In such a chain structure, the order of base learners is critical: better order can lead to less evaluation time. In this paper, we present a novel method for ordering. We base our discussion on the data structure representing Boosting’s decision function. Viewing the decision function a boolean expression, we propose a Binary Valued Tree for its representation. As a secondary contribution, such a representation unifies the work by previous researchers and helps devise new representation. Also, its connection to Binary Decision Diagram(BDD) is discussed.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a trained boosting classifier can make predictions without evaluating every base learner. Existing methods evaluate learners sequentially and permit early stopping when the decision function is sufficiently confident. In this arrangement, evaluation order matters because some orderings can reach a decision with less work.

The authors propose a new ordering method based on the representation of the boosting decision function. They view that function as a Boolean expression and introduce a Binary Valued Tree to represent it. This makes the structure of the combined decision central to the problem of choosing an evaluation order.

The representation also provides a common perspective on earlier work and helps motivate additional representations. The paper discusses its connection to Binary Decision Diagrams as well. Its contribution is therefore both operational and conceptual: it addresses the order in which a trained classifier's components are evaluated while offering a structural language for understanding and developing ways to compute the final decision.
summary.tldr: A Binary Valued Tree representation motivates a new base-learner ordering method intended to reduce boosting prediction time.

title: Saving Evaluation Time for the Decision Function in Boosting: Representation and Reordering Base Learner

abstract: We study the problem of building generative models of natural source code (NSC); that is, source code written and understood by humans. Our primary contribution is to describe a family of generative models for NSC that have two key properties: First, they incorporate both sequential and hierarchical structure. Second, they are capable of integrating closely with a compiler, which allows leveraging compiler logic and abstractions when building structure into the model. We also develop an extension that includes more complex structure, refining how the model generates identifier tokens based on what variables are currently in scope. Our models can be learned efficiently, and we show empirically that including appropriate structure greatly improves the probability of generating test programs.

paragraphs: The paper studies generative models of source code written and understood by people. Its central idea is that code has both a sequential organization and a hierarchical structure, and a model can incorporate both. The authors describe a family of models designed to represent these aspects together.

A second defining feature is close integration with a compiler. This allows compiler logic and abstractions to help determine the structure built into the model. The authors also develop an extension for generating identifier tokens that takes account of which variables are currently in scope, adding programming-context information to the generation process.

The models can be learned efficiently, and the empirical results show that appropriate structure substantially increases the probability assigned to test programs. That finding concerns how well the models account for observed programs. It supports the value of incorporating compiler-informed organization and scope information into probabilistic code modeling, rather than treating the program solely as a sequence of tokens.
summary.tldr: Efficient generative code models combine sequence, hierarchy, and compiler-informed scope structure to assign higher probability to test programs.

title: Structured Generative Models of Natural Source Code

abstract: We consider a generalization of the classic linear regression problem to the case when the loss is an Orlicz norm. An Orlicz norm is parameterized by a non-negative convex function G: R_+ - > R_+ with G(0) = 0: the Orlicz norm of a n-dimensional vector x is defined as |x|_G = inf{ alpha > 0 | sum_{i = 1}^n G( |x_i| / alpha ) < = 1 }. We consider the cases where the function G grows subquadratically. Our main result is based on a new oblivious embedding which embeds the column space of a given nxd matrix A with Orlicz norm into a lower dimensional space with L2 norm. Specifically, we show how to efficiently find an mxn embedding matrix S (m < n), such that for every d-dimensional vector x, we have Omega(1/(d log n)) |Ax|_G < = |SAx|_2 < = O(d^2 log n) |Ax|_G. By applying this subspace embedding technique, we show an approximation algorithm for the regression problem min_x |Ax-b|_G, up to a O( d log^2 n ) factor. As a further application of our techniques, we show how to also use them to improve on the algorithm for the Lp low rank matrix approximation problem for 1 < = p < 2.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes linear regression by measuring residuals with an Orlicz norm. Such a norm is defined through a nonnegative convex function G that vanishes at zero. The authors focus on functions G with subquadratic growth, giving a specified family of losses for which they develop efficient approximation methods.

Their main tool is an oblivious subspace embedding that maps the column space of an n-by-d matrix into a lower-dimensional space measured with the Euclidean norm. The guarantee holds for every vector in that column space. The embedded norm lies between an Omega(1/(d log n)) multiple and an O(d² log n) multiple of the original Orlicz norm.

This controlled distortion allows the authors to obtain an O(d log² n)-factor approximation for Orlicz-norm regression. The contribution is a reduction from a more general norm geometry to a smaller Euclidean representation with explicit guarantees. They also apply their techniques to improve an algorithm for low-rank matrix approximation under l_p losses when 1 ≤ p < 2.
summary.tldr: A lower-dimensional Euclidean embedding enables provable approximation algorithms for regression with subquadratic Orlicz norms.

title: Subspace Embedding and Linear Regression with Orlicz Norm

abstract: We present an extension of the cut-pursuit algorithm, introduced by Landrieu and Obozinski (2017), to the graph total-variation regularization of functions with a separable nondifferentiable part. We propose a modified algorithmic scheme as well as adapted proofs of convergence. We also present a heuristic approach for handling the cases in which the values associated to each vertex of the graph are multidimensional. The performance of our algorithm, which we demonstrate on difficult, ill-conditioned large-scale inverse and learning problems, is such that it may in practice extend the scope of application of the total-variation regularization.

We propose a modified algorithmic scheme as well as adapted proofs of convergence. paragraphs: Graph total-variation regularization uses relationships between graph vertices to constrain an optimization problem's solution. This paper extends the cut-pursuit algorithm to objectives containing a separable nondifferentiable component. That setting matters because useful objectives can contain terms for which ordinary derivatives are unavailable, requiring an algorithm designed to accommodate them.

The authors modify the algorithmic scheme and adapt its convergence proofs to the extended setting. They also consider problems where each vertex carries several values rather than a single scalar. For this multidimensional case, they present a heuristic approach, keeping its status distinct from the convergence analysis of the main algorithm.

The method is demonstrated on large inverse and learning problems described as difficult and ill-conditioned. Its observed performance suggests that it may make total-variation regularization practical for a wider range of applications. This is a qualified practical implication of the demonstrations, alongside the more formal contribution of extending the algorithm and its convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: An extended cut-pursuit algorithm handles graph total-variation objectives with separable nondifferentiable terms and shows promising large-scale performance.

title: Cut-Pursuit Algorithm for Regularizing Nonsmooth Functionals with Graph Total Variation

abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings offer excellent quality with few dimensions when embedding hierarchical data structures. We give a combinatorial construction that embeds trees into hyperbolic space with arbitrarily low distortion without optimization. On WordNet, this algorithm obtains a mean-average-precision of 0.989 with only two dimensions, outperforming existing work by 0.11 points. We provide bounds characterizing the precision-dimensionality tradeoff inherent in any hyperbolic embedding. To embed general metric spaces, we propose a hyperbolic generalization of multidimensional scaling (h-MDS). We show how to perform exact recovery of hyperbolic points from distances, provide a perturbation analysis, and give a recovery result that enables us to reduce dimensionality. Finally, we extract lessons from the algorithms and theory above to design a scalable PyTorch-based implementation that can handle incomplete information.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic space can represent hierarchical data well using few dimensions. This paper investigates both how to construct such representations and what they demand from numerical precision. It gives a combinatorial procedure that embeds trees with arbitrarily low distortion without optimization, providing a direct construction rather than requiring an embedding to be learned.

On WordNet, the construction achieves mean average precision of 0.989 in two dimensions, exceeding existing work by 0.11 points. The authors also derive bounds on the tradeoff between precision and dimensionality inherent in hyperbolic embeddings. This connects compact representations with the precision needed to express them, making dimensionality only one part of the representation question.

For general metric spaces, the paper proposes hyperbolic multidimensional scaling. It establishes exact recovery of hyperbolic points from distances, analyzes perturbations, and provides a recovery result supporting dimensionality reduction. These theoretical and algorithmic lessons inform a scalable PyTorch implementation that can work with incomplete information, extending the work beyond the tree-specific construction.
summary.tldr: Direct constructions and recovery algorithms clarify how hyperbolic embeddings trade dimensionality against numerical precision.

title: Representation Tradeoffs for Hyperbolic Embeddings

abstract: We present a novel way of generating Lyapunov functions for proving linear convergence rates of first-order optimization methods. Our approach provably obtains the fastest linear convergence rate that can be verified by a quadratic Lyapunov function (with given states), and only relies on solving a small-sized semidefinite program. Our approach combines the advantages of performance estimation problems (PEP, due to Drori and Teboulle (2014)) and integral quadratic constraints (IQC, due to Lessard et al. (2016)), and relies on convex interpolation (due to Taylor et al. (2017c;b)).
originalAbstract: We present a novel way of generating Lyapunov functions for proving linear convergence rates of first-order optimization methods. Our approach provably obtains the fastest linear convergence rate that can be verified by a quadratic Lyapunov function (with given states), and only relies on solving a small-sized semidefinite program. Our approach combines the advantages of performance estimation problems (PEP, due to Drori and Teboulle (2014)) and integral quadratic constraints (IQC, due to Lessard et al. (2016)), and relies on convex interpolation (due to Taylor et al. (2017c;b)).

paragraphs: This paper develops an automated way to construct Lyapunov functions for analyzing first-order optimization methods. Such a function provides a quantity whose behavior can certify progress toward convergence. The authors focus on proving linear convergence rates, turning the search for a suitable certificate into a computational problem.

Their method requires solving only a small semidefinite program. For a given choice of states, it provably finds the fastest linear rate that a quadratic Lyapunov function can verify. This qualification defines the strength of the result: the rate is optimal within that specified class of certificates and with those states.

The construction combines advantages of performance estimation problems and integral quadratic constraints, using convex interpolation as a mathematical foundation. These ingredients support a systematic procedure for producing convergence guarantees. The main contribution is therefore both computational and theoretical: a manageable optimization problem generates a certificate, and the result establishes that the chosen certificate class cannot verify a faster rate.
summary.tldr: A small semidefinite program finds the fastest linear convergence rate certifiable by quadratic Lyapunov functions with specified states.

title: Lyapunov Functions for First-Order Methods: Tight Automated Convergence Guarantees

abstract: We propose a fixed-point iteration approach to the maximum likelihood estimation for the incomplete multinomial model, which provides a unified framework for ranking data analysis. Incomplete observations typically fall in a subset of categories, and thus cannot be distinguished as belonging to a unique category. We develop a minorization–maximization (MM) type of algorithm, which requires relatively fewer iterations and shorter time to achieve convergence. Under such a general framework, incomplete multinomial models can be reformulated to include several well-known ranking models as special cases, such as the Bradley–Terry, Plackett–Luce models and their variants. The simple form of iteratively updating equations in our algorithm involves only basic matrix operations, which makes it efficient and easy to implement with large data. Experimental results show that our algorithm runs faster than existing methods on synthetic data and real data.

paragraphs: An incomplete multinomial observation identifies a subset of possible categories rather than one definite category. Estimating a model from such observations requires accounting for that ambiguity. The paper develops a maximum likelihood estimation framework for this setting and shows how it also provides a common treatment of several ranking models.

The proposed estimator uses fixed-point iterations through a minorization–maximization type of algorithm. Its update equations involve basic matrix operations, giving the procedure a simple implementation suitable for large datasets. Within the same framework, familiar ranking models such as Bradley–Terry and Plackett–Luce, along with their variants, appear as special cases.

This unification matters because computational improvements to the general estimator can apply across multiple ranking formulations. The authors report that the algorithm needs relatively fewer iterations and less time to converge, and experiments on synthetic and real data show faster execution than existing methods. The contribution combines a shared statistical formulation with an efficient iterative solution, connecting ambiguous categorical observations to practical ranking-data analysis.
summary.tldr: A simple fixed-point algorithm accelerates maximum likelihood estimation for incomplete multinomial models and several ranking models.

title: Fast and Stable Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Incomplete Multinomial Models

abstract: We consider the setting of distributed empirical risk minimization where multiple machines compute the gradients in parallel and a centralized server updates the model parameters. In order to reduce the number of communications required to reach a given accuracy, we propose a preconditioned accelerated gradient method where the preconditioning is done by solving a local optimization problem over a subsampled dataset at the server. The convergence rate of the method depends on the square root of the relative condition number between the global and local loss functions. We estimate the relative condition number for linear prediction models by studying uniform concentration of the Hessians over a bounded domain, which allows us to derive improved convergence rates for existing preconditioned gradient methods and our accelerated method. Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate the benefits of acceleration in the ill-conditioned regime.

In order to reduce the number of communications required to reach a given accuracy, we propose a preconditioned accelerated gradient method where the preconditioning is done by solving a local optimization problem over a subsampled dataset at the server. The convergence rate of the method depends on the square root of the relative condition number between the global and local loss functions. paragraphs: In distributed empirical risk minimization, several machines calculate gradients while a central server updates the model. Repeated communication between them can be costly. This paper proposes an accelerated gradient method designed to reduce the number of communication rounds needed to reach a chosen accuracy by making additional use of data at the server.

The server solves a local optimization problem on a subsampled dataset to precondition the updates. The method’s convergence rate depends on the square root of the relative condition number between the global and local losses. This quantity captures how the local optimization problem relates to the global one, making their relationship central to the convergence analysis.

For linear prediction models, the authors bound this relative condition number by studying uniform concentration of Hessians over a bounded domain. The analysis yields improved rates for both existing preconditioned gradient methods and the proposed accelerated method. Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate acceleration’s benefits in ill-conditioned problems, linking the theoretical improvement to settings where optimization is difficult.
summary.tldr: Server-side optimization on subsampled data preconditions an accelerated distributed method, improving convergence guarantees and showing benefits on ill-conditioned problems.

title: Statistically Preconditioned Accelerated Gradient Method for Distributed Optimization

abstract: Most real-world tasks are compound tasks that consist of multiple simpler sub-tasks. The main challenge of learning compound tasks is that we have no explicit supervision to learn the hierarchical structure of compound tasks. To address this challenge, previous imitation learning methods exploit task-specific knowledge, e.g., labeling demonstrations manually or specifying termination conditions for each sub-task. However, the need for task-specific knowledge makes it difficult to scale imitation learning to real-world tasks. In this paper, we propose an imitation learning method that can learn compound tasks without task-specific knowledge. The key idea behind our method is to leverage a self-supervised learning framework to learn the hierarchical structure of compound tasks. Our work also proposes a task-agnostic regularization technique to prevent unstable switching between sub-tasks, which has been a common degenerate case in previous works. We evaluate our method against several baselines on compound tasks. The results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on compound tasks, outperforming prior imitation learning methods.

The key idea is to learn the structure of compound behavior without requiring task-specific annotations or termination rules. The authors also introduce a task-agnostic regularizer aimed at preventing unstable switching between subtasks, a degenerate behavior observed in prior methods.

These components address both discovering the task hierarchy and keeping the resulting subtask behavior stable. The results support learning useful hierarchical behavior from demonstrations without the task-specific structural knowledge required by those earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised hierarchy learning and a task-agnostic switching regularizer improve imitation of compound tasks without task-specific structural guidance.

title: Learning Compound Tasks without Task-specific Knowledge via Imitation and Self-supervised Learning

abstract: In order to compute fast approximations to the singular value decompositions (SVD) of very large matrices, randomized sketching algorithms have become a leading approach. However, a key practical difficulty of sketching an SVD is that the user does not know how far the sketched singular vectors/values are from the exact ones. Indeed, the user may be forced to rely on analytical worst-case error bounds, which may not account for the unique structure of a given problem. As a result, the lack of tools for error estimation often leads to much more computation than is really necessary. To overcome these challenges, this paper develops a fully data-driven bootstrap method that numerically estimates the actual error of sketched singular vectors/values. Furthermore, the method is computationally inexpensive, because it operates only on sketched objects, and hence it requires no extra passes over the full matrix being factored.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching makes singular value decomposition practical for very large matrices by working with smaller representations. The resulting singular values and vectors are approximations, however, and users need to know how far they may be from the exact quantities. Computing an approximation is therefore only part of the practical problem.

The paper develops a data-driven bootstrap method to estimate these errors numerically. Its target is the error associated with the particular matrix and sketch being used. This addresses a weakness of relying on analytical worst-case bounds, which may fail to reflect the structure of an individual problem and can encourage unnecessary computation.

The method operates entirely on sketched objects, so error estimation requires no additional passes over the full matrix. That design keeps the extra computation inexpensive and preserves a central benefit of sketching. The contribution is a practical way to assess approximation quality alongside the approximate decomposition, helping users judge the accuracy of the result they have actually computed.
summary.tldr: A bootstrap method estimates sketched SVD errors cheaply using only the sketch, without rereading the full matrix.

title: Error Estimation for Sketched SVD via the Bootstrap

abstract: Reliably predicting the products of chemical reactions presents a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry. Existing machine learning approaches typically produce a reaction product by sequentially forming its subparts or intermediate molecules. Such autoregressive methods, however, not only require a pre-defined order for the incremental construction but preclude the use of parallel decoding for efficient computation. To address these issues, we devise a non-autoregressive learning paradigm that predicts reaction in one shot. Leveraging the fact that chemical reactions can be described as a redistribution of electrons in molecules, we formulate a reaction as an arbitrary electron flow and predict it with a novel multi-pointer decoding network. Experiments on the USPTO-MIT dataset show that our approach has established a new state-of-the-art top-1 accuracy and achieves at least 27 times inference speedup over the state-of-the-art methods. Also, our predictions are easier for chemists to interpret owing to predicting the electron flows.

paragraphs: Predicting a chemical reaction's products is difficult, and many machine-learning approaches construct the answer sequentially from molecular pieces or intermediate structures. That process requires a predefined construction order and prevents parallel decoding. This paper develops a one-shot prediction approach intended to remove those sequential dependencies.

The model represents a reaction through the redistribution of electrons within molecules. It formulates the transformation as electron flow and predicts that flow using a multi-pointer decoding network. This choice gives the prediction a chemically meaningful representation while enabling non-autoregressive decoding. The model can describe the transformation without first selecting an order in which to assemble the product's parts.

On the USPTO-MIT dataset, the authors report a new leading top-1 accuracy and at least a 27-fold inference speedup over the leading methods used for comparison. They also report that electron-flow predictions are easier for chemists to interpret. The findings connect the representation choice to three benefits in the evaluated setting: accurate product prediction, faster inference, and a more understandable account of the predicted transformation.
summary.tldr: One-shot electron-flow prediction improves reported reaction-prediction accuracy and achieves at least 27-fold faster inference on USPTO-MIT.

title: Non-Autoregressive Electron Redistribution Modeling for Reaction Prediction

abstract: We characterize the measurement complexity of compressed sensing of signals drawn from a known prior distribution, even when the support of the prior is the entire space (rather than, say, sparse vectors). We show for Gaussian measurements and \emph{any} prior distribution on the signal, that the posterior sampling estimator achieves near-optimal recovery guarantees. Moreover, this result is robust to model mismatch, as long as the distribution estimate (e.g., from an invertible generative model) is close to the true distribution in Wasserstein distance. We implement the posterior sampling estimator for deep generative priors using Langevin dynamics, and empirically find that it produces accurate estimates with more diversity than MAP.

Moreover, this result is robust to model mismatch, as long as the distribution estimate (e.g., from an invertible generative model) is close to the true distribution in Wasserstein distance. paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from a limited collection of measurements. This paper studies how many measurements are needed when the signal is drawn from a known prior distribution. The prior need not restrict signals to sparse vectors or another narrow subset; its support may cover the entire signal space.

For Gaussian measurements and any signal prior, the authors show that sampling from the posterior achieves near-optimal recovery guarantees. The posterior combines the prior with the observed measurements, so reconstruction is expressed as drawing a signal consistent with that information. The guarantee also tolerates a mismatched prior estimate when it is sufficiently close to the true distribution in Wasserstein distance.

The authors implement posterior sampling with deep generative priors using Langevin dynamics. Empirically, the resulting reconstructions are accurate and more diverse than those obtained by maximum a posteriori estimation. Together, the theory and implementation support posterior sampling as a recovery strategy with broad prior coverage, while making clear that the stated robustness to prior error depends on distributional closeness.
summary.tldr: With Gaussian measurements, posterior sampling provides near-optimal compressed-sensing recovery for any prior and tolerates sufficiently small Wasserstein model mismatch.

title: Instance-Optimal Compressed Sensing via Posterior Sampling

abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are a staple of mathematical modelling of temporal dynamics. However, a fundamental limitation has been that such models have typically been relatively inflexible, which recent work introducing Neural SDEs has sought to solve. Here, we show that the current classical approach to fitting SDEs may be approached as a special case of (Wasserstein) GANs, and in doing so the neural and classical regimes may be brought together. The input noise is Brownian motion, the output samples are time-evolving paths produced by a numerical solver, and by parameterising a discriminator as a Neural Controlled Differential Equation (CDE), we obtain Neural SDEs as (in modern machine learning parlance) continuous-time generative time series models. Unlike previous work on this problem, this is a direct extension of the classical approach without reference to either prespecified statistics or density functions. Arbitrary drift and diffusions are admissible, so as the Wasserstein loss has a unique global minima, in the infinite data limit \textit{any} SDE may be learnt.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe temporal processes that combine structured evolution with randomness. Classical versions have often offered limited flexibility, motivating neural versions. This paper connects the two by showing that a classical approach to fitting these equations can be viewed as a special case of a Wasserstein generative adversarial network.

In this formulation, Brownian motion provides the input randomness and a numerical solver generates entire time-evolving paths. A neural controlled differential equation serves as the discriminator. The adversarial learning problem therefore compares temporal paths, yielding a continuous-time generative model for time series without requiring prespecified summary statistics or density functions.

The framework admits arbitrary drift and diffusion terms, which describe the structured and random parts of the dynamics. The authors connect this flexibility and the unique global minimum of the Wasserstein loss to the possibility of learning any SDE in the infinite-data limit. That qualification is central: the statement concerns the limiting learning formulation, while the conceptual contribution unifies classical SDE fitting and neural adversarial modeling.
summary.tldr: A Wasserstein GAN formulation unifies classical and neural SDE fitting by learning distributions over continuous-time paths.

title: Neural SDEs as Infinite-Dimensional GANs

abstract: The bulk of existing research in defending against adversarial examples focuses on defending against a single (typically bounded $\ell_p$-norm) attack, but for a practical setting, machine learning (ML) models should be robust to a wide variety of attacks. In this paper, we present the first unified framework for considering multiple attacks against ML models. Our framework is able to model different levels of learner’s knowledge about the test-time adversary, allowing us to model robustness against unforeseen attacks and robustness against unions of attacks. Using our framework, we present the first leaderboard, MultiRobustBench (https://multirobustbench.github.io), for benchmarking multiattack evaluation which captures performance across attack types and attack strengths. We evaluate the performance of 16 defended models for robustness against a set of 9 different attack types, including $\ell_p$-based threat models, spatial transformations, and color changes, at 20 different attack strengths (180 attacks total). Additionally, we analyze the state of current defenses against multiple attacks. Our analysis shows that while existing defenses have made progress in terms of average robustness across the set of attacks used, robustness against the worst-case attack is still a big open problem as all existing models perform worse than random guessing.
