paragraphs: Defenses against adversarial examples are often developed for one attack type, while practical models may face many kinds of changes. MultiRobustBench introduces a unified framework for evaluating this broader challenge. It represents different levels of knowledge about the test-time adversary, covering both unforeseen attacks and situations where the adversary can choose among several attack families.

The accompanying leaderboard evaluates robustness across attack types and strengths. The authors test 16 defended models against nine attack types, including norm-bounded perturbations, spatial transformations, and color changes. With 20 strengths per type, the evaluation contains 180 attacks. This makes it possible to examine how defenses behave across a varied collection of threats within one framework.

The results reveal a substantial difference between average robustness and worst-case robustness. Existing defenses show progress on the average across the evaluated attacks, but every evaluated model performs worse than random guessing under the worst-case attack. The finding exposes a weakness that averaging can obscure and identifies worst-case multiattack robustness as an unresolved problem in the evaluated defenses.
summary.tldr: MultiRobustBench finds that improved average robustness can coexist with worse-than-random worst-case performance across multiple attacks.

title: MultiRobustBench: Benchmarking Robustness Against Multiple Attacks

abstract: Clustering aims to group unlabelled samples based on their similarities and is widespread in high-dimensional data analysis. However, most of the clustering methods merely generate pseudo labels and thus are unable to simultaneously present the similarities between different clusters and outliers. This paper proposes a new framework called High-dimensional Clustering onto Hamiltonian Cycle (HCHC) to solve the above problems. First, HCHC combines global structure with local structure in one objective function for deep clustering, improving the labels as relative probabilities, to mine the similarities between different clusters while keeping the local structure in each cluster. Then, the anchors of different clusters are sorted on the optimal Hamiltonian cycle generated by the cluster similarities and mapped on the circumference of a circle. Finally, a sample with a higher probability of a cluster will be mapped closer to the corresponding anchor. In this way, our framework allows us to appreciate three aspects visually and simultaneously - clusters (formed by samples with high probabilities), cluster similarities (represented as circular distances), and outliers (recognized as dots far away from all clusters). The theoretical analysis and experiments illustrate the superiority of HCHC.

paragraphs: Clustering usually assigns unlabeled examples to groups, but those assignments alone do not show how groups relate or where outliers lie. HCHC combines clustering with a visualization designed to display all three. It represents assignments through relative probabilities, allowing a sample's relationship to several clusters to influence its placement.

The method first learns clusters using an objective that combines global relationships with local structure within each cluster. It then orders cluster anchors along an optimal Hamiltonian cycle derived from cluster similarities and places those anchors around a circle. Samples are positioned so that a higher probability of belonging to a cluster brings them closer to that cluster's anchor.

The resulting view uses concentrated samples to show clusters, circular distances to convey relationships among clusters, and points far from all clusters to indicate outliers. The authors report theoretical analysis and experiments supporting the framework's superiority. Its distinctive contribution is to make probabilistic clustering assignments drive a common visual representation of group membership, relationships between groups, and unusual samples.
summary.tldr: HCHC maps probabilistic clusters onto a circular arrangement that jointly displays clusters, their similarities, and outliers.

title: High-dimensional Clustering onto Hamiltonian Cycle

abstract: In many real-world sequential decision-making problems, an action does not immediately reflect on the feedback and spreads its effects over a long time frame. For instance, in online advertising, investing in a platform produces an instantaneous increase of awareness, but the actual reward, i.e., a conversion, might occur far in the future. Furthermore, whether a conversion takes place depends on: how fast the awareness grows, its vanishing effects, and the synergy or interference with other advertising platforms. Previous work has investigated the Multi-Armed Bandit framework with the possibility of delayed and aggregated feedback, without a particular structure on how an action propagates in the future, disregarding possible dynamical effects. In this paper, we introduce a novel setting, the Dynamical Linear Bandits (DLB), an extension of the linear bandits characterized by a hidden state. When an action is performed, the learner observes a noisy reward whose mean is a linear function of the hidden state and of the action. Then, the hidden state evolves according to linear dynamics, affected by the performed action too. We start by introducing the setting, discussing the notion of optimal policy, and deriving an expected regret lower bound. Then, we provide an optimistic regret minimization algorithm, Dynamical Linear Upper Confidence Bound (DynLin-UCB), that suffers an expected regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}} \Big( \frac{d \sqrt{T}}{(1-\overline{\rho})^{3/2}} \Big)$, where $\overline{\rho}$ is a measure of the stability of the system, and $d$ is the dimension of the action vector. Finally, we conduct a numerical validation on a synthetic environment and on real-world data to show the effectiveness of DynLin-UCB in comparison with several baselines.

Advertising illustrates the issue: spending can build awareness that later produces conversions, while effects fade or interact with other platforms. Dynamical Linear Bandits model this persistence through a hidden state that carries the influence of previous actions.

This provides an explicit structure for how decisions affect the future. The authors define the setting, discuss optimal policies, and establish a lower bound on expected regret.

They introduce DynLin-UCB, an optimistic algorithm with an expected-regret upper bound proportional to d times the square root of T, multiplied by a system-stability factor, up to logarithmic terms. The bound worsens as the stated stability parameter approaches one. Numerical tests on synthetic and real-world data support its effectiveness against several baselines, connecting the theoretical model to decisions with persistent effects.
summary.tldr: Dynamical Linear Bandits model persistent action effects through a hidden linear state and provide an optimistic algorithm with stability-dependent regret guarantees.

title: Dynamical Linear Bandits

abstract: Automated decision support systems promise to help human experts solve multiclass classification tasks more efficiently and accurately. However, existing systems typically require experts to understand when to cede agency to the system or when to exercise their own agency. Otherwise, the experts may be better off solving the classification tasks on their own. In this work, we develop an automated decision support system that, by design, does not require experts to understand when to trust the system to improve performance. Rather than providing (single) label predictions and letting experts decide when to trust these predictions, our system provides sets of label predictions constructed using conformal prediction—prediction sets—and forcefully asks experts to predict labels from these sets. By using conformal prediction, our system can precisely trade-off the probability that the true label is not in the prediction set, which determines how frequently our system will mislead the experts, and the size of the prediction set, which determines the difficulty of the classification task the experts need to solve using our system. In addition, we develop an efficient and near-optimal search method to find the conformal predictor under which the experts benefit the most from using our system. Simulation experiments using synthetic and real expert predictions demonstrate that our system may help experts make more accurate predictions and is robust to the accuracy of the classifier the conformal predictor relies on.

In addition, we develop an efficient and near-optimal search method to find the conformal predictor under which the experts benefit the most from using our system. paragraphs: Decision support can fail when experts must decide for themselves whether to trust each automated recommendation. This paper changes the interaction: the system supplies a set of candidate labels, and the expert must choose from that set. The expert therefore solves a restricted classification problem instead of judging whether to accept a single machine prediction.

Conformal prediction controls the trade-off between set size and the probability of excluding the true label. Smaller sets simplify the expert's task but can remove the correct answer; larger sets preserve more choices while leaving a harder decision. The authors develop an efficient, near-optimal search procedure to find the conformal predictor under which experts benefit most.

Simulations using both synthetic predictions and real expert predictions indicate that the system may improve expert accuracy. They also show robustness to the accuracy of the underlying classifier. The evidence supports this constrained-choice design as a potentially useful form of assistance, while preserving the central trade-off: excluding the true label directly prevents an expert from selecting it.
summary.tldr: Conformal prediction sets can improve expert decisions by restricting choices while balancing task difficulty against exclusion of the correct label.

title: Improving Expert Predictions with Conformal Prediction

abstract: We investigate novel random graph embeddings that can be computed in expected polynomial time and that are able to distinguish all non-isomorphic graphs in expectation. Previous graph embeddings have limited expressiveness and either cannot distinguish all graphs or cannot be computed efficiently for every graph. To be able to approximate arbitrary functions on graphs, we are interested in efficient alternatives that become arbitrarily expressive with increasing resources. Our approach is based on Lovász’ characterisation of graph isomorphism through an infinite dimensional vector of homomorphism counts. Our empirical evaluation shows competitive results on several benchmark graph learning tasks.

To be able to approximate arbitrary functions on graphs, we are interested in efficient alternatives that become arbitrarily expressive with increasing resources. Our approach is based on Lovász’ characterisation of graph isomorphism through an infinite dimensional vector of homomorphism counts. Our empirical evaluation shows competitive results on several benchmark graph learning tasks.

paragraphs: Graph representations need enough detail to distinguish different graph structures, but richer representations can be expensive to compute. This paper studies random embeddings that balance these demands. Its target is a representation whose expressive power can grow as more resources become available, supporting the broader aim of approximating arbitrary functions on graphs.

The construction builds on a characterization of graph isomorphism using an infinite vector of homomorphism counts. These counts describe structure-preserving mappings between graphs. The proposed random embeddings can distinguish every pair of non-isomorphic graphs in expectation and can be computed in expected polynomial time. Both qualifications matter: the guarantees concern expectations, rather than requiring every individual random embedding to distinguish every graph.

Empirical evaluation finds competitive performance on several graph learning benchmarks. The theoretical contribution is a route toward increasingly expressive representations with an expected computational guarantee. The experiments complement that result by showing that the approach can also be useful on practical learning tasks, beyond its ability to separate graph structures in expectation.
summary.tldr: Random homomorphism-based embeddings distinguish all non-isomorphic graphs in expectation while remaining computable in expected polynomial time.

title: Expectation-Complete Graph Representations with Homomorphisms

abstract: We present an algorithm for minimizing an objective with hard-to-compute gradients by using a related, easier-to-access function as a proxy. Our algorithm is based on approximate proximal-point iterations on the proxy combined with relatively few stochastic gradients from the objective. When the difference between the objective and the proxy is $\delta$-smooth, our algorithm guarantees convergence at a rate matching stochastic gradient descent on a $\delta$-smooth objective, which can lead to substantially better sample efficiency. Our algorithm has many potential applications in machine learning, and provides a principled means of leveraging synthetic data, physics simulators, mixed public and private data, and more.

When the difference between the objective and the proxy is $\delta$-smooth, our algorithm guarantees convergence at a rate matching stochastic gradient descent on a $\delta$-smooth objective, which can lead to substantially better sample efficiency. paragraphs: Optimizing a useful objective can be expensive when its gradients are difficult to obtain. This paper studies how a related, more accessible function can help. The central idea is to use that cheaper proxy for much of the optimization while still consulting the true objective to guide progress toward the intended solution.

The algorithm combines approximate proximal-point iterations on the proxy with relatively few stochastic gradients from the objective. Its theoretical guarantee depends on the smoothness of the difference between the two functions. If that difference is δ-smooth, the convergence rate matches stochastic gradient descent on a δ-smooth objective.

This makes the relationship between the proxy and the objective central to the potential efficiency gain. Under the stated condition, the method can substantially improve sample efficiency. The authors identify synthetic data, physics simulators, and mixtures of public and private data as potential applications. Those examples illustrate ways an accessible proxy might arise; the abstract presents them as opportunities for the algorithm rather than reported application-specific experimental results.
summary.tldr: A cheaper proxy can reduce expensive gradient use, with convergence governed by the smoothness of its difference from the true objective.

title: Two Losses Are Better Than One: Faster Optimization Using a Cheaper Proxy

abstract: Deep equilibrium (DEQ) models replace the multiple-layer stacking of conventional deep networks with a fixed-point iteration of a single-layer transformation. Having been demonstrated to be competitive in a variety of real-world scenarios, the adversarial robustness of general DEQs becomes increasingly crucial for their reliable deployment. Existing works improve the robustness of general DEQ models with the widely-used adversarial training (AT) framework, but they fail to exploit the structural uniquenesses of DEQ models. To this end, we interpret DEQs through the lens of neural dynamics and find that AT under-regulates intermediate states. Besides, the intermediate states typically provide predictions with a high prediction entropy. Informed by the correlation between the entropy of dynamical systems and their stability properties, we propose reducing prediction entropy by progressively updating inputs along the neural dynamics. During AT, we also utilize random intermediate states to compute the loss function. Our methods regulate the neural dynamics of DEQ models in this manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods substantially increase the robustness of DEQ models and even outperform the strong deep network baselines.
originalAbstract: Deep equilibrium (DEQ) models replace the multiple-layer stacking of conventional deep networks with a fixed-point iteration of a single-layer transformation. Having been demonstrated to be competitive in a variety of real-world scenarios, the adversarial robustness of general DEQs becomes increasingly crucial for their reliable deployment. Existing works improve the robustness of general DEQ models with the widely-used adversarial training (AT) framework, but they fail to exploit the structural uniquenesses of DEQ models. To this end, we interpret DEQs through the lens of neural dynamics and find that AT under-regulates intermediate states. Besides, the intermediate states typically provide predictions with a high prediction entropy. Informed by the correlation between the entropy of dynamical systems and their stability properties, we propose reducing prediction entropy by progressively updating inputs along the neural dynamics. During AT, we also utilize random intermediate states to compute the loss function. Our methods regulate the neural dynamics of DEQ models in this manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods substantially increase the robustness of DEQ models and even outperform the strong deep network baselines.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models repeatedly apply a single transformation until reaching a fixed point, instead of using a conventional stack of distinct layers. This paper argues that adversarial training should account for that iterative structure. The authors find that existing adversarial training insufficiently regulates the intermediate states encountered during the model's computation.

Those intermediate states also tend to produce high-entropy predictions, meaning that their predictions are spread across possibilities. Motivated by a relationship between dynamical-system entropy and stability, the authors propose progressively updating inputs along the neural dynamics to reduce prediction entropy. They also compute the adversarial-training loss using randomly selected intermediate states.

Together, these interventions regulate the path toward equilibrium rather than focusing only on the final prediction. Extensive experiments report substantial gains in adversarial robustness, including performance above strong deep-network baselines. The results support using the distinctive computation of equilibrium models to design robustness methods; the entropy-and-stability connection provides motivation for those interventions rather than an unconditional robustness guarantee.
summary.tldr: Regulating intermediate states during equilibrium-model computation substantially improves adversarial robustness in the reported experiments.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness of Deep Equilibrium Models with Explicit Regulations Along the Neural Dynamics

abstract: We study reward-free reinforcement learning (RL) with linear function approximation, where the agent works in two phases: (1) in the exploration phase, the agent interacts with the environment but cannot access the reward; and (2) in the planning phase, the agent is given a reward function and is expected to find a near-optimal policy based on samples collected in the exploration phase. The sample complexities of existing reward-free algorithms have a polynomial dependence on the planning horizon, which makes them intractable for long planning horizon RL problems. In this paper, we propose a new reward-free algorithm for learning linear mixture Markov decision processes (MDPs), where the transition probability can be parameterized as a linear combination of known feature mappings. At the core of our algorithm is uncertainty-weighted value-targeted regression with exploration-driven pseudo-reward and a high-order moment estimator for the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. When the total reward is bounded by $1$, we show that our algorithm only needs to explore $\tilde O\left( d^2\varepsilon^{-2}\right)$ episodes to find an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping. The sample complexity of our algorithm only has a polylogarithmic dependence on the planning horizon and therefore is "horizon-free”. In addition, we provide an $\Omega\left(d^2\varepsilon^{-2}\right)$ sample complexity lower bound, which matches the sample complexity of our algorithm up to logarithmic factors, suggesting that our algorithm is optimal.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates exploration from planning. An agent first collects experience without observing rewards, then receives a reward function and must use that experience to find a good policy. This paper addresses the high exploration cost of long planning horizons for linear mixture Markov decision processes, whose transitions are linear combinations of known feature mappings.

The algorithm combines uncertainty-weighted regression, a pseudo-reward that drives exploration, and a high-order moment estimator. Its uncertainty estimates account for both randomness in the environment and uncertainty arising from incomplete knowledge. These components guide data collection before the eventual reward function is available, supporting later planning from the collected samples.

When total reward is bounded by one, the required number of exploration episodes scales as d squared divided by epsilon squared, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is feature dimension and epsilon specifies policy accuracy. Horizon dependence is only polylogarithmic, which is the sense of “horizon-free.” A matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors establishes near-optimal sample complexity in this setting.
summary.tldr: For linear mixture MDPs with total reward bounded by one, the algorithm achieves nearly optimal reward-free exploration with only polylogarithmic horizon dependence.

title: Optimal Horizon-Free Reward-Free Exploration for Linear Mixture MDPs

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has witnessed remarkable progress, resulting in the emergence of numerous method variations. However, practitioners often encounter challenges when attempting to deploy these methods due to their subpar performance. In this paper, we present a novel SSL approach named FineSSL that significantly addresses this limitation by adapting pre-trained foundation models. We identify the aggregated biases and cognitive deviation problems inherent in foundation models, and propose a simple yet effective solution by imposing balanced margin softmax and decoupled label smoothing. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FineSSL sets a new state of the art for SSL on multiple benchmark datasets, reduces the training cost by over six times, and can seamlessly integrate various fine-tuning and modern SSL algorithms. The source code is available at https://github.com/Gank0078/FineSSL.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses labeled and unlabeled examples together, but the growing number of available methods has not eliminated disappointing performance in practical deployment. FineSSL approaches this problem by adapting pretrained foundation models. The paper examines problems within those models that can interfere with their use in semi-supervised learning.

The authors identify what they call aggregated biases and cognitive deviation, then introduce balanced margin softmax and decoupled label smoothing as a simple remedy. Both changes concern the learning objective used during adaptation. The resulting approach makes correcting these model biases a central part of fine-tuning, rather than relying solely on the strength of pretraining.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, FineSSL achieves a new reported state of the art and reduces training cost by more than a factor of six in the authors’ experiments. It can also integrate with different fine-tuning methods and modern semi-supervised algorithms. These findings support its usefulness as an adaptable training approach, with both predictive performance and training expense motivating the design.
summary.tldr: FineSSL adjusts foundation-model fine-tuning to address bias, improving semi-supervised benchmark performance while substantially reducing training cost.

title: Erasing the Bias: Fine-Tuning Foundation Models for Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Transformer-based architectures achieved breakthrough performance in natural language processing and computer vision, yet they remain inferior to simpler linear baselines in multivariate long-term forecasting. To better understand this phenomenon, we start by studying a toy linear forecasting problem for which we show that transformers are incapable of converging to their true solution despite their high expressive power. We further identify the attention of transformers as being responsible for this low generalization capacity. Building upon this insight, we propose a shallow lightweight transformer model that successfully escapes bad local minima when optimized with sharpness-aware optimization. We empirically demonstrate that this result extends to all commonly used real-world multivariate time series datasets. In particular, SAMformer surpasses current state-of-the-art methods and is on par with the biggest foundation model MOIRAI while having significantly fewer parameters. The code is available at https://github.com/romilbert/samformer.

paragraphs: Transformers have strong results in language and vision, yet simpler linear models can outperform them in long-term forecasting of multiple time series. This paper investigates that gap through a toy linear forecasting problem. In that setting, the authors show that transformers fail to converge to the true solution despite having enough expressive power.

The analysis identifies attention as responsible for the poor generalization in the studied problem. Building on that finding, the authors propose SAMformer, a shallow, lightweight transformer using channel-wise attention and sharpness-aware optimization. They report that this optimization approach allows the model to escape bad local minima, connecting forecasting performance to how the model is trained.

Experiments extend the findings to commonly used real-world multivariate time-series datasets. SAMformer surpasses the compared state-of-the-art methods and matches the largest MOIRAI foundation model while using substantially fewer parameters. The results support the paper's emphasis on attention and optimization: a compact transformer can perform strongly when its training avoids the failure behavior identified in the analysis.
summary.tldr: SAMformer combines a lightweight transformer with sharpness-aware optimization to improve multivariate long-term forecasting.

title: SAMformer: Unlocking the Potential of Transformers in Time Series Forecasting with Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Channel-Wise Attention

abstract: As a dominant force in text-to-image generation tasks, Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) face a critical challenge in controllability, struggling to adhere strictly to complex, multi-faceted instructions. In this work, we aim to address this alignment challenge for conditional generation tasks. First, we provide an alternative view of state-of-the-art DPMs as a way of inverting advanced Vision-Language Models (VLMs). With this formulation, we naturally propose a training-free approach that bypasses the conventional sampling process associated with DPMs. By directly optimizing images with the supervision of discriminative VLMs, the proposed method can potentially achieve a better text-image alignment. As proof of concept, we demonstrate the pipeline with the pre-trained BLIP-2 model and identify several key designs for improved image generation. To further enhance the image fidelity, a Score Distillation Sampling module of Stable Diffusion is incorporated. By carefully balancing the two components during optimization, our method can produce high-quality images with near state-of-the-art performance on T2I-Compbench. The code is available at https://github.com/Pepper-lll/VLMinv.

paragraphs: Text-to-image systems can struggle to satisfy instructions containing several interacting requirements. This paper explores using a vision-language model's ability to judge image-text correspondence as a guide for creating images. It first offers a view of diffusion generation as a form of inversion of an advanced vision-language model.

That perspective motivates a training-free approach that directly optimizes an image under supervision from a discriminative vision-language model. The authors demonstrate the pipeline using pretrained BLIP-2 and identify design choices that improve generation. Direct supervision from the model that evaluates image-text relationships could potentially improve how closely an image follows a prompt.

To improve visual fidelity, the method also incorporates Score Distillation Sampling from Stable Diffusion. Image generation therefore balances the vision-language model's supervision with the diffusion-based component during optimization. The reported outcome is high-quality imagery with near state-of-the-art performance on T2I-Compbench. The proof of concept supports model inversion as an alternative route to conditional generation, with alignment guidance and image fidelity addressed through complementary components.
summary.tldr: A training-free method optimizes images using vision-language supervision and diffusion-based guidance for conditional generation.

title: Referee Can Play: An Alternative Approach to Conditional Generation via Model Inversion

abstract: Layer normalization (LN) is a ubiquitous technique in deep learning but our theoretical understanding to it remains elusive. This paper investigates a new theoretical direction for LN, regarding to its nonlinearity and representation capacity. We investigate the representation capacity of a network with layerwise composition of linear and LN transformations, referred to as LN-Net. We theoretically show that, given $m$ samples with any label assignment, an LN-Net with only 3 neurons in each layer and $O(m)$ LN layers can correctly classify them. We further show the lower bound of the VC dimension of an LN-Net. The nonlinearity of LN can be amplified by group partition, which is also theoretically demonstrated with mild assumption and empirically supported by our experiments. Based on our analyses, we consider to design neural architecture by exploiting and amplifying the nonlinearity of LN, and the effectiveness is supported by our experiments.

paragraphs: Layer normalization is widely used, but its contribution to what a network can represent remains incompletely understood. This paper studies it as a source of nonlinearity. The authors analyze an LN-Net, a network constructed by repeatedly composing linear transformations with layer normalization, to isolate the expressive capacity of that combination.

They prove that an LN-Net with just three neurons per layer and O(m) normalization layers can correctly classify m samples with any assignment of labels. They also establish a lower bound on its VC dimension. These results show substantial capacity in a narrow network when sufficient depth is available; the classification theorem concerns representing the supplied sample labels.

The paper further shows, under a mild assumption, that dividing features into groups can amplify layer normalization's nonlinearity. Experiments support this effect and the effectiveness of architectures designed to exploit it. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical account of normalization's expressive power to a concrete architectural direction: using and strengthening that nonlinearity when designing neural networks.
summary.tldr: Layer normalization supplies substantial representational nonlinearity, and grouping can amplify it under the paper's stated assumption.

title: On the Nonlinearity of Layer Normalization

abstract: An open problem in differentially private deep learning is hyperparameter optimization (HPO). DP-SGD introduces new hyperparameters and complicates existing ones, forcing researchers to painstakingly tune hyperparameters with hundreds of trials, which in turn makes it impossible to account for the privacy cost of HPO without destroying the utility. We propose an adaptive HPO method that uses cheap trials (in terms of privacy cost and runtime) to estimate optimal hyperparameters and scales them up. We obtain state-of-the-art performance on 22 benchmark tasks, across computer vision and natural language processing, across pretraining and finetuning, across architectures and a wide range of $\varepsilon \in [0.01,8.0]$, all while accounting for the privacy cost of HPO.

paragraphs: Training with differential privacy creates a tuning problem: the training method introduces new hyperparameters and makes existing choices harder to set. Trying hundreds of configurations can consume substantial privacy resources as well as computation. Consequently, the privacy cost of finding a good configuration can undermine the usefulness of the final model.

The paper proposes an adaptive search method that starts with trials designed to be inexpensive in both privacy cost and runtime. It uses these trials to estimate promising hyperparameters and then scales them up. The central idea is to make small, affordable searches informative enough to guide the more expensive training configuration.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on 22 benchmark tasks while including hyperparameter search in the privacy accounting. Their evaluation spans vision and language, pretraining and fine-tuning, multiple architectures, and privacy parameters from 0.01 to 8.0. These findings support the practical value of treating tuning as part of the private learning procedure rather than an unaccounted preliminary expense.
summary.tldr: An adaptive method uses inexpensive private tuning trials to select and scale hyperparameters, achieving strong benchmark results while accounting for search privacy costs.

title: A New Linear Scaling Rule for Private Adaptive Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: In order to stabilize nonlinear systems modeled by stochastic differential equations, we design a Fast Exponentially Stable and Safe Neural Controller (FESSNC) for fast learning controllers. Our framework is parameterized by neural networks, and realizing both rigorous exponential stability and safety guarantees. Concretely, we design heuristic methods to learn the exponentially stable and the safe controllers, respectively, in light of the classical theory of stochastic exponential stability and our established theorem on guaranteeing the almost-sure safety for stochastic dynamics. More significantly, to rigorously ensure the stability and the safety guarantees for the learned controllers, we develop a projection operator, projecting to the space of exponentially-stable and safe controllers. To reduce the highly computational cost for solving the projection operation, approximate projection operators are delicately proposed with closed forms that map the learned controllers to the target controller space. Furthermore, we employ Hutchinson’s trace estimator for a scalable unbiased estimate of the Hessian matrix that is used in the projection operator, which thus allows for reducing computational cost and, therefore, can accelerate the training and testing processes. More importantly, our approximate projection operations are applicable to the nonparametric control methods, improving their stability and safety performance. We empirically demonstrate the superiority of the FESSNC over the existing methods.

paragraphs: FESSNC learns controllers for nonlinear systems described by stochastic differential equations. The objective combines exponential stability with safety despite randomness in the dynamics. The authors use neural networks to parameterize controllers and develop learning methods informed by stochastic stability theory and a theorem establishing almost-sure safety.

The framework adds a projection operator to give learned controllers rigorous stability and safety guarantees. Projection maps a candidate controller into the space satisfying both requirements. Because solving this operation can be computationally expensive, the authors also construct approximate projection operators with closed-form expressions that map controllers into the target space.

For further efficiency, the method uses Hutchinson's trace estimator to obtain scalable, unbiased estimates for Hessian-related computations in the projection. These changes reduce computational costs during training and testing. The approximate projections can also be applied to nonparametric control methods to improve stability and safety performance. Empirical comparisons favor FESSNC over existing methods, supporting the combination of learned control, mathematical guarantees, and computationally cheaper enforcement.
summary.tldr: FESSNC combines neural controller learning with efficient projection methods to enforce exponential stability and safety for stochastic nonlinear systems.

title: FESSNC: Fast Exponentially Stable and Safe Neural Controller

abstract: We design differentially private algorithms for the problem of prediction with expert advice under dynamic regret, also known as tracking the best expert. Our work addresses three natural types of adversaries, stochastic with shifting distributions, oblivious, and adaptive, and designs algorithms with sub-linear regret for all three cases. In particular, under a shifting stochastic adversary where the distribution may shift $S$ times, we provide an $\epsilon$-differentially private algorithm whose expected dynamic regret is at most $O\left( \sqrt{S T \log (NT)} + \frac{S \log (NT)}{\epsilon}\right)$, where $T$ and $N$ are the time horizon and number of experts, respectively. For oblivious adversaries, we give a reduction from dynamic regret minimization to static regret minimization, resulting in an upper bound of $O\left(\sqrt{S T \log(NT)} + \frac{S T^{1/3}\log(T/\delta) \log(NT)}{\epsilon ^{2/3}}\right)$ on the expected dynamic regret, where $S$ now denotes the allowable number of switches of the best expert. Finally, similar to static regret, we establish a fundamental separation between oblivious and adaptive adversaries for the dynamic setting: while our algorithms show that sub-linear regret is achievable for oblivious adversaries in the high-privacy regime $\epsilon \le \sqrt{S/T}$, we show that any $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm must suffer linear dynamic regret under adaptive adversaries for $\epsilon \le \sqrt{S/T}$. Finally, to complement this lower bound, we give an $\epsilon $-differentially private algorithm that attains sub-linear dynamic regret under adaptive adversaries whenever $\epsilon \gg \sqrt{S/T}$.

paragraphs: Prediction with expert advice becomes harder when the best expert changes over time. This paper studies that tracking problem under differential privacy, measuring performance through dynamic regret against a changing expert sequence. It considers shifting stochastic distributions, oblivious adversaries, and adaptive adversaries, with privacy constraints affecting each setting differently.

For stochastic distributions that shift S times, the authors provide a private algorithm whose expected regret combines a square-root learning term with a privacy cost proportional to S divided by epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. For oblivious adversaries, they reduce dynamic regret minimization to static regret minimization, where the comparison expert remains fixed, obtaining a further bound that accounts for permitted switches.

The strongest distinction concerns adaptive adversaries. In the high-privacy regime where epsilon is at most the square root of S divided by T, oblivious adversaries permit sublinear regret, but adaptive adversaries force linear regret. The paper complements this impossibility result with an adaptive-adversary algorithm achieving sublinear regret when epsilon is sufficiently larger than that threshold.
summary.tldr: Private expert-tracking algorithms achieve sublinear regret in several settings, with a sharp privacy-dependent obstruction for adaptive adversaries.

title: Tracking The Best Expert Privately

abstract: Proteins typically exist in complexes, interacting with other proteins or biomolecules to perform their specific biological roles. Research on single-chain protein modeling has been extensively and deeply explored, with advancements seen in models like the series of ESM and AlphaFold2. Despite these developments, the study and modeling of multi-chain proteins remain largely uncharted, though they are vital for understanding biological functions. Recognizing the importance of these interactions, we introduce APM (all-Atom Protein generative Model), a model specifically designed for modeling multi-chain proteins. By integrating atom-level information and leveraging data on multi-chain proteins, APM is capable of precisely modeling inter-chain interactions and designing protein complexes with binding capabilities from scratch. It also performs folding and inverse-folding tasks for multi-chain proteins. Moreover, APM demonstrates versatility in downstream applications: it achieves enhanced performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) while also supporting zero-shot sampling in certain tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results. We released our code at https://github.com/bytedance/apm.

paragraphs: Proteins often perform their biological roles through interactions with other proteins or biomolecules. Modeling a single protein chain therefore addresses only part of the problem. This paper introduces APM, an all-atom generative model developed specifically for proteins containing multiple chains and for the interactions that hold protein complexes together.

APM combines atom-level information with training data on multi-chain proteins. The authors report that this enables precise modeling of interactions between chains and the generation of protein complexes with binding capabilities from scratch. The model also supports multi-chain folding and inverse folding, connecting the tasks of determining structures and designing sequences within the same modeling approach.

The paper further evaluates APM in downstream applications. Supervised fine-tuning improves its performance, while certain tasks also support zero-shot sampling, with state-of-the-art results reported. These findings position APM as a versatile approach to multi-chain protein modeling. The central advance is its explicit treatment of atomic detail and interactions across chains, bringing complex design into the model’s scope.
summary.tldr: APM uses atom-level information to model multi-chain proteins and generate protein complexes with binding capabilities.

title: An All-Atom Generative Model for Designing Protein Complexes

abstract: To design reward that align with human goals, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a prominent technique for learning reward functions from human preferences and optimizing models using reinforcement learning algorithms. However, existing RLHF methods often misinterpret trajectories as being generated by an optimal policy, causing inaccurate likelihood estimation and suboptimal learning. To address this, we propose Policy-labeled Preference Learning (PPL) within the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) framework, which resolves these likelihood mismatch problems by modeling human preferences with regret, reflecting the efficiency of executed policies. Additionally, we introduce a contrastive KL regularization term derived from regret-based principles to enhance sequential contrastive learning. Experiments in high-dimensional continuous control environments demonstrate PPL’s significant improvements in offline RLHF performance and its effectiveness in online settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses preferences to help align behavior with human goals. The paper identifies a likelihood-estimation problem in existing approaches: they can treat observed trajectories as if an optimal policy generated them. When that interpretation is inaccurate, it can undermine the learning process.

Policy-labeled Preference Learning, or PPL, addresses the mismatch within the Direct Preference Optimization framework. It models preferences using regret, incorporating the efficiency of the policies that produced the trajectories. The authors also derive a contrastive KL regularization term from regret-based principles to strengthen sequential contrastive learning. Both changes connect preference learning more directly to the behavior of the executed policies.

Experiments in high-dimensional continuous-control environments show significant improvements in offline reinforcement learning from human feedback, along with effectiveness in online settings. The findings support accounting for policy quality when interpreting trajectory preferences. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a revised preference model and an accompanying regularizer, evaluated in control tasks where behavior unfolds over sequences of actions.
summary.tldr: PPL models preferences through policy regret to correct likelihood mismatches and improve feedback-based learning in continuous control.

title: Policy-labeled Preference Learning: Is Preference Enough for RLHF?

abstract: Robust training methods typically defend against specific attack types, such as $\ell_p$ attacks with fixed budgets, and rarely account for the fact that defenders may encounter new attacks over time. A natural solution is to adapt the defended model to new adversaries as they arise via fine-tuning, a method which we call continual robust training (CRT). However, when implemented naively, fine-tuning on new attacks degrades robustness on previous attacks. This raises the question: how can we improve the initial training and fine-tuning of the model to simultaneously achieve robustness against previous and new attacks? We present theoretical results which show that the gap in a model’s robustness against different attacks is bounded by how far each attack perturbs a sample in the model’s logit space, suggesting that regularizing with respect to this logit space distance can help maintain robustness against previous attacks. Extensive experiments on 3 datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNette) and over 100 attack combinations demonstrate that the proposed regularization improves robust accuracy with little overhead in training time. Our findings and open-source code lay the groundwork for the deployment of models robust to evolving attacks.

Updating it on the new attack is a natural response, but ordinary fine-tuning can weaken defenses against attacks it previously handled. The paper studies how to make this ongoing adaptation preserve earlier robustness while acquiring new protection.

The theory supplies a bound that motivates the method, while the experiments demonstrate its benefits across the tested combinations of previous and new attacks.
summary.tldr: Regularizing attack-induced changes in model output scores helps models adapt to new adversaries while retaining robustness against earlier attacks.

title: Adapting to Evolving Adversaries with Regularized Continual Robust Training

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has achieved significant progress in large-scale traffic control, autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Drawing inspiration from biological systems where roles naturally emerge to enable coordination, role-based MARL methods have been proposed to enhance cooperation learning for complex tasks. However, existing methods exclusively derive roles from an agent’s past experience during training, neglecting their influence on its future trajectories. This paper introduces a key insight: an agent’s role should shape its future behavior to enable effective coordination. Hence, we propose Role Discovery and Diversity through Dynamics Models (R3DM), a novel role-based MARL framework that learns emergent roles by maximizing the mutual information between agents’ roles, observed trajectories, and expected future behaviors. R3DM optimizes the proposed objective through contrastive learning on past trajectories to first derive intermediate roles that shape intrinsic rewards to promote diversity in future behaviors across different roles through a learned dynamics model. Benchmarking on SMAC and SMACv2 environments demonstrates that R3DM outperforms state-of-the-art MARL approaches, improving multi-agent coordination to increase win rates by up to 20%. The code is available at https://github.com/UTAustin-SwarmLab/R3DM.

R3DM starts from the idea that a useful role should both reflect experience and shape what an agent goes on to do.

Tests on SMAC and SMACv2 show R3DM outperforming state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning approaches, with win-rate increases of up to 20%. The reported improvement supports incorporating expected future behavior into role learning. The contribution is a training framework in which roles actively guide agents toward distinct behaviors, giving the team a stronger basis for coordinated action.
summary.tldr: R3DM learns agent roles that connect past experience to diverse future behaviors, improving coordination on SMAC benchmarks.

title: R3DM: Enabling Role Discovery and Diversity Through Dynamics Models in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Shuffling-type gradient methods are favored in practice for their simplicity and rapid empirical performance. Despite extensive development of convergence guarantees under various assumptions in recent years, most require the Lipschitz smoothness condition, which is often not met in common machine learning models. We highlight this issue with specific counterexamples. To address this gap, we revisit the convergence rates of shuffling-type gradient methods without assuming Lipschitz smoothness. Using our stepsize strategy, the shuffling-type gradient algorithm not only converges under weaker assumptions but also match the current best-known convergence rates, thereby broadening its applicability. We prove the convergence rates for nonconvex, strongly convex, and non-strongly convex cases, each under both random reshuffling and arbitrary shuffling schemes, under a general bounded variance condition. Numerical experiments further validate the performance of our shuffling-type gradient algorithm, underscoring its practical efficacy.

paragraphs: Shuffling-based gradient methods are widely used because they are simple and work well empirically. Their theoretical guarantees, however, often rely on Lipschitz smoothness, a condition controlling how quickly gradients can change. The authors provide counterexamples showing that this condition need not hold in common machine-learning models, creating a gap between practice and existing analysis.

The paper develops a step-size strategy and convergence analysis that do not assume Lipschitz smoothness. Under weaker assumptions, including a general bounded-variance condition, the resulting method converges while matching current best-known convergence rates. The result broadens the settings covered by theory without claiming that convergence holds without any assumptions.

The analysis includes nonconvex, strongly convex, and convex but not strongly convex objectives. For each category, it covers both random reshuffling and arbitrary shuffling schemes. Numerical experiments also support the method's practical performance. The main contribution is a wider theoretical foundation for shuffling-based optimization, paired with a step-size strategy that preserves strong rates under the stated weaker conditions.
summary.tldr: A new step-size strategy gives shuffling-based gradient methods strong convergence rates without assuming Lipschitz smoothness.

title: Revisiting Convergence: Shuffling Complexity Beyond Lipschitz Smoothness

abstract: We study the relationship between gradient-based optimization of parametric models (e.g., neural networks) and optimization of linear combinations of random features. Our main result shows that if a parametric model can be learned using mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (bSGD) without making assumptions about the data distribution, then with high probability, the target function can also be approximated using a polynomial-sized combination of random features. The size of this combination depends on the number of gradient steps and numerical precision used in the bSGD process. This finding reveals fundamental limitations of distribution-free learning in neural networks trained by gradient descent, highlighting why making assumptions about data distributions is often crucial in practice. Along the way, we also introduce a new theoretical framework called average probabilistic dimension complexity (adc), which extends the probabilistic dimension complexity developed by Kamath et al. (2020). We prove that adc has a polynomial relationship with statistical query dimension, and use this relationship to demonstrate an infinite separation between adc and standard dimension complexity.

paragraphs: This paper compares learning a parametric model through gradient updates with learning a linear combination of random features. Its focus is distribution-free learning, where the learning guarantee makes no assumptions about the data distribution. The authors ask how much additional expressive learning power gradient-based training provides under that demanding requirement.

Their main theorem is conditional: if mini-batch stochastic gradient descent can learn the parametric model distribution-free, then random features can approximate the target with high probability using a polynomial-sized combination. The authors also introduce average probabilistic dimension complexity, prove a polynomial relationship with statistical query dimension, and establish an infinite separation from standard dimension complexity. Together, these results characterize limits of distribution-free gradient learning. They help explain why assumptions about data distributions can be consequential when seeking advantages from neural-network training beyond what random-feature combinations can already represent.
summary.tldr: Anything learnable distribution-free by the analyzed mini-batch gradient method can also be approximated with polynomially many random features, with high probability.

title: The Power of Random Features and the Limits of Distribution-Free Gradient Descent

abstract: We investigate the Sobolev IPM problem for probability measures supported on a graph metric space. Sobolev IPM is an important instance of integral probability metrics (IPM), and is obtained by constraining a critic function within a unit ball defined by the Sobolev norm. In particular, it has been used to compare probability measures and is crucial for several theoretical works in machine learning. However, to our knowledge, there are no efficient algorithmic approaches to compute Sobolev IPM effectively, which hinders its practical applications. In this work, we establish a relation between Sobolev norm and weighted $L^p$-norm, and leverage it to propose a novel regularization for Sobolev IPM. By exploiting the graph structure, we demonstrate that the regularized Sobolev IPM provides a closed-form expression for fast computation. This advancement addresses long-standing computational challenges, and paves the way to apply Sobolev IPM for practical applications, even in large-scale settings. Additionally, the regularized Sobolev IPM is negative definite. Utilizing this property, we design positive-definite kernels upon the regularized Sobolev IPM, and provide preliminary evidences of their advantages for comparing probability measures on a given graph for document classification and topological data analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compare probability distributions supported on a graph. Sobolev integral probability metrics perform such comparisons through critic functions constrained by a Sobolev norm. Although these metrics are useful theoretically, a lack of efficient computation has limited their practical application. The authors develop a regularized version aimed at addressing that obstacle.

The construction begins with a relationship between the Sobolev norm and a weighted Lp norm. Using that relationship and the structure of the graph, the authors derive a closed-form expression for the regularized metric. This gives a direct route to fast computation and creates opportunities to use the comparison in larger-scale applications.

The regularized metric also has a negative-definiteness property, which the authors use to construct positive-definite kernels. These kernels allow the distribution comparison to become a building block for kernel-based methods. Experiments in document classification and topological data analysis provide preliminary evidence of advantages. The computational result concerns the proposed regularized metric, while the application findings are presented as early supporting evidence.
summary.tldr: A regularized Sobolev metric on graphs admits fast closed-form computation and supports positive-definite kernels for comparing distributions.

title: Scalable Sobolev IPM for Probability Measures on a Graph

abstract: Applying Gaussian processes (GPs) to very large datasets remains a challenge due to limited computational scalability. Matrix structures, such as the Kronecker product, can accelerate operations significantly, but their application commonly entails approximations or unrealistic assumptions. In particular, the most common path to creating a Kronecker-structured kernel matrix is by evaluating a product kernel on gridded inputs that can be expressed as a Cartesian product. However, this structure is lost if any observation is missing, breaking the Cartesian product structure, which frequently occurs in real-world data such as time series. To address this limitation, we propose leveraging latent Kronecker structure, by expressing the kernel matrix of observed values as the projection of a latent Kronecker product. In combination with iterative linear system solvers and pathwise conditioning, our method facilitates inference of exact GPs while requiring substantially fewer computational resources than standard iterative methods. We demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art sparse and variational GPs on real-world datasets with up to five million examples, including robotics, automated machine learning, and climate applications.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes become expensive on large datasets because their inference involves large kernel matrices. Kronecker structure can accelerate these operations, but a common construction requires product kernels evaluated on a complete Cartesian grid. Missing observations break that directly visible structure, creating a difficulty for data such as incomplete time series.

The paper retains a structured latent matrix and expresses the kernel matrix for observed values as its projection. In this formulation, missing entries need not erase the underlying computational structure. The authors combine this representation with iterative linear system solvers and pathwise conditioning to perform inference for exact Gaussian processes using fewer resources than standard iterative methods.

Experiments cover real-world datasets with up to five million examples in robotics, automated machine learning, and climate applications. The method outperforms state-of-the-art sparse and variational Gaussian processes in those evaluations. Its contribution is a way to use latent matrix structure despite incomplete observations, expanding the practical reach of exact Gaussian process modeling in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Latent Kronecker structure enables resource-efficient exact Gaussian process inference when missing observations disrupt a complete grid.

title: Scalable Gaussian Processes with Latent Kronecker Structure

abstract: Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a downstream task often degrades its original capabilities, a phenomenon known as "catastrophic forgetting". This is especially an issue when one does not have access to the data and recipe used to develop the pre-trained model. Under this constraint, most existing methods for mitigating forgetting are inapplicable. To address this challenge, we propose a sample weighting scheme for the fine-tuning data solely based on the pre-trained model’s losses. Specifically, we upweight the easy samples on which the pre-trained model’s loss is low and vice versa to limit the drift from the pre-trained model. Our approach is orthogonal and yet complementary to existing methods; while such methods mostly operate on parameter or gradient space, we concentrate on the sample space. We theoretically analyze the impact of fine-tuning with our method in a linear setting, showing that it stalls learning in a certain subspace, which inhibits overfitting to the target task. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our method on both language and vision tasks. As an example, when fine-tuning Gemma 2 2B on MetaMathQA, our method results in only a $0.8$% drop in accuracy on GSM8K (another math dataset) compared to standard fine-tuning, while preserving $5.4$% more accuracy on the pre-training datasets.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can improve a model on a new task while weakening capabilities it already had. Addressing this forgetting is especially difficult without access to the original training data or recipe. This paper proposes a method that needs only the fine-tuning examples and the pretrained model’s losses on them.

The method gives more weight to examples the pretrained model already finds easy and less weight to difficult ones. This is intended to limit movement away from the pretrained model. Because it changes sample weights, it can complement methods acting on parameters or gradients. In a linear setting, the authors show that it stalls learning in a particular subspace, inhibiting overfitting to the target task.

summary.tldr: Giving greater fine-tuning weight to examples a pretrained model already handles well mitigates forgetting without requiring its original training data.

title: Upweighting Easy Samples in Fine-Tuning Mitigates Forgetting

abstract: Multi-objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) seeks to develop policies that simultaneously optimize multiple conflicting objectives, but it requires extensive online interactions. Offline MORL provides a promising solution by training on pre-collected datasets to generalize to any preference upon deployment. However, real-world offline datasets are often conservatively and narrowly distributed, failing to comprehensively cover preferences, leading to the emergence of out-of-distribution (OOD) preference areas. Existing offline MORL algorithms exhibit poor generalization to OOD preferences, resulting in policies that do not align with preferences. Leveraging the excellent expressive and generalization capabilities of diffusion models, we propose MODULI (Multi-objective Diffusion Planner with Sliding Guidance), which employs a preference-conditioned diffusion model as a planner to generate trajectories that align with various preferences and derive action for decision-making. To achieve accurate generation, MODULI introduces two return normalization methods under diverse preferences for refining guidance. To further enhance generalization to OOD preferences, MODULI proposes a novel sliding guidance mechanism, which involves training an additional slider adapter to capture the direction of preference changes. Incorporating the slider, it transitions from in-distribution (ID) preferences to generating OOD preferences, patching, and extending the incomplete Pareto front. Extensive experiments on the D4MORL benchmark demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art Offline MORL baselines, exhibiting excellent generalization to OOD preferences.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning must accommodate different preferences among conflicting goals. Learning offline avoids extensive new interactions, but collected data may cover only a narrow set of those preferences. MODULI addresses the resulting problem: a policy can behave poorly when asked to follow a preference outside the dataset's coverage.

The method uses a preference-conditioned diffusion model to plan trajectories and derive actions. Two return-normalization methods refine the guidance used during generation. MODULI also trains a slider adapter to capture directions of preference change. Its sliding guidance mechanism moves from preferences represented in the data toward out-of-distribution preferences, helping extend the available set of trade-offs.

The paper describes this as filling gaps in and extending an incomplete Pareto front, the collection of competing objective trade-offs. On the D4MORL benchmark, MODULI outperforms state-of-the-art offline multi-objective reinforcement learning baselines and shows strong generalization to unseen preference regions. The results support guided diffusion planning as a way to produce behavior better aligned with requested trade-offs beyond those well represented in the offline data.
summary.tldr: MODULI uses preference-conditioned diffusion planning and sliding guidance to improve offline reinforcement learning for preferences outside the training data's coverage.

title: MODULI: Unlocking Preference Generalization via Diffusion Models for Offline Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Scaling multi-dimensional transformers to long sequences is indispensable across various domains. However, the challenges of large memory requirements and slow speeds of such sequences necessitate sequence parallelism. All existing approaches fall under the category of embedded sequence parallelism, which are limited to shard along a single sequence dimension, thereby introducing significant communication overhead. However, the nature of multi-dimensional transformers involves independent calculations across multiple sequence dimensions. To this end, we propose Dynamic Sequence Parallelism (DSP) as a novel abstraction of sequence parallelism. DSP dynamically switches the parallel dimension among all sequences according to the computation stage with efficient resharding strategy. DSP offers significant reductions in communication costs, adaptability across modules, and ease of implementation with minimal constraints. Experimental evaluations demonstrate DSP’s superiority over state-of-the-art embedded sequence parallelism methods by remarkable throughput improvements ranging from 32.2% to 10x, with less than 25% communication volume.

paragraphs: Long sequences make multidimensional transformers expensive in both memory and computation. Sequence parallelism distributes sequence processing, but the existing approaches described in this paper divide work along a single sequence dimension. That fixed choice can require substantial communication even when different computation stages expose independent work along different dimensions.

Dynamic Sequence Parallelism, or DSP, changes the dimension used to distribute work as computation proceeds. An efficient resharding strategy rearranges the distribution between stages. The central idea is to make the parallel layout follow the structure of the current calculation, taking advantage of the multiple sequence dimensions already present in these transformers.

The authors describe DSP as adaptable across modules and implementable with few constraints. In their evaluations, it improves throughput by amounts ranging from 32.2% to tenfold compared with state-of-the-art embedded sequence parallelism methods, while using less than one quarter of their communication volume. These experimental results show how changing work distribution can improve execution efficiency without requiring a single parallel dimension to serve every stage.
summary.tldr: DSP switches the sequence dimension used for parallel computation across stages, reducing communication and substantially improving measured transformer throughput.

title: DSP: Dynamic Sequence Parallelism for Multi-Dimensional Transformers

abstract: A generalist foundation model agent needs to have a large and diverse skill repertoire, such as finding directions between two travel locations and buying specific items from the Internet. If each skill needs to be specified manually through a fixed set of human-annotated instructions, the agent’s skill repertoire will necessarily be limited due to the scalability of human-annotated instructions. In this work, we address this challenge by proposing Proposer-Agent-Evaluator (PAE), an effective learning system that enables foundation model agents to autonomously discover and practice skills in the wild. After a context-aware task proposer generates instructions based on website information, the agent policy attempts those tasks in the real world with resulting trajectories evaluated by an autonomous VLM-based success evaluator. The success evaluation serves as the reward signal for the agent to refine its policies through RL. We validate PAE on challenging vision-based web navigation, using both real-world and selfhosted websites from WebVoyager and WebArena. Our results show that PAE significantly improves the zero-shot generalization capability of VLM Internet agents (around 50% relative improvement) to both unseen tasks and websites.

paragraphs: An Internet agent needs a broad range of skills, but manually writing instructions for every skill limits how much training can scale. Proposer-Agent-Evaluator, or PAE, organizes learning around automatically generated tasks and automatically assessed attempts. Its aim is to let agents discover and practice useful behavior on websites.

A context-aware proposer first examines website information and generates task instructions. The agent attempts those tasks, producing interaction trajectories. A vision-language model then evaluates whether each attempt succeeded. Those evaluations become reward signals for reinforcement learning, connecting task creation, practice, and policy improvement in one learning system.

The authors evaluate PAE on vision-based web navigation using real-world and self-hosted websites from WebVoyager and WebArena. They report approximately 50% relative improvement in zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and websites. This is a relative gain in the evaluated capability, not a percentage-point increase. The findings support autonomously generated practice as a way to expand web-agent skills beyond a fixed collection of human-written instructions.
summary.tldr: PAE lets web agents generate tasks, practice them, and learn from automated success judgments, improving generalization in the reported evaluations.

title: Proposer-Agent-Evaluator (PAE): Autonomous Skill Discovery For Foundation Model Internet Agents

abstract: Motivated by liability and intellectual property concerns over open-weight models we consider the following problem: given the weights of two models, can we test whether they were trained independently—i.e., from independent random initializations? We consider two settings: constrained and unconstrained. In the constrained setting, we make assumptions about model architecture and training and propose statistical tests that yield exact p-values with respect to the null hypothesis that the models are trained from independent random initializations. We compute the p-values by simulating exchangeable copies of each model under our assumptions and comparing various similarity measures between the original two models versus these copies. We report p-values on pairs of 21 open-weight models (210 total pairs) and find we correctly identify all pairs of non-independent models. In the unconstrained setting we make none of the prior assumptions and allow for adversarial evasion attacks that do not change model output. We thus propose a new test which matches hidden activations between two models, which is robust to these transformations and to changes in model architecture and can also identify specific non-independent components of models. Though we no longer obtain exact p-values from this test, empirically we find it reliably distinguishes non-independent models like a p-value. Notably, we can use the test to identify specific parts of one model that are derived from another (e.g., how Llama 3.1-8B was pruned to initialize Llama 3.2-3B, or shared layers between Mistral-7B and StripedHyena-7B), and it is even robust to retraining individual layers of either model from scratch.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether two models were trained independently from separate random initializations. It develops two approaches that trade statistical guarantees against flexibility. The question concerns model lineage: detecting whether models, or particular components within them, share a training origin.

In the constrained setting, assumptions about architecture and training allow tests with exact p-values for independent initialization. The tests simulate exchangeable model copies and compare their similarities with those of the original pair. Across 210 pairs drawn from 21 open-weight models, the authors report identifying every non-independent pair.

The unconstrained test matches hidden activations and handles architecture changes and output-preserving transformations intended to evade detection. It no longer provides exact p-values, but empirically distinguishes non-independent models and identifies shared components. Examples include pruning relationships between Llama models and shared layers between Mistral and StripedHyena. The test also withstands retraining individual layers from scratch. Its broader applicability therefore comes with a different evidential status: empirical reliability rather than the constrained test’s exact statistical guarantee.
summary.tldr: Two model-lineage tests offer either exact p-values under assumptions or broader empirical detection through hidden-activation matching.

title: Independence Tests for Language Models

abstract: The rapid evolution of generative models has unlocked new potentials in protein binder design, a pivotal task in structural biology, by facilitating end-to-end generation via joint sequence-structure modeling or hallucination. However, existing approaches are predominantly implemented under a single-target, single-state assumption, limiting their ability to model multi-target or multi-state interactions required for advanced function-oriented protein design. Here, we introduce Chamaileon, which unifies multi-target and multi-state binder design by formulating the problem as cross-context binding landscape modeling. The framework is underpinned by a training paradigm termed In-Context Complex Co-Design (I3CD) for context-aware sequence-structure co-modeling. During inference, we employ Mixture-of-Paths Sampling (MoPS), a scalable strategy that optimizes a single sequence across contexts while alleviating the scarcity of high-quality multi-conformational paired data. Extensive evaluation on our newly constructed benchmark, CROSS, demonstrates that Chamaileon effectively generates sequences adaptable to diverse conformational landscapes and multi-target requirements.

paragraphs: Protein binder design becomes more demanding when one sequence must work across several targets or several structural states. Existing generative approaches largely assume a single target in a single state, which restricts their ability to address these broader requirements. Chamaileon treats the different binding situations as contexts within a shared design problem.

Its training approach, In-Context Complex Co-Design, models protein sequence and structure together while accounting for context. This gives the framework a way to represent binding requirements across different situations. At inference time, Mixture-of-Paths Sampling optimizes a single sequence across contexts, addressing the need for a common design while alleviating the scarcity of high-quality paired data covering multiple conformations.

The authors evaluate the framework on a newly constructed benchmark called CROSS. They report that Chamaileon generates sequences adaptable to varied conformational landscapes and multiple targets. The contribution is a unified approach to requirements that single-state design handles only narrowly: the generated sequence is assessed against several binding contexts within the same modeling framework.
summary.tldr: Chamaileon jointly models sequence and structure to design protein binders that accommodate multiple targets or structural states.

title: Chamaileon: Cross-Context Binder Design with Contextualized Modeling and Mixed Sampling

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at code generation, yet ensuring the functional correctness of their outputs remains a persistent challenge. Recent studies have applied Test-Driven Development (TDD) to refine code, leveraging execution feedback to guide the model toward correct solutions. However, such feedback is often noisy and uninformative, stemming from the scarcity of high-quality test cases and the abundance of noisy, auto-generated ones. In this work, we shift the focus from test-case generation to feedback quality. We introduce the Property-Generated Solver (PGS), a novel feedback-centric framework designed to generate highly effective feedback via two principles: it must provide semantic guidance beyond simple I/O mismatches through property validation, and be structurally minimal, to reduce cognitive load and isolate root causes. PGS operates by checking high-level program properties (e.g., a sorting function must produce a non-decreasing sequence) then providing the simplest failing counterexample to the LLM. This property-driven, minimal feedback steers LLMs toward correct and generalizable solutions. Across diverse benchmarks, PGS demonstrates superior performance, achieving a bug fix rate 1.4x-1.6x higher than the strongest debugging-based approaches and establishing a new state-of-the-art in automated code refinement.
