paragraphs: Execution feedback can help language models repair generated code, but its usefulness depends on what the feedback reveals. A large collection of noisy tests may provide little guidance about the underlying defect. The Property-Generated Solver, or PGS, focuses on producing feedback that explains the relevant program requirement and presents a simple failure exposing its violation.

PGS checks high-level properties of a program, such as whether a sorting function returns a non-decreasing sequence. When a property fails, it supplies the simplest failing counterexample to the language model. Property validation adds semantic guidance beyond a mismatch between expected and observed outputs, while structural minimality reduces distracting detail and helps isolate the cause.

Across the reported benchmarks, PGS achieves bug-fix rates 1.4 to 1.6 times those of the strongest debugging-based approaches and establishes a new state of the art in automated code refinement. The findings support improving the information content of feedback as a route to more effective repair and more generalizable solutions, rather than relying solely on generating additional test cases.
summary.tldr: PGS improves language-model code repair by pairing violated program properties with the simplest failing counterexamples.

title: PGS: Effective LLM Code Refinement via Property-Oriented and Structurally Minimal Feedback

abstract: Existing machine learning models for network simulation excel at predicting average performance but, due to their reliance on mean squared error, systematically fail to capture the critical tail-latency and jitter that define modern network stability. This ’tail-blindness’ renders them unreliable for latency-sensitive systems. We bridge this gap by introducing Accurate Neural Architecture Search (ANAS), a paradigm that automates the discovery of architectures for high-precision, distribution-aware network simulation. ANAS corrects the evaluation inaccuracies of weight-sharing NAS via a similarity-constrained search, employs a hybrid search space to model complex traffic, and uses a Wasserstein loss to optimize for the entire delay distribution, not just its mean. Empirically, the ANAS-discovered architecture is holistically superior: it reduces overall validation loss by 25.8% compared to DeepQueueNet, demonstrating strong average-case performance, while simultaneously excelling at tail-sensitive metrics by lowering the normalized Wasserstein distance ($W_n$) by up to 69.8%. This confirms its ability to faithfully model a comprehensive performance spectrum, encompassing both average and critical tail behaviors. The ANAS framework provides a practical methodology for automatically creating high-fidelity model of network devices, enabling more reliable validation of next-generation network protocols and algorithms.

paragraphs: A network simulator can predict average delay accurately while missing rare long delays and fluctuations in timing. The paper identifies this weakness in machine learning simulators trained around mean squared error. Those missed behaviors matter for latency-sensitive systems, where average performance alone gives an incomplete picture of network stability.

Accurate Neural Architecture Search, or ANAS, automates the search for models that capture delay distributions. It combines a hybrid architecture search space with a similarity constraint intended to correct evaluation inaccuracies in weight-sharing search. A Wasserstein loss then trains the chosen model against the full delay distribution, giving distributional behavior a direct role in optimization.

The discovered architecture reduces overall validation loss by 25.8% relative to DeepQueueNet and lowers normalized Wasserstein distance by up to 69.8%. These results support improved modeling of both typical delays and tail behavior in the evaluated setting. The framework offers a way to design network-device simulators whose accuracy accounts for the performance spectrum relevant to protocol and algorithm validation.
summary.tldr: ANAS searches for network simulation architectures that model full delay distributions, improving average and tail-sensitive prediction metrics.

title: Optimizing Network Simulation: Enhancing Performance Prediction Accuracy via Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often employ Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to improve factuality. However, this also increases the risk of sensitive private information leakage. Differential Privacy (DP) has therefore been integrated into LLM inference and is widely regarded as a standard safeguard; yet most studies focus narrowly on the privacy–utility trade-off, leaving the trustworthiness of DP outputs underexplored. To assess trustworthiness, we employ the confidence gap (CG), which quantifies an LLM’s internal knowledge conflict. We show that CG correlates with both hallucination and exposure of personally identifiable information (PII). Building on this insight, we propose PEARL, a CG-guided, entropy-aware private decoding framework. PEARL adaptively allocates the privacy budget across tokens and sentences based on CG, concentrating protection on PII-bearing spans while stabilizing low-confidence, hallucination-prone regions. In experiments, PEARL improves both trustworthiness and robustness against PII extraction attacks. Notably, while applying DP alone significantly increases hallucination, our framework demonstrates that it is possible to preserve privacy while reducing hallucination.

paragraphs: Retrieval can improve language-model factuality while also exposing sensitive information to the generation process. Differential privacy offers a safeguard, but this paper examines another concern: whether private outputs remain trustworthy. The authors report that applying differential privacy alone significantly increases hallucination in their experiments.

They study the confidence gap, a measure of conflict in the model’s internal knowledge, and find that it correlates with both hallucination and exposure of personally identifiable information. PEARL uses this signal in an entropy-aware private decoding framework. It adaptively distributes the privacy budget across tokens and sentences, concentrating protection on sensitive spans while stabilizing uncertain regions prone to hallucination.

Experiments show improved trustworthiness and greater robustness against attempts to extract personal information. The result demonstrates that privacy protection and reduced hallucination can coexist within the tested approach. The confidence gap provides a common signal for guiding both goals, rather than treating all parts of a generated answer as having the same privacy and reliability needs.
summary.tldr: PEARL uses confidence-gap-guided private decoding to improve resistance to personal-information extraction while reducing hallucination in experiments.

title: PEARL: Differentially Private and Entropy-Aware Regulated Language Generation

abstract: We study the relation between the total variation (TV) and Hellinger distances between two Gaussian location mixtures. Our first result establishes a general upper bound: for any two mixing distributions supported on a compact set, the Hellinger distance between the two mixtures is controlled by the TV distance raised to a power $1-o(1)$, where the $o(1)$ term is of order $1/\log\log(1/\mathrm{TV})$. We also construct two sequences of mixing distributions that demonstrate the sharpness of this bound. Taken together, our results resolve an open problem raised in Jia et al. (2023) and thus lead to an entropic characterization of learning Gaussian mixtures in total variation. Our inequality also yields optimal robust estimation of Gaussian mixtures in Hellinger distance, which has a direct implication for bounding the minimax regret of empirical Bayes under Huber contamination.

paragraphs: Total variation and Hellinger distance provide different ways to measure how far apart probability distributions are. This paper studies how tightly they are connected for Gaussian location mixtures. Establishing a precise relationship makes it possible to transfer statistical guarantees expressed in one distance into guarantees expressed in the other.

For mixing distributions supported on a compact set, the authors bound the Hellinger distance by total variation raised to a power of 1−o(1). The correction term has order 1/log log(1/TV), so the exponent approaches one as total variation becomes small. They also construct two sequences of mixing distributions demonstrating that the bound is sharp.

The upper bound and matching constructions resolve the stated open problem and yield an entropic characterization of learning Gaussian mixtures in total variation. The inequality additionally supports optimal robust estimation in Hellinger distance, with an implication for bounding empirical Bayes minimax regret under Huber contamination. The compact-support condition is part of the stated result; the paper’s contribution is a sharp mathematical relationship and the statistical consequences that follow from it.
summary.tldr: A sharp bound links Hellinger and total variation distances for compactly supported Gaussian location mixtures, yielding learning and robust-estimation consequences.

title: Sharp Inequalities between Total Variation and Hellinger Distances for Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: Transforming a large language model (LLM) into a vision-language model (VLM) can be achieved by mapping the visual tokens from a vision encoder into the embedding space of an LLM. Intriguingly, this mapping can be as simple as a shallow MLP transformation. To understand why LLMs can so readily process visual tokens, we need interpretability methods that reveal what is encoded in the visual token representations at every layer of LLM processing. In this work, we introduce LatentLens, a novel approach for mapping latent representations to descriptions in natural language. LatentLens encodes a large text corpus and stores contextualized token representations for each token in that corpus. Visual token representations are then compared to these contextualized representations and the top-$k$ nearest neighbor representations serve as descriptions of the visual token. We evaluate this method on 15 different VLMs, showing that commonly used methods, such as LogitLens, substantially underestimate the interpretability of visual tokens. With LatentLens instead, the majority of visual tokens are interpretable across all studied models and all layers. Qualitatively, we show that the descriptions produced by LatentLens are semantically meaningful and provide more fine-grained interpretations for humans compared to individual tokens. More broadly, our findings contribute new evidence on the alignment between vision and language representations and open up new directions for analyzing the latent representations of LLMs.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can connect an image encoder to a language model through a shallow mapping, yet understanding what the resulting visual tokens mean throughout processing remains difficult. LatentLens addresses this by translating internal visual representations into natural-language descriptions at different layers of the language model.

The method first encodes a large text corpus and stores the internal representation of each token in its textual context. It then compares visual token representations with this collection and uses the nearest contextualized text representations as descriptions. Because the reference tokens carry context, the resulting interpretations can express finer semantic distinctions than isolated vocabulary tokens.

Across 15 vision-language models, the authors find that most visual tokens are interpretable at every studied layer using LatentLens. Common methods such as LogitLens substantially underestimate that interpretability in the comparison. Qualitative examples show semantically meaningful, detailed descriptions. The findings provide evidence of alignment between vision and language representations and make that alignment easier to inspect throughout the model's processing.
summary.tldr: LatentLens describes visual tokens using nearby contextualized text representations, revealing interpretability across all studied layers of 15 vision-language models.

title: LatentLens: Revealing Highly Interpretable Visual Tokens in LLMs

abstract: Despite high accuracy, Vision Transformer (ViT) predictions can be driven by spurious cues, raising the need to understand their inner workings before safe deployment. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising lens for decomposing model representations into human-interpretable concepts, yet adapting SAE-based interpretation to ViTs remains challenging due to limited control over concept coverage and subjective, non-scalable feature interpretation. To fill the gaps, motivated by neuroscience-inspired principles, we propose ViSAE, a mechanistic interpretability toolbox for understanding ViT inner workings through concept circuits. ViSAE consists of three components: (1) A probing suite with 64K images and a 16K visually grounded concept vocabulary, improving concept coverage efficiency by 20$\times$ over ImageNet and interpretation accuracy by 28.7% over existing concept sets. (2) Top-down concept reading and Bottom-up circuit tracing algorithms that automatically recover ViT inner workings via concept circuits. (3) Applications for auditing and steering ViT behavior. Through concept editing, ViSAE improves the worst-group accuracy on WaterBirds by 48.2%, outperforming existing methods by 23.8%. Our data and code: https://github.com/deep-real/ViSAE.

paragraphs: A vision transformer can make accurate predictions while relying on misleading visual cues. ViSAE aims to expose and modify such behavior through interpretable concept circuits. It builds on sparse autoencoders, which decompose internal representations into features, while addressing limited concept coverage and the difficulty of interpreting features consistently at scale.

The toolbox includes a probing collection of 64,000 images and 16,000 visually grounded concepts. The authors report twentyfold better concept-coverage efficiency than ImageNet and 28.7% better interpretation accuracy than existing concept sets. The paper also applies these circuits to auditing and steering model behavior. Through concept editing, ViSAE improves worst-group accuracy on WaterBirds by a reported 48.2%, outperforming existing methods by 23.8%. This connects interpretation to intervention: the recovered concepts support changes to model behavior, with the reported application targeting performance on groups that the model handles least well.
summary.tldr: ViSAE identifies concept circuits in vision transformers and uses concept editing to improve reported worst-group performance.

title: Inside the Visual Mind: Neuroscience-Motivated Concept Circuits for Interpreting and Steering Vision Transformers

abstract: Egocentric reasoning fundamentally differs from third-person understanding in LVLMs. Third-person settings offer wide and stable contexts with consistent global regularities, allowing models to utilize broad statistical correlations. In contrast, egocentric scenes are highly dynamic and heterogeneous, where decisive cues are localized and atypical. Therefore, robust egocentric reasoning requires models to focus on ”what is seen now”, i.e., the immediate visual input. However, existing methods tend to exhibit "inertial thinking”, relying excessively on language priors and global context. To address this limitation, we propose a novel three-stage Ego3S framework to ground models’ reasoning in interaction evidence. Specifically, before training, we first utilize the counterfactual-based paradigm to select high-value samples that effectively activate multimodal reasoning, thus mitigating the over-reliance on language priors and global context. Moreover, we introduce an interaction-centric reward for reinforcement learning that strengthens the model’s sensitivity to localized interaction cues. Finally, during training, we employ a variance-aware learning schedule that monitors reward distributions to dynamically synchronize data selection with the evolving model competence. Experiments on five datasets show that our Ego3S consistently achieves superior performance using only 26.5% of the training data, while reducing computational costs by over 46%. Code is available at https://github.com/Mrshenshen/Ego3S.

paragraphs: First-person visual reasoning depends heavily on immediate, localized evidence. Unlike relatively stable third-person scenes, egocentric views can change rapidly and contain unusual cues that determine what is happening. The paper identifies a tendency for large vision-language models to rely too heavily on language expectations and broad context, weakening their sensitivity to those cues.

Ego3S addresses this through three coordinated training components. Before training, counterfactual-based selection identifies examples that activate multimodal reasoning. During reinforcement learning, an interaction-focused reward encourages attention to localized evidence. A variance-aware schedule then monitors reward distributions and adjusts data selection as the model’s competence changes, connecting the examples it receives to its evolving learning needs.

Across five datasets, the authors report consistently superior performance while using only 26.5% of the training data and reducing computational costs by more than 46%. These findings suggest that carefully selecting examples and rewarding interaction evidence can improve both reasoning and efficiency. The contribution ties data selection, learning feedback, and training progression to the same grounding objective.
summary.tldr: Ego3S improves first-person visual reasoning by coordinating sample selection, interaction-focused rewards, and adaptive training schedules.

title: Ego3S: Select, Strengthen, and Synchronize for Efficient Egocentric Reasoning

abstract: Multi-device inference can reduce Transformer latency by parallelizing computation. However, existing methods require high inter-device bandwidth, making them impractical for bandwidth-constrained environments. We present ASTRA, a communication-efficient framework that integrates sequence parallelism with mixed-precision attention, where non-local token embeddings are transmitted as low-bit vector-quantized codes while local attention remains full precision. To preserve accuracy under aggressive compression, ASTRA introduces Noise-Augmented Quantization and Distributed Class Tokens. Across vision and language models (e.g., ViT and GPT2), ASTRA achieves up to 2.64$\times$ speedup over single-device inference and up to 15.25$\times$ over prior multi-device baselines while operating at bandwidths as low as 10 Mbps. ASTRA remains robust on large models (e.g., Llama-3-8B) even under non-ideal network conditions such as packet loss and dynamic networks.

paragraphs: Splitting Transformer inference across devices can reduce computation time, but exchanging information between devices can erase those savings when network bandwidth is limited. ASTRA addresses this communication bottleneck. It combines sequence parallelism, which distributes tokens across devices, with attention that uses different numerical precision for local information and information received from elsewhere.

The main design choice is to send non-local token embeddings as compact, low-bit vector-quantized codes while retaining full precision for local attention. This reduces the information transmitted between devices. To preserve accuracy despite aggressive compression, the framework adds Noise-Augmented Quantization and Distributed Class Tokens. Together, these components target the accuracy and communication costs of distributed inference.

Across vision and language models, the authors report speedups reaching 2.64 times over single-device inference and 15.25 times over earlier multi-device methods, at bandwidths as low as 10 Mbps. They also report robustness on Llama-3-8B under packet loss and changing networks. These findings support distributing inference even when connections are constrained, with the quoted speedups representing the strongest reported results.
summary.tldr: ASTRA compresses communication between devices while preserving local attention precision to accelerate Transformer inference over constrained networks.

title: ASTRA: Communication-Efficient Acceleration for Multi-Device Transformer Inference

abstract: Reinforcement learning usually assumes a given or sometimes even fixed environment in which an agent seeks an optimal policy to maximize its long-term discounted reward. In contrast, we consider agents that are not limited to passive adaptations: they instead have model-changing actions that actively modify the RL model of world dynamics itself. Reconfiguring the underlying transition processes can potentially increase the agents’ rewards. Motivated by this setting, we introduce the multi-layer configurable time-varying Markov decision process (MCTVMDP). In an MCTVMDP, the lower-level MDP has a non-stationary transition function that is configurable through upper-level model-changing actions. The agent’s objective consists of two parts: Optimize the configuration policies in the upper-level MDP and optimize the primitive action policies in the lower-level MDP to jointly improve its expected long-term reward.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement-learning agents that can alter the rules governing their environment’s transitions. In the usual formulation, an agent chooses actions within a given environment to maximize long-term discounted reward. Here, some actions can reconfigure the underlying dynamics themselves, potentially making future interaction more rewarding.

The proposed formalism is a multi-layer configurable time-varying Markov decision process. At the lower level, a conventional action policy operates in an environment whose transition function can change over time. At the upper level, configuration actions determine changes to that transition function. The layers distinguish acting within a configuration from choosing how the environment is configured.

The learning objective therefore combines two policy problems: choosing useful configurations and choosing effective primitive actions under those configurations. Both contribute to expected long-term reward, so they must be considered jointly. The abstract presents this modeling framework and objective rather than an empirical performance result. Its contribution is to make deliberate modification of world dynamics an explicit part of the agent’s decision problem.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes reinforcement learning in which agents jointly learn ordinary actions and higher-level actions that reconfigure environment dynamics.

title: Learn to change the world: Multi-level reinforcement learning with model-changing actions

abstract: Stem retrieval, the task of matching missing stems to a given audio submix, is a key challenge currently limited by models that discard temporal information. We introduce PHALAR, a contrastive framework achieving a relative accuracy increase of up to $\approx 70$% over the state-of-the-art while requiring $<50$% of the parameters and a 7$\times$ training speedup. By utilizing a Learned Spectral Pooling layer and a complex-valued head, PHALAR enforces pitch-invariant and phase-equivariant biases. PHALAR establishes new retrieval state-of-the-art across MoisesDB, Slakh, and ChocoChorales, correlating significantly higher with human coherence judgment than semantic baselines. Finally, zero-shot beat tracking and linear chord probing confirm that PHALAR captures robust musical structures beyond the retrieval task.

paragraphs: Stem retrieval asks which missing musical component belongs with a given audio submix. The paper argues that discarding temporal information limits existing approaches to this task. PHALAR addresses that problem through a contrastive learning framework designed to preserve musically relevant relationships in its audio representations.

Its design combines a learned spectral pooling layer with a complex-valued output head. Together, these impose pitch-invariant and phase-equivariant biases: the representation is designed to handle pitch changes consistently while retaining structured responses to phase changes. This gives the model explicit guidance about which changes to treat as irrelevant and which temporal relationships to preserve.

PHALAR establishes new retrieval results across MoisesDB, Slakh, and ChocoChorales, with relative accuracy gains of up to approximately 70%, fewer than half the parameters, and sevenfold faster training. Zero-shot beat tracking and linear chord probing further support the finding that the representations capture musical structure useful beyond the retrieval objective.
summary.tldr: PHALAR uses structured musical audio representations to improve stem retrieval accuracy and efficiency while capturing information useful for beats and chords.

title: PHALAR: Phasors for Learned Musical Audio Representations

abstract: The rise of bot accounts on social media poses significant risks to public discourse. To address this threat, modern bot detectors increasingly rely on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). However, the effectiveness of these GNN-based detectors in real-world settings remains poorly understood. In practice, attackers continuously adapt their strategies and must operate under domain-specific and temporal constraints, which can fundamentally limit the applicability of existing attack methods. As a result, there is a critical need for robust GNN-based bot detection methods under realistic, constraint-aware attack scenarios. We introduce BOCLOAK to systematically evaluate the robustness of GNN-based bot detection via both edge editing and node injection adversarial attacks under realistic constraints. BOCLOAK constructs a probability measure over spatio-temporal neighbor features and learns an optimal transport (OT) geometry that separates human and bot behaviors. It then decodes transport plans into sparse, plausible edge edits that evade detection while obeying real-world constraints. We evaluate BOCLOAK across three social bot datasets, five state-of-the-art bot detectors, three adversarial defenses, and compare it against four leading graph adversarial attack baselines. BOCLOAK achieves up to 80.13% higher attack success rates while using 99.80% less GPU memory under real-world constraints. BOCLOAK shows that OT provides a lightweight, principled framework for bridging adversarial attacks and real-world bot detection.

These results support optimal transport as a computationally lightweight way to test weaknesses in graph-based bot detection under more realistic attack conditions.

title: BOCLOAK: Optimal Transport-Guided Adversarial Attacks on Graph Neural Network-Based Bot Detection

abstract: Diffusion-based language models (dLLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, but existing decoding strategies collapse to single-token generation under low confidence, severely limiting throughput. Unlike autoregressive models where speculative decoding operates on token sequences in a fixed left-to-right order, dLLMs require speculating over denoising trajectories—sequences of multi-token updates with explicit positions and unmasking orders. We develop a trajectory-level speculative framework that constructs draft denoising trajectories via confidence-stratified tree exploration and verifies them through blockwise parallel evaluation with bidirectional attention masking. Our method further introduces inter-block speculation, exploiting diffusion models’ bidirectional structure to perform cross-block lookahead. We formally characterize when this approach is exact and identify trajectory drift as the fundamental cost of increased parallelism. Building on Fast-dLLM’s dual-cache infrastructure, our framework reduces denoising iterations by 30-40% and increases tokens-per-step from 2.6 to 4.3, achieving 7-14$\times$ speedup over vanilla dLLMs and 1.3$\times$ over Fast-dLLM with less than 1% accuracy change across reasoning and code benchmarks.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can update multiple tokens in parallel, but low-confidence decoding can reduce them to generating one token at a time. This paper adapts speculative decoding to their iterative denoising process. The object being drafted is a trajectory of updates, including token positions and unmasking order, rather than a fixed left-to-right token sequence.

The framework explores a confidence-stratified tree to propose denoising trajectories, then checks them through parallel blockwise evaluation with bidirectional attention masking. It also looks ahead across blocks, exploiting the model's bidirectional structure. The results show substantial practical acceleration, while the theoretical analysis makes clear that exactness depends on the trajectory conditions.
summary.tldr: Speculating over denoising trajectories accelerates diffusion language models while explicitly accounting for the trajectory drift introduced by greater parallelism.

title: Trajectory-Level Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Two-sample comparison is a fundamental problem in machine learning, with broad applications such as generative modeling. Although the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is widely used, MMD-based tests often exhibit poor or even counterintuitive performance under covariance- and location-shift alternatives, partly due to cancellation effects induced by their sum-of-differences construction. To address this issue, we propose a kernel-based maximum-of-difference (MOD) test, which maximizes the squared discrepancy between within-sample and between-sample average distances, thereby improving sensitivity to subtle distributional differences. We further develop a fused MOD procedure to adaptively combine multiple kernels. Extensive experiments demonstrate clear performance gains over existing MMD-based methods.

paragraphs: Two-sample testing asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution, a question that appears in applications such as evaluating generative models. A common approach is maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. This paper examines why MMD-based tests can behave poorly when distributions differ in location or covariance, which describe their positioning and patterns of variation.

The authors identify cancellation within a sum-of-differences construction as part of the problem: combining discrepancies can weaken the signal that the distributions differ. They propose a maximum-of-difference test, called MOD. It maximizes the squared discrepancy between average distances within samples and average distances between samples, aiming to make subtle differences easier to detect.

The paper also develops a fused version that adaptively combines multiple kernels, allowing the procedure to use more than one kernel-based comparison. Extensive experiments report clear gains over existing MMD-based methods. The findings show that the way discrepancies are aggregated can materially affect a test’s sensitivity, alongside the choice of kernel used to compare observations.
summary.tldr: The MOD test changes how kernel discrepancies are aggregated to improve sensitivity to distribution differences that can trouble MMD.

title: Kernel-based Maximum-of-difference Test for Two-sample Comparison

abstract: Personalization techniques for image generation models have increasingly been misused for malicious purposes, including unauthorized style imitation and copyrighted content replication. In response, recent mimicry protection methods embed carefully designed perturbations into images to disrupt a model’s ability to learn genuine semantic representations. Despite their growing adoption, the robustness of these protection mechanisms remains poorly understood, raising concerns about their reliability in real-world deployment. In this work, we present the first systematic analysis showing that DDIM inversion inherently acts as a perturbation amplifier, causing protected images to suffer severe structural distortions during reconstruction. Building on this observation, we propose DDIM Inversion-based Reconstruction Purification (DIRP), a novel purification approach that removes protective perturbations by explicitly minimizing DDIM inversion reconstruction error under perceptual constraints. Extensive experiments on six existing mimicry protection methods demonstrate that DIRP consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art attack baselines, achieving superior perturbation removal while better preserving image quality. Our results expose fundamental vulnerabilities in current mimicry protection strategies and highlight the urgent need for more robust and principled defenses.

paragraphs: Some image-protection methods add carefully designed perturbations that interfere with a generative model’s ability to learn an image’s underlying content or style. These methods aim to obstruct unauthorized imitation and replication. This paper investigates their robustness by examining what happens when protected images undergo DDIM inversion and reconstruction.

The analysis finds that DDIM inversion amplifies protective perturbations, producing pronounced structural distortions in reconstructed images. The authors turn that response into a signal for purification. Their method, DIRP, minimizes the error between an image and its DDIM-based reconstruction while imposing perceptual constraints. The reconstruction objective targets the disruptive perturbations, and the perceptual constraints help preserve the image’s visible content.

Experiments cover six mimicry-protection methods and compare DIRP with five leading attack baselines. DIRP consistently achieves better perturbation removal while preserving image quality more effectively. These findings expose vulnerabilities in the evaluated protections: a transformation that magnifies their effects can also provide an objective for removing them, motivating stronger protection designs.
summary.tldr: DIRP uses DDIM reconstruction errors to remove image-protection perturbations, exposing weaknesses in six evaluated mimicry defenses.

title: DDIM Inversion as a Perturbation Amplifier: Breaking Mimicry Protection via Reconstruction Error Minimization

abstract: This paper develops a finite-sample statistical theory for in-context learning (ICL), analyzed within a meta-learning framework that accommodates mixtures of diverse task types. We leverage a Bayes risk identity that separates the total ICL risk into two orthogonal components: Bayes Gap and Posterior Variance. The Bayes Gap quantifies how well the trained model approximates the Bayes-optimal in-context predictor. For a uniform-attention Transformer, we derive a non-asymptotic upper bound on this gap, which explicitly clarifies the dependence on the number of pretraining prompts and their context length. The Posterior Variance is a model-independent risk representing the intrinsic task uncertainty. Our key finding is that this term is determined solely by the difficulty of the true underlying task, while the uncertainty arising from the task mixture vanishes exponentially fast with only a few in-context examples. Together, these results provide a unified view of ICL: the uniform-attention Transformer selects the optimal meta-algorithm during pretraining and rapidly converges to the optimal algorithm for the true task at test time.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model use examples inside a prompt to respond to a task. This paper studies that behavior through a finite-sample meta-learning framework that allows mixtures of different task types. Its central tool separates prediction risk into two components, distinguishing the model’s approximation error from uncertainty inherent in the inference problem.

The Bayes Gap measures how closely the trained model matches the best Bayesian in-context predictor. For a Transformer with uniform attention, the authors bound this gap and make explicit how it depends on the number of pretraining prompts and their context lengths. Posterior Variance captures model-independent uncertainty, separating what training can improve from the difficulty associated with the underlying task.

Within the analysis, uncertainty about which task in the mixture generated the examples disappears exponentially quickly as in-context examples accumulate. The remaining uncertainty is governed by the true task’s difficulty. These results support a Bayesian interpretation for the analyzed Transformer: pretraining selects a meta-level strategy, and prompt examples rapidly specialize that strategy to the current task.
summary.tldr: A finite-sample theory explains Bayesian in-context learning for a uniform-attention Transformer by separating approximation error from task uncertainty.

title: In-Context Learning Is Provably Bayesian Inference: A Generalization Theory for Meta-Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become pivotal for improving model capabilities yet suffers from rollout efficiency bottlenecks due to the long-tail response length distribution. While existing works mitigate the impact of long tails via prompt-level tail scheduling, we focus on the root source of inefficiency: the distribution itself. Specifically, we characterize the long-tail distribution at a finer granularity, identifying intra-prompt long tails, and revealing that they frequently consist of ineffective verbosity. To address this, we propose a novel paradigm of active distribution shaping to shape the rollout distribution towards conciseness and certainty, thereby fundamentally resolving tail-induced overheads. We achieve this through a distribution-aware trajectory sampling mechanism, which selects trajectories from a redundant exploration space for each prompt, and an adaptive redundancy allocation scheme to maximize both shaping effectiveness and system efficiency. Experiments demonstrate significant acceleration over state-of-the-art systems by up to 1.77$\times$ without compromising model performance.

paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning generates response trajectories during training, and unusually long responses can create substantial delays. This paper examines that long tail within individual prompts: even responses to the same question can differ greatly in length. The authors find that these especially long trajectories frequently contain ineffective verbosity, making their extra generation work a target for improvement.

DARTS changes which trajectories are selected rather than only scheduling prompts around slow responses. For each prompt, it samples from a redundant exploration space using a mechanism that accounts for the response distribution. The aim is to favor conciseness and certainty. An adaptive allocation scheme controls the redundancy so that the benefit of selection is balanced against the work needed to create alternatives.

Experiments report acceleration of up to 1.77 times over the state-of-the-art systems evaluated without reducing model performance. These findings support shaping the rollout distribution itself as an effective efficiency strategy. They also make variation among responses to the same prompt relevant to training-system design.
summary.tldr: DARTS accelerates language-model reinforcement learning by selecting trajectories that reduce costly, often unproductive long responses.

title: DARTS: Distribution-Aware Active Rollout Trajectory Shaping for Accelerating LLM Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is essential for extremely low-bit large language models (LLMs). Current QAT methods are mainly based on scalar quantization (SQ), which enables efficient optimization but suffers from severe performance degradation at 2-bit precision. On the other hand, vector quantization (VQ) provides substantially higher representational capacity, but its discrete codebook lookup prevents end-to-end training. We propose LC-QAT, a 2-bit weight-only VQ-QAT framework that represents quantized weights via a learned affine mapping over discrete vectors, which yields a high-quality PTQ initialization and enables fully differentiable end-to-end optimization without explicit codebook lookup in the training forward pass. This strong post-training initialization makes LC-QAT highly data-efficient. Experiments across diverse LLMs demonstrate that LC-QAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art QAT methods while using only 0.1%–10% of the training data. Our results establish LC-QAT as a practical and scalable solution for extreme low-bit model deployment.

paragraphs: Compressing language-model weights to two bits creates a difficult representation and optimization problem. Scalar quantization is easy to optimize but can severely reduce performance at this precision. Vector quantization offers greater representational capacity, yet selecting discrete entries from a codebook obstructs straightforward end-to-end training. LC-QAT aims to combine useful properties of both approaches.

The framework represents quantized weights through a learned affine mapping over discrete vectors. This supplies a strong post-training quantization initialization and allows fully differentiable optimization without an explicit codebook lookup during the training forward pass. Its two-bit setting applies to weights. The paper connects its data efficiency to the quality of the starting quantized model.

Across diverse language models, LC-QAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art quantization-aware training methods while using only 0.1%–10% of their training data. These findings suggest that improving the quantized representation and its initialization can substantially reduce the data needed for subsequent training. The contribution is a trainable vector-quantization framework aimed at practical deployment under extreme weight compression.
summary.tldr: LC-QAT enables differentiable two-bit weight quantization and outperforms compared QAT methods using a small fraction of their training data.

title: LC-QAT: Data-Efficient 2-Bit QAT for LLMs via Linear-Constrained Vector Quantization

abstract: Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) has emerged as a transformative approach for solving combinatorial optimization problems. While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise, they predominantly rely on fixed evolutionary operators and struggle to effectively accumulate and reuse historical search experience. This paper proposes RefineEvo, a novel evolutionary framework that transforms AHD from a static trial-and-error process into a planning-guided, experience-driven system. RefineEvo introduces a Planner to dynamically schedule evolutionary operators and trigger refinement based on the current search state, and a Reflector to distill valuable lessons into a Bidirectional Experience Pool containing both positive insights and negative pitfalls. This synergistic framework enables the system to adapt its search tools to the evolving complexity of the problem and leverage trajectory-aware, situation-conditioned insights to guide generation. Experiments on several classic combinatorial optimization benchmarks demonstrate that RefineEvo consistently outperforms strong baselines. In particular, RefineEvo delivers superior solution quality while improving token efficiency, enabling more efficient and autonomous heuristic design.

paragraphs: Automatic heuristic design uses search to develop procedures for combinatorial optimization problems. Language models can help generate these procedures, but fixed evolutionary operators and poor reuse of search history can limit the process. RefineEvo introduces planning and reflection so that both the search actions and the guidance used to generate candidates can adapt over time.

A Planner chooses evolutionary operators according to the current search state and decides when refinement should occur. A Reflector distills lessons from previous search trajectories into an experience pool containing both successful ideas and pitfalls. This gives the system access to positive and negative experience conditioned on the situation it currently faces.

The two components connect historical learning to present search decisions: experience informs generation, while planning adjusts which search tools are used. On several classic combinatorial optimization benchmarks, RefineEvo consistently outperforms strong baselines, with better solution quality and improved token efficiency. These results suggest that organizing and reusing search experience can improve heuristic development while reducing the language-model resources needed to obtain strong solutions.
summary.tldr: RefineEvo adapts heuristic search through planning and reusable lessons from both successful and unsuccessful search trajectories.

title: RefineEvo: Planning-Guided Heuristic Evolution with Bidirectional Experience

abstract: Accurate RNA structure modeling remains difficult because RNA backbones are highly flexible, non-canonical interactions are prevalent, and experimentally determined 3D structures are comparatively scarce. We introduce RiboSphere, a framework that learns discrete geometric representations of RNA by combining vector quantization with flow matching. Our design is motivated by the modular organization of RNA architecture: complex folds are composed from recurring structural motifs. RiboSphere uses a geometric transformer encoder trained using mean-centered coordinates and random rotation augmentation to produce geometry-aware features, which are discretized with finite scalar quantization (FSQ) into a finite vocabulary of latent codes. Conditioned on these discrete codes, a flow-matching decoder reconstructs atomic coordinates, enabling high-fidelity structure generation. We find that the learned code indices are enriched for specific RNA motifs, suggesting that the model captures motif-level compositional structure rather than acting as a purely compressive bottleneck. Across benchmarks, RiboSphere achieves strong performance in structure reconstruction (RMSD 1.25 {Å}, TM-score 0.84), and its pretrained discrete representations transfer effectively to inverse folding and RNA–ligand binding prediction, with robust generalization in data-scarce regimes.

paragraphs: RNA structure modeling is difficult because backbones are flexible, interactions are varied, and experimentally determined 3D structures are scarce. RiboSphere draws on the recurring motifs that make up complex RNA folds. It learns a finite vocabulary of geometric codes intended to represent structural information compactly and support reconstruction and downstream prediction.

A geometric transformer encodes coordinates after centering, with random rotations used during training. Finite scalar quantization converts the resulting features into discrete codes. A flow-matching decoder then reconstructs atomic coordinates conditioned on those codes. The learned code indices are enriched for particular RNA motifs, suggesting that they capture motif-level composition as well as compressing geometry.

Across benchmarks, RiboSphere achieves reconstruction RMSD of 1.25 Å and a TM-score of 0.84. Its pretrained representations also transfer effectively to inverse folding and RNA–ligand binding prediction, including robust generalization when data are scarce. Together, these findings indicate that the discrete representation retains structural information useful both for rebuilding RNA coordinates and for other RNA modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: RiboSphere learns discrete RNA geometry codes that support accurate reconstruction and transfer to inverse folding and ligand-binding prediction.

title: RiboSphere: Learning Unified and Efficient Representations of RNA Structures

abstract: Although diffusion models have revolutionized continuous domains like image synthesis through high quality generations and controllable guidance mechanisms, bringing this controllability to the discrete, sequential nature of text remains an open challenge. Meanwhile, current sampling strategies and guidance methods adjust token likelihoods without capturing the broader semantic landscape, leading to a suboptimal balance between fidelity and diversity. In this work, we introduce a novel training-free Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy (SAKE) guidance method. Our method computes the order-2 Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix that captures both cross-token semantic interactions and relative token positions. By linearizing this objective in the embedding space, we derive a tractable guidance signal that dynamically adjusts the sampling distribution—flattening it to encourage exploration during redundancy and sharpening it for fidelity when diverse. Empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity, and improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as code and mathematics generation, compared to temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines.

paragraphs: Text diffusion generation needs to balance producing faithful outputs with exploring meaningfully different possibilities. Adjusting individual token probabilities does not necessarily capture whether the resulting text is semantically repetitive. This paper introduces Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy, or SAKE, a training-free guidance method that incorporates relationships among tokens and their relative positions.

SAKE measures order-2 Rényi entropy using a kernel Gram matrix that reflects those semantic and positional relationships. The authors linearize this objective in embedding space to obtain a manageable guidance signal for sampling. When generation becomes redundant, the signal flattens the sampling distribution to encourage exploration; when diversity is already present, it sharpens the distribution to support fidelity.

The experiments show a better empirical fidelity–diversity Pareto frontier than temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines. They also report improved performance when generating multiple candidate answers for reasoning-heavy tasks, including code and mathematics. The result suggests that guidance informed by semantic relationships can make multiple samples more useful, rather than merely making their token choices more random.
summary.tldr: SAKE guides text diffusion with semantic entropy, improving the measured balance between output fidelity, diversity, and multi-sample reasoning performance.

title: Exploring More to Solve More: Boosting Diversity in Text Diffusion Models via Entropy-Based Guidance

abstract: This position paper argues that vision-language model benchmarks for causal reasoning contain two blind spots. First, benchmarks presuppose temporal constitution, the understanding of time as the medium through which causes bring about effects, without testing it. Second, they provide scaffolding through prompts that may substitute for internalized capability instead of accessing it. A camera records one instant from one position. Human visual intelligence works differently. Post-impressionist painter Paul Cézanne grasped this a century before cognitive science would articulate it. He painted how we see, not what is seen. We draw on his technique to distinguish camera-like processing from Cézanne-like construction of understanding through temporal integration. Preliminary evidence shows systematic disparity between fluent causal text and valid causal structure, and divergent responses to identical scaffolding manipulation. Progress requires benchmarks that go beyond output accuracy to test temporal understanding and scaffolding-invariance.

paragraphs: This position paper identifies two blind spots in benchmarks of causal reasoning for vision-language models. First, benchmarks may assume without testing that models understand time as the medium through which causes produce effects. Second, helpful prompt structure may supply reasoning support that substitutes for a capability the model has not internalized.

The authors draw on Cézanne’s painting technique to distinguish recording a single visual instant from constructing understanding through temporal integration. This serves as a conceptual lens for asking what visual intelligence requires. A fluent account of causation may still fail to represent a valid causal structure, so the form of the answer alone is insufficient to settle that question.

Preliminary evidence shows systematic differences between fluent causal text and valid causal structure, along with divergent responses to identical changes in scaffolding. The authors therefore call for benchmarks that test temporal understanding and robustness to scaffolding changes alongside output accuracy. The findings motivate closer examination of what prompt-assisted success reveals about the model’s underlying visual and causal capabilities.
summary.tldr: Preliminary evidence motivates visual-reasoning benchmarks that test temporal understanding and distinguish internal capability from prompt-provided scaffolding.

title: Position: What Cézanne Knew About Visual Intelligence That Vision-Language Models Miss

abstract: Ground truth datasets play a fundamental role as reference values in the training and evaluation of machine learning models. This position paper argues that ground truths are not neutral objective measurements that are naturally given, but instead that they are constructed by arrangements of humans and technologies. We argue that the ML community will benefit from articulating and discussing these often invisible or unreported choices and acknowledging that reference data sets are contingent, not universal. Focusing on the situated and context-dependent nature of ground truths can improve reliability by enabling a better informed perspective on where, when, and how the datasets, and the models they have shaped, can best be used. We argue for increasing "situated reliability" which includes articulating the limits and strengths of models and their truth claims. Finally, paying more attention to the construction of ground truths can support transparency, accountability, and interdisciplinary work.

paragraphs: This position paper questions how machine learning treats the reference datasets commonly called ground truth. The authors argue that these datasets emerge from arrangements of people and technologies, rather than arriving as neutral, naturally given measurements. Choices involved in their construction therefore matter to what models learn and how their performance is judged.

The paper calls for making those often invisible or unreported choices explicit. Its emphasis is on context: a reference dataset is contingent on how it was produced and should not automatically be treated as universally applicable. Understanding that context can support better decisions about where, when, and how a dataset or the models shaped by it should be used.

The authors describe this goal as situated reliability. It requires articulating both the strengths and limits of models and the truth claims associated with them. Their argument connects reliability to a clearer account of reference data, rather than simply accepting the authority of its label. Greater attention to dataset construction could also strengthen transparency, accountability, and collaboration across disciplines.
summary.tldr: Making the human and technical choices behind ground truth explicit can improve the context-sensitive reliability of machine learning.

abstract: Minimum rank problems arise frequently in machine learning applications and are notoriously difficult to solve due to the non-convex nature of the rank objective. In this paper, we present the first online learning approach for the problem of rank minimization of matrices over polyhedral sets. In particular, we present two online learning algorithms for rank minimization - our first algorithm is a multiplicative update method based on a generalized experts framework, while our second algorithm is a novel application of the online convex programming framework [Zinkevich, 2003]. In the latter, we flip the role of the decision maker by making the decision maker search over the constraint space instead of feasible points, as is usually the case in online convex programming. A salient feature of our online learning approach is that it allows us to give the first provable approximation guarantees for the rank minimization problem over polyhedral sets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on synthetic examples, and on the real-life application of low-rank kernel learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses matrix rank minimization over polyhedral sets, a difficult optimization problem because rank is a nonconvex objective. It introduces an online learning approach to this setting, using learning algorithms as tools for solving a constrained matrix optimization problem.

Two algorithms are proposed. The first uses multiplicative updates within a generalized experts framework. The second adapts online convex programming by changing what the decision maker searches over: it searches the constraint space instead of the feasible points. This change in roles is the distinctive step that connects the online framework to the rank-minimization task.

The approach yields provable approximation guarantees, which the authors identify as the first for rank minimization over polyhedral sets. These are approximation guarantees rather than claims of exact minimum-rank solutions. Experiments on synthetic examples and low-rank kernel learning demonstrate the methods' effectiveness. The contribution combines a new algorithmic viewpoint with theoretical guarantees and evidence from both constructed problems and a practical learning application.
summary.tldr: Two online learning algorithms provide provable approximation guarantees for matrix rank minimization over polyhedral sets.

title: Rank minimization via online learning

abstract: The Support Vector Machine (SVM) is an acknowledged powerful tool for building classifiers, but it lacks flexibility, in the sense that the kernel is chosen prior to learning. Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) enables to learn the kernel, from an ensemble of basis kernels, whose combination is optimized in the learning process. Here, we propose Composite Kernel Learning to address the situation where distinct components give rise to a group structure among kernels. Our formulation of the learning problem encompasses several setups, putting more or less emphasis on the group structure. We characterize the convexity of the learning problem, and provide a general wrapper algorithm for computing solutions. Finally, we illustrate the behavior of our method on multi-channel data where groups correspond to channels.

paragraphs: A support vector machine ordinarily starts with a chosen kernel, which determines how examples are compared during learning. Multiple kernel learning adds flexibility by optimizing a combination of basis kernels. This paper addresses a further structure in that choice: kernels may belong to groups because they arise from distinct components of the data.

Composite Kernel Learning incorporates those groups into the learning formulation. The framework covers several setups that place different amounts of emphasis on group structure. This matters when the relationships among candidate kernels are meaningful, because the learning problem can reflect those relationships as well as the individual kernels available for combination.

The authors characterize the convexity of the resulting optimization problem and provide a general wrapper algorithm for computing solutions. They illustrate the method with multi-channel data, where each channel corresponds to a group of kernels. The stated contribution is a flexible formulation and a way to solve it, together with an illustration of its behavior; the abstract does not claim a universal accuracy advantage.
summary.tldr: Composite Kernel Learning extends multiple kernel learning to account for meaningful groups among candidate kernels.

title: Composite kernel learning

abstract: Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) is an efficient no-regret learning algorithm for decision problems modeled as extensive games. CFR's regret bounds depend on the requirement of perfect recall: players always remember information that was revealed to them and the order in which it was revealed. In games without perfect recall, however, CFR's guarantees do not apply. In this paper, we present the first regret bound for CFR when applied to a general class of games with imperfect recall. In addition, we show that CFR applied to any abstraction belonging to our general class results in a regret bound not just for the abstract game, but for the full game as well. We verify our theory and show how imperfect recall can be used to trade a small increase in regret for a significant reduction in memory in three domains: die-roll poker, phantom tic-tac-toe, and Bluff.

paragraphs: Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, is a learning algorithm for sequential decision problems represented as extensive-form games. Its established regret guarantees require perfect recall: players remember previously revealed information and its order. Forgetting information can simplify a game representation, but the usual guarantees do not automatically carry over to that setting.

The paper establishes what the authors describe as the first CFR regret bound for a general class of imperfect-recall games. It also proves that when an abstraction belongs to this class, the regret bound applies to the full game as well as the abstraction. This connects the behavior learned in a simplified representation to the original decision problem.

The authors examine die-roll poker, phantom tic-tac-toe, and Bluff to verify the theory and demonstrate the memory tradeoff. In these domains, imperfect recall can substantially reduce memory use at the cost of a small increase in regret. The result supports a principled use of forgetting within the analyzed class, with guarantees that remain relevant beyond the simplified game itself.
summary.tldr: CFR gains regret guarantees for a class of imperfect-recall games, supporting substantial memory savings with small regret increases in three domains.

title: No-Regret Learning in Extensive-Form Games with Imperfect Recall

abstract: Recently, prediction markets have shown considerable promise for developing flexible mechanisms for machine learning. In this paper agents with isoelastic utilities are considered, and it is shown that the costs associated with homogeneous markets of agents with isoelastic utilities produce equilibrium prices corresponding to alpha-mixtures, with a particular form of mixing component relating to each agent's wealth. We also demonstrate that wealth accumulation for logarithmic and other isoelastic agents (through payoffs on prediction of training targets) can implement both Bayesian model updates and mixture weight updates by imposing different market payoff structures. An efficient variational algorithm is given for market equilibrium computation. We demonstrate that inhomogeneous markets of agents with isoelastic utilities outperform state of the art aggregate classifiers such as random forests, as well as single classifiers (neural networks, decision trees) on a number of machine learning benchmarks, and show that isoelastic combination methods are generally better than using logarithmic agents.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction markets as mechanisms for combining machine learning predictions. Its agents use isoelastic utility functions, and their wealth influences the resulting combination. For homogeneous markets of these agents, the authors connect equilibrium prices to alpha-mixtures, with a particular relationship between each agent's wealth and its mixing component.

The market also provides a learning mechanism. Agents accumulate wealth through payoffs tied to predictions of training targets. By choosing different payoff structures, the authors show that this process can implement Bayesian model updates or mixture-weight updates for logarithmic and other isoelastic agents. An efficient variational algorithm computes the market equilibrium.

Experiments use heterogeneous markets of isoelastic agents and report better performance than random forests, neural networks, and decision trees on a number of benchmarks. Isoelastic combinations are also generally better than combinations using logarithmic agents in the reported study. The work therefore links market behavior to recognizable statistical updates and evaluates that connection as a practical approach to combining classifiers.
summary.tldr: Isoelastic prediction markets connect wealth and payoffs to statistical model combination, with heterogeneous markets performing well on reported classification benchmarks.

title: Isoelastic Agents and Wealth Updates in Machine Learning Markets

abstract: We consider the ℓ_1 -regularized least-squares problem for sparse recovery and compressed sensing. Since the objective function is not strongly convex, standard proximal gradient methods only achieve sublinear convergence. We propose a homotopy continuation strategy, which employs a proximal gradient method to solve the problem with a sequence of decreasing regularization parameters. It is shown that under common assumptions in compressed sensing, the proposed method ensures that all iterates along the homotopy solution path are sparse, and the objective function is effectively strongly convex along the solution path. This observation allows us to obtain a global geometric convergence rate for the procedure. Empirical results are presented to support our theoretical analysis.

We propose a homotopy continuation strategy, which employs a proximal gradient method to solve the problem with a sequence of decreasing regularization parameters. It is shown that under common assumptions in compressed sensing, the proposed method ensures that all iterates along the homotopy solution path are sparse, and the objective function is effectively strongly convex along the solution path. This observation allows us to obtain a global geometric convergence rate for the procedure. Empirical results are presented to support our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper tackles L1-regularized least squares, a problem used in sparse recovery and compressed sensing. The objective encourages solutions with few nonzero entries, but it is not strongly convex. As a result, standard proximal gradient methods have only sublinear convergence guarantees for this problem, motivating a different way to organize the optimization.

The proposed approach solves a sequence of problems whose regularization parameters gradually decrease. This homotopy strategy still uses proximal gradient steps, but follows a path through related optimization problems. Under common compressed-sensing assumptions, the authors show that every iterate on this path remains sparse and that the objective behaves as strongly convex along the path.

That path-specific property is what enables a global geometric convergence rate for the overall procedure. The result does not require claiming that the objective becomes strongly convex everywhere; the useful curvature is established where the algorithm travels, under the stated assumptions. Empirical results support the theoretical analysis, linking the faster convergence guarantee to observed behavior.
summary.tldr: A decreasing-regularization strategy gives proximal gradient sparse recovery global geometric convergence under common compressed-sensing assumptions.

title: A Proximal-Gradient Homotopy Method for the L1-Regularized Least-Squares Problem
